Yield: About ⅔ cup

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why it’s healthy

A baste is a flavor delivery system, and this one is built from the right parts: olive oil, whose fat is mostly monounsaturated — the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance — carrying a ground paste of rosemary, garlic and lemon. The garlic is minced and never cooked on its own, so its protective compound forms in the paste; the lemon goes in raw, vitamin C intact; and the rosemary's intensity is the point — food that tastes this seasoned needs less salt.

The honest cost

It is, at bottom, oil: a full serving would be 221 calories of almost pure fat, though its saturated fat is low — 3.5 g, 18% of a day's limit. Choosing extra virgin olive oil improves that fat itself, with the bitter polyphenols that protect blood vessels and that refined oil has little of. The honest framing is dose: nobody eats a baste by the spoonful, and brushed on, it replaces fattier finishes rather than adding to them.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Grind the paste, then give it a few minutes before it meets the grill. The mortar work mixes the garlic's building block with the enzyme that uses it — a short rest in the bowl lets the protective compound form before the fire can destroy it. Allicin doesn't exist in a whole clove: alliin and alliinase sit in separate compartments until crushing or grinding brings them together, and the compound builds over about 10 minutes. A baste is the kind case — the garlic rests raw in oil and lemon, and only the thin film on the food ever sees hard heat.
  • Brush it on in films, not ladles. Two-thirds of a cup bastes a lot of grilling; a thin coat carries the rosemary and lemon at full volume, which is all the baste is for.
  • Use the week's fridge life. It keeps up to a week refrigerated, so one batch can season several lean meals — chicken, fish, vegetables — instead of richer sauces being made fresh each time.
Ingredients
  • 1 tablespoon finely chopped fresh rosemary
  • ½ teaspoon fine kosher or sea salt
  • 2 garlic cloves, minced
  • ½ cup olive oil
  • Zest and juice of 1 lemon
  • Freshly ground black pepper to taste
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Mortar-and-pestle method: Grind 1 tablespoon rosemary, ½ teaspoon salt and 2 garlic cloves together in the mortar to a fine paste. Drizzle in ½ cup olive oil and grind again. Add the zest and juice of 1 lemon, grind, taste, and add more salt if wanted and season with pepper.
  2. Step 2: Food-processor alternative: Pulse rosemary, salt and garlic just until chopped into a paste. Add olive oil and pulse again. Add lemon zest and juice and pulse, then season with salt and pepper as needed.
  3. Step 3: Keeps in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.
Intro describes it as looser than a paste — a basting sauce/drizzle for garden vegetables, beef, pork, chicken or leg of lamb before, during and after grilling; suggested on High-Heat Grilled Romaine Salad (page 109), brushed on bread or pizza dough, and drizzled over grilled asparagus, greens and tomatoes. A mortar and pestle is recommended for best texture; a food processor may also be used.

Yield: 2 cups

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why it’s healthy

A finishing butter with a real béarnaise spine — tarragon, shallot, vinegar and a little heat — so one spoonful makes plain grilled meat or vegetables taste finished. It's made from scratch, from whole ingredients you can name, with no preservatives and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose. Its health story is mostly about dose: the flavor is concentrated, so a little genuinely goes a long way.

The honest cost

It's butter. A serving carries 7.8 g of saturated fat — 39% of a day's limit — in 116 calories, so the spoon is the serving size that matters. Grass-fed butter improves the profile a little, with more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than conventional butter. It stays a rich finishing sauce — best spent over something lean, where it balances.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Shape it as a roll and slice it. The recipe's own trick: a chilled log cuts into coins, and a coin per plate keeps the portion honest without any measuring.
  • Freeze it in portions. It keeps three months frozen — portioned, it's a finishing touch you reach for deliberately, not a tub that drifts into everything.
Ingredients
  • 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter, at room temperature
  • 2 tablespoons chopped shallots
  • 1 tablespoon white wine vinegar
  • 2 tablespoons chopped fresh tarragon leaves
  • ¼ teaspoon sea salt
  • ½ teaspoon hot sauce or to taste
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a medium bowl stir all ingredients together with a fork: 1 cup unsalted butter, 2 tablespoons chopped shallots, 1 tablespoon white wine vinegar, 2 tablespoons chopped fresh tarragon leaves, ¼ teaspoon sea salt, ½ teaspoon hot sauce.
  2. Step 2: Either spoon into a ramekin or small bowl for serving, or shape into a roll, wrap in waxed paper, and chill.
  3. Step 3: For freezer storage up to 3 months, wrap tightly first in waxed paper, then in layers of plastic wrap and aluminum foil.
Intro suggests spreading on a bread crouton to top Smoked Tomato Bisque (page 128), adding pats to Grilled Spring Platter of Asparagus and Leeks (page 161), and serving at room temperature with grill-roasted potatoes (page 8), grilled bread, asparagus, poultry or steaks. The recipe halves easily; the extra half can be labelled, dated and frozen ready for use.

Servings: 2 to 4

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why it’s healthy

A snack that actually feeds you. Edamame — young soybeans, still in the pod — is a rare nibble with both protein and fiber together: about 7 g of protein and 3 g of fiber in a serving, the fiber feeding gut bacteria and slowing digestion so you stay full. The pods are grilled whole in a slick of oil, from ingredients you can name, with nothing hidden and nothing processed.

The honest cost

Almost none. A serving carries barely half a gram of saturated fat and, before the finishing salt, almost no sodium at all. The oil is the only real addition, and it is a coating on pods you throw away, not a sauce you drink. The flaked salt at the table is the one dial you control — a light dip is the whole cost.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Grill them crisp-tender, not soft. Four to five minutes a side in a single layer, as written — a pod that still has bite eats slower and satisfies more than one grilled limp.
  • Eat them from the pod. Tearing each pod open is built-in pacing: the protein and fiber get time to register before you have emptied the bowl.
  • Dip, don't shower. The beans meet the flaked salt one dip at a time, so the salt lands on the surface where you taste it — full flavor for a fraction of a salted-through dish.
Ingredients
  • 1 pound fresh edamame in the pod
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil
  • 2 teaspoons toasted sesame oil
  • Flaked salt for serving
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Preheat grill to medium-high. In a large bowl toss 1 pound edamame pods with both oils (1 tablespoon vegetable oil and 2 teaspoons toasted sesame oil).
  2. Step 2: Put pods on a perforated grill rack or in a disposable aluminum pan, arranged in a single layer on the grill over medium-high heat. Grill-roast (page 8), covered, 4 to 5 minutes.
  3. Step 3: Flip, cover, and grill a few minutes more, until pods are crisp-tender when pierced with a knife. If unsure, remove a pod, open it and taste a bean to check.
  4. Step 4: To eat, tear open the pods and dip the beans into flaked salt.
Headnote says edamame meant for fresh eating can be grilled right in the pod and served on a platter with a small dish of flaked salt. A separate "Growing Edamame" box gives growing notes in paraphrase: edamame is the Japanese name for soybeans eaten fresh; plant like green beans after frost danger, seeds in full sun about 1 inch deep and 2 inches apart, can be grown in large pots around a wire frame/trellis, best in spring or fall as a cool-weather crop; about 3 soybeans per pod, pick when beans within the pod are young and tender, about ½ inch long.

Servings: 4

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why it’s healthy

The vegetable itself is nearly free: bok choy brings calcium for bones and vitamin A for eyes and immune system in a green that's mostly water and crunch. The sauce is where the interest is — ginger, whose bite comes from gingerol, a compound that helps calm nausea and eases everyday inflammation, and olive oil, whose fat helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance and carries the greens' fat-soluble vitamins.

The honest cost

The butter in the baste. A quarter cup melts into the ginger-soy sauce, and a serving picks up about 8.7 g of saturated fat — over 40% of a day's limit — from a vegetable side. Grass-fed butter improves that fat a little, with more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than conventional. Pouring all the leftover sauce over the top at serving gives back whatever the grill spared.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Rest the garlic and ginger in the sauce while the grill heats. The sauce is whisked raw, so the garlic's protective compound gets its 10 minutes to form before the baste ever meets the fire. A whole clove holds no allicin at all — the compound is assembled only when mincing brings a stored building block together with the enzyme that activates it. Hard heat destroys it fast, so in a grilled dish the rest beforehand is the only chance it gets: form it in the bowl, then baste.
  • Lean the sauce toward the olive oil. More oil, less butter keeps the baste glossy — and olive oil's fat improves cholesterol mainly by replacing saturated fat, so the swap is the mechanism, not just a lighter taste.
  • Brush, don't pour. Baste as written, and serve what's left in a small dish for the table rather than over the top — the charred leaves carry plenty.
Ingredients
  • 2 small heads bok choy, trimmed and halved lengthwise
  • Fresh ginger soy sauce
  • ¼ cup (½ stick) unsalted butter, melted
  • 2 tablespoons olive oil
  • 2 teaspoons soy sauce
  • 2 teaspoons fresh ginger, minced
  • 1 garlic clove, minced
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Prepare a medium-hot fire in the grill. Rinse the 2 small heads bok choy, drain well, and pat dry.
  2. Step 2: Make the Ginger-Soy Sauce (see separate sub-recipe entry below): whisk together ¼ cup melted butter, 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 teaspoons soy sauce, 2 teaspoons ginger and 1 garlic clove.
  3. Step 3: Brush bok choy with the sauce and place cut side down directly over the fire. Grill about 10 minutes.
  4. Step 4: Baste the leaves, turn, and continue grilling about another 10 minutes until bok choy is fork-tender.
  5. Step 5: Serve with any remaining sauce.
Intro notes late spring/early summer dwarf bok choy heads (also called pak choi) are tender and sweet, the sturdy leafy stalks suit breaking apart and serving with a dipping sauce such as Satay-Style Peanut Dipping Sauce (page 23), and the Fresh Ginger-Soy sauce is versatile — try it with grilled asparagus, eggplant and zucchini.

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why it’s healthy

A sauce built to be brushed on, not poured — a small amount carries a lot of flavor. The garlic goes in raw and minced, its strongest form, and the ginger brings gingerol, the compound behind ginger's stomach-settling, inflammation-easing bite. The olive oil pulls real weight too: mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels.

The honest cost

The butter is half the sauce. Melted butter and olive oil split the base, and a serving picks up 4.3 g of saturated fat — about a fifth of a day's limit — from a condiment. Grass-fed butter and extra virgin olive oil both shrink that a little: the butter carries more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than conventional, and the oil brings protective polyphenols refined oil lacks. Still a butter sauce — just better built.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Whisk it, then wait a few minutes before brushing. The sauce is never cooked on its own, so the garlic keeps everything — but its compound still has to be built after mincing. Raw keeps the full yield because no heat ever touches the enzyme that builds allicin — yet a whole clove contains none; mince, wait a few minutes, and the compound forms right in the sauce. Eaten raw like this, garlic arrives at full strength — the sharpness is what the strength tastes like.
  • Lean the base toward the olive oil. More oil, less butter keeps the sauce glossy and brushable — and the swap itself is the health mechanism. Olive oil's monounsaturated fat improves cholesterol mainly by replacing saturated fat, so trading butter for oil is what does the work, not adding oil on top. Its bitter bite is oleocanthal, a polyphenol that calms inflammation and shields blood-vessel walls; cheap, refined oil has little of it.
  • Brush it on; serve the rest beside, not over. As written, it coats the food before and during grilling and the remainder goes to the table — a brushed coat flavors every bite for a fraction of a poured sauce.
Ingredients
  • ¼ cup (½ stick) unsalted butter, melted
  • 2 tablespoons olive oil
  • 2 teaspoons soy sauce
  • 2 teaspoons fresh ginger, minced
  • 1 garlic clove, minced
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Whisk ¼ cup melted butter, 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 teaspoons soy sauce, 2 teaspoons ginger and 1 garlic clove together. Use to brush the bok choy before and during grilling, and serve any remainder alongside.

Servings: 6

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why it’s healthy

The corn is the substance: fiber for digestion and lutein, a yellow pigment that collects in your eyes and helps protect your vision as you age. The butter on top is seasoned hard — raw garlic, ancho chile and lime zest — so a brush of it tastes like a lot, and the ancho's gentle heat makes a rich ear satisfying sooner.

The honest cost

The butter, as always — but portioned by the recipe itself. A quarter cup is divided across six ears, so a serving lands at about 5 g of saturated fat, a quarter of a day's limit, on an otherwise lean vegetable. Grass-fed butter improves that brush a little, with more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than conventional butter. The ear is light; the brush is the bill, and it is a small one.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Make the butter ahead and rest the garlic in it. Mince the clove and give it about 10 minutes in the butter before serving — the butter is never cooked, so the compound that forms stays in it. Allicin does not exist in a whole clove: a building block and the enzyme that uses it sit in separate compartments, and mincing mixes them. Here the butter only melts over hot corn at the table, so nothing destroys what the rest built — this is garlic at nearly full strength, hidden in a finishing brush.
  • Let the husk do the cooking. Soaked and tied shut, the ears steam over the fire with no fat at all — every bit of butter in the dish is the brush you choose at the end.
  • Brush after grilling, and brush once. The butter goes on hot kernels at serving, where it melts into every ridge — one coat reads as buttery; a second is just more of the same. Lutein gathers in the macula, the sharp center of the retina, where it filters blue light and absorbs the oxidative wear that comes with seeing. The body makes none of it — the supply is entirely what meals bring. Corn is a modest, steady contributor rather than a headline source.
Ingredients
  • 6 ears sweet corn, in the husk
  • 1 garlic clove, minced
  • ¼ cup (½ stick) unsalted butter, at room temperature
  • ½ teaspoon ground ancho chile powder
  • ½ teaspoon grated lime zest
  • Fine kosher or sea salt to taste
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Peel husks back without detaching them, remove the corn silk, then pull husks back over the corn and tie them securely closed with kitchen string or a strip of corn husk. Soak the 6 ears sweet corn in cold water 15 minutes; drain well.
  2. Step 2: Make the Ancho-Lime Butter (see separate sub-recipe entry below): stir 1 garlic clove, ¼ cup butter, ½ teaspoon ancho chile powder and ½ teaspoon lime zest together in a bowl until well blended; add salt to taste and set aside.
  3. Step 3: Prepare a hot fire in the grill.
  4. Step 4: Grill corn directly over the heat, turning often, about 10 minutes, until husks are slightly charred and steam rises from the ears. Let cool slightly and remove the string.
  5. Step 5: To serve, pull husks back and brush kernels with the Ancho-Lime Butter.
Intro says grilling in the husk keeps sweet corn very tender while giving a gentle grill flavour; varieties suggested include Silver Queen, Purdue Super Sweet, Peaches and Cream, and the heirloom Country Gentleman.

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why it’s healthy

This is a flavor tool, not a food group — and that's its virtue. Garlic, ancho chile and lime zest carry so much flavor that a thin brush over grilled corn is plenty, so the butter stays a seasoning instead of becoming the dish. The garlic goes in raw and minced, which is the strongest way to eat it: its protective compound forms on crushing, and no cooking heat ever gets at it.

The honest cost

The butter itself. A serving carries 3.8 g of saturated fat — about a fifth of a day's limit — in just 55 calories, so the dose is the whole question. Grass-fed butter shrinks the cost a little: it carries more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than conventional butter. Still butter — just better built.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Rest the garlic first. Mince it and wait about 10 minutes before stirring it into the butter, so its protective compound forms while nothing can destroy it. Allicin doesn't exist in a whole clove — a building block and the enzyme that uses it sit in separate compartments, and mincing mixes them. In this butter the compound forms right in the bowl and stays there, because the butter is never cooked hard; it only melts over hot corn at the table.
  • Brush it thin. The ancho and lime are loud on purpose — a light coat over hot corn gives the full effect for a fraction of a pat.
Ingredients
  • 1 garlic clove, minced
  • ¼ cup (½ stick) unsalted butter, at room temperature
  • ½ teaspoon ground ancho chile powder
  • ½ teaspoon grated lime zest
  • Fine kosher or sea salt to taste
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Stir 1 garlic clove, ¼ cup butter, ½ teaspoon ancho chile powder and ½ teaspoon lime zest together in a bowl until well blended. Add salt to taste and set aside until serving; brush onto grilled corn kernels.

Servings: 2–6

Adapted from Salt & Shore.

Why it’s healthy

The shrimp carry the plate: lean, complete protein — 24.5 g in a serving, half a day's worth — for very few calories, plus selenium, a mineral your thyroid needs to make its hormones and your cells need to defend themselves. The peanut chile crisp brings plant protein and monounsaturated fat along with its heat, and a full half cup of cilantro and a lime's zest land fresh at the end, where their brightness survives.

The honest cost

The butter the shrimp swim in. Four tablespoons of salted butter melt with the chile crisp, and a serving carries 8.6 g of saturated fat — 43% of a day's limit — with cholesterol at 71% of a day's limit from the butter and shrimp together. Grass-fed butter betters its part of the fat: more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than conventional butter carries. Rich sauce, lean shrimp — the balance is the dish.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Keep the cilantro and lime off the heat. The recipe folds the cilantro in after the pan leaves the burner and grates the zest over at serving — vitamin C breaks down in heat, so the finish is where it survives. Weight check on vitamin C: it does not prevent colds in ordinary life, and its collagen role is maintenance, not transformation. Its strongest trick is iron — in the same meal, vitamin C can multiply the absorption of plant iron severalfold. Served over greens or beans, this shrimp's lime finish does real work.
  • Let the heat do the satisfying. The chile crisp's capsaicin makes a rich sauce taste bigger than it is — a spoon of sauce over the shrimp, rather than the shrimp spooned up with all of it, keeps the butter in its place. Capsaicin works by tripping the nerves that sense heat — a signal, not damage — and the body answers with widened blood vessels and a small rise in calorie burn. Honest size: the metabolic effect is minor; the way heat makes rich food satisfying in smaller portions is the bigger gift, and this dish is built on it.
  • Treat the crusty bread as optional — it is. The recipe lists it that way. The bread's job is mopping up butter; the shrimp are complete without it.
Ingredients
  • 4 tablespoons salted butter
  • 1/4 cup Peanut Chile Crisp or a mix of store-bought chile crisp and finely chopped peanuts
  • 1 lb large shrimp (preferably from Sun Shrimp), peeled and deveined
  • Kosher salt
  • 1/2 cup finely chopped fresh cilantro
  • 1 lime
  • Crusty bread slices, for serving (optional)
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat a large cast-iron skillet, Dutch oven, or sauté pan over medium heat for 3 minutes.
  2. Step 2: Add 4 tablespoons butter, ¼ cup chile crisp, and 1 lb shrimp; stir until well mixed.
  3. Step 3: Season lightly with salt and cook, stirring somewhat frequently, 3–5 minutes until shrimp are cooked.
  4. Step 4: Remove from heat and fold in ½ cup cilantro.
  5. Step 5: Spoon into a cazuela, cocotte, or serving bowl, grate the zest of 1 lime directly over the dish, and serve.
Intro notes the dish is inspired by Spanish gambas al ajillo, balances spicy/buttery/citrus, peanuts add depth; quick and easy, traditionally enjoyed pinchos-style skewered with toothpicks; Florida-based Sun Shrimp (p. 88) preferred when possible. Serving note: delightful as is, sometimes served with crusty bread for dipping.

Yield: 3 cups

Adapted from Salt & Shore.

Why it’s healthy

A condiment with real substance behind the heat. The peanuts bring plant protein plus monounsaturated fat — the heart-friendly kind — and that combination keeps you full for a long time. A full cup of gochugaru chile flakes brings capsaicin, the heat compound, which warms you up and opens blood flow a little, and makes rich food satisfying in smaller amounts. A spoonful transforms plain rice, eggs or vegetables — flavor that pulls plain food onto the plate.

The honest cost

It's mostly oil by design — three-quarters of a cup of avocado and sesame oil carrying the peanuts and chile — so a serving runs about 105 calories with 10 g of fat, though only 1.4 g of it saturated. The tablespoon of brown sugar across three cups of crisp is a whisper. The cost here isn't any single ingredient; it's that something this good is easy to spoon like a sauce instead of a seasoning.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Spoon it like the condiment it is. A tablespoon over a bowl does the whole job — the heat and crunch register in every bite without turning the dish into an oil course. The burn is a signal, not an injury: capsaicin fires the heat-sensing nerves, and the body's answer — wider blood vessels, a touch more calorie burn — is the whole effect. Honest size: the metabolism bump is small. The real gift is satiety: food that tastes this intense satisfies sooner, which is what keeps the spoon small.
  • Pulse it fine, as written. Finely chopped, the crisp spreads its flavor across a whole dish instead of landing in a few heavy clumps — more coverage per spoonful.
  • Store it airtight, in the dark. It keeps three months in a cool, dark cupboard; oils and chile compounds both fade with light and air, so the jar you protect stays the jar that satisfies.
Ingredients
  • 1 cup unsalted roasted peanuts
  • 1 cup Korean chile flakes (gochugaru)
  • 1 tablespoon firmly packed organic dark brown sugar
  • 1 tablespoon granulated garlic
  • 1 teaspoon kosher salt
  • 1/2 cup avocado or canola oil
  • 1/4 cup toasted sesame oil
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a food processor, combine 1 cup peanuts, 1 cup chile flakes, 1 tablespoon brown sugar, 1 tablespoon granulated garlic, and 1 teaspoon kosher salt; pulse until finely chopped, about 30 seconds.
  2. Step 2: Add both oils (½ cup avocado or canola oil and ¼ cup toasted sesame oil) and process until well incorporated, about 30 seconds.
  3. Step 3: Use right away, or store in an airtight container in a cool, dark cupboard for up to 3 months.
Best enjoyed at room temperature or in a cooked dish.

Servings: 4

Adapted from Poole's.

Why it’s healthy

Sirloin is the steak for this: trimmed of excess fat before it ever sees the pan, it delivers 51 g of protein and a quarter of a day's iron in a serving, with the cracked-pepper crust doing the seasoning work. The sauce is built from the pan itself — red onion, garlic, wine, stock and a spoon of tomato paste, whose lycopene helps protect the heart and blood vessels and absorbs better cooked, the way it is here.

The honest cost

The beef's own fat, plus a tablespoon of butter melted into the sauce: 6.3 g of saturated fat in a serving — about 31% of a day's limit — in 414 calories. The butter's share gets a small upgrade from grass-fed: more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than conventional butter. The wine reduces down in the pan as a flavoring, not a drink — the sauce is a coating, and that's how the cost stays proportionate.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Rest the steaks while the sauce cooks. Tenting them under foil for the sauce's few minutes keeps the juices in the meat — a juicy steak reads as richer than it is, no extra butter required.
  • Give the garlic its rest first. Mince it about 10 minutes ahead; the sauce gives it only 3 to 5 minutes in the pan, so the compound needs its head start. Allicin doesn't exist in a whole clove: crushing mixes a building block with the enzyme that uses it, and the compound builds over about 10 minutes, then relaxes blood-vessel walls. In a quick pan sauce, forming it before the pan is the only window it gets.
  • Spoon the sauce, pass the rest. The recipe serves a generous spoonful over each steak and passes the extra at the table — take the spoonful; the second pour is where butter and salt quietly double. The tomato paste earns its spoonful: lycopene lodges in cell membranes and neutralizes the oxidative damage linked to vessel aging, and heat reshapes it into the form your gut absorbs best, with the pan's fat ferrying it across. Cooked tomato is one of the few cases where processing clearly helps.
Ingredients
  • 4 boneless beef sirloin steaks, at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick, trimmed of excess fat
  • Salt
  • 1 tablespoon cracked black peppercorns
  • 1 tablespoon olive oil
  • For the pan sauce:
  • 1 tablespoon unsalted butter
  • 1/2 red onion, finely chopped
  • 1 clove garlic, minced
  • 1/2 cup (4 fl oz/125 ml) dry red wine
  • 1 cup (8 fl oz/250 ml) beef stock (page 110) or prepared broth, plus more if needed
  • 1 tablespoon tomato paste
  • 1 tablespoon cornstarch (cornflour) combined with 2 tablespoons water
  • 2 tablespoons chopped fresh flat-leaf (Italian) parsley
  • Salt and freshly ground pepper
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Slash edges of the 4 sirloin steaks in 1 or 2 places to prevent curling. Sprinkle all sides generously with salt and 1 tablespoon cracked black peppercorns, pressing pepper into the surface. Let stand at room temperature at least 15 minutes and up to 1 hour before cooking.
  2. Step 2: In a large, heavy frying pan over medium-high heat, heat 1 tablespoon olive oil. Add steaks and cook to desired doneness, turning once, 3–5 minutes on each side. Test with an instant-read thermometer or by cutting into the meat. Remove steaks when they are red at the center for rare (120°F/49°C) or deep pink at the center for medium-rare (130°F/54°C). Transfer to a platter, tent loosely with aluminum foil, and rest while making the pan sauce.
  3. Step 3: Pan sauce: In the same frying pan over medium-high heat, melt 1 tablespoon butter. Add ½ red onion and 1 clove garlic and sauté until onion is softened, 3–5 minutes. Add ½ cup dry red wine and 1 cup beef stock and boil until reduced by half, 4–5 minutes.
  4. Step 4: Reduce heat to medium, whisk in 1 tablespoon tomato paste and the 1 tablespoon cornstarch mixture, and simmer, whisking occasionally, until slightly thickened, 3–5 minutes. Add more stock if sauce seems too thick. Stir in 2 tablespoons parsley and season to taste with salt and pepper.
  5. Step 5: To serve, spoon a generous amount of sauce over steaks and serve at once; pass extra sauce at the table.
Sidebar "Making Pan Sauces" (paraphrased): To make a sauce in the pan used to cook meat, first add a little olive oil and sauté minced garlic or shallot, then pour in wine, stock, or another liquid to deglaze, scraping up browned bits. Next stir in seasonings such as herbs, mustard, tomato paste, Worcestershire sauce, or soy sauce. Thicken by reducing over high heat or by stirring in a little cornstarch mixed with water and cooking a few minutes longer. For a richer sauce, stir in 2 tablespoons heavy (double) cream or chilled unsalted butter at the end.

Servings: 8–10 · Oven: 350°F (180°C)

Why it’s healthy

Beef's real gifts are here in strength: iron in the form your body absorbs best, vitamin B12 for making red blood cells and keeping nerves working, and 40 g of protein in a serving. The crust is the smart part — Dijon mustard, horseradish, rosemary and garlic deliver huge flavor for almost no calories, so the meat needs no rich sauce to taste finished. The horseradish cream on top works the same way: a spoonful goes a long way.

The honest cost

Prime rib is the celebration cut and eats like it: 26 g of saturated fat in a serving — 131% of a day's 20 g limit — in 762 calories, with 901 mg of sodium, about 39% of a day's ceiling, much of it from the salted crust. Nothing in the preparation adds the cost; the marbling is the cost, and it is also the point of the cut. Make it knowingly: an occasion roast, carved with the occasion in mind.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Give the crust its full stand. At least 15 minutes and up to overnight, as written — the minced garlic sits in the mustard paste before any heat arrives, which is the one window its protective compound gets. Allicin forms only after crushing mixes garlic's building block (alliin) with the enzyme that uses it (alliinase), building over about 10 minutes; roasting heat then destroys it. A crust mixed and rested ahead keeps whatever forms during the stand — garlic added straight to a hot pan gets no such chance.
  • Rest the roast the full 10 to 12 minutes, tented. The juices settle back into the meat instead of flooding the carving board — a juicy slice satisfies without the sauce doing the work.
  • Carve thinner than the celebration urges. The recipe leaves thick or thin to you; thin slices of a marbled roast deliver the full flavor across more bites for less meat per plate.
  • Keep the horseradish sauce a spoonful, not a blanket. Horseradish is nearly free and intensely flavored — it is there to cut the richness, and a little genuinely does. The beef underneath needs no help being absorbed: its iron is heme iron, taken up at roughly 15–35%, against 2–20% for plant iron — that gap is red meat's real nutritional advantage. B12 is the quieter half; your liver stores years' worth, so it supports steadily rather than dramatically.
Ingredients
  • For the crust:
  • 1/2 cup (4 oz/125 g) Dijon mustard
  • 1/4 cup (2 oz/60 g) prepared horseradish
  • 1/4 cup (3 oz/90 g) dried bread crumbs
  • 2 tablespoons chopped fresh rosemary or 1 tablespoon dried
  • 6 cloves garlic, minced
  • 2 teaspoons salt
  • 2 teaspoons freshly ground pepper
  • 1 standing prime rib roast (4 ribs), 6–8 lb (3–4 kg), chine bone removed by the butcher
  • 1/2 cup (4 oz/125 g) prepared horseradish
  • 1/2 cup (4 oz/125 g) sour cream
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Crust: In a small bowl, mix ½ cup Dijon mustard, ¼ cup horseradish, ¼ cup dried bread crumbs, 2 tablespoons rosemary, 6 cloves garlic, 2 teaspoons salt, and 2 teaspoons pepper. Rub mixture all over the meat and let stand at room temperature for at least 15 minutes or up to 1 hour, or cover and refrigerate overnight; bring to room temperature, if necessary, before cooking.
  2. Step 2: Preheat oven to 350°F (180°C). Oil a roasting pan just large enough to hold the roast. Place the 1 standing prime rib roast fat side up in the pan and roast until nicely browned, about 1 hour. Check doneness with an instant-read thermometer inserted away from the bone or by cutting into meat near the bone: for rare beef remove roast at 120°–125°F (49°–52°C) when meat is red near the bone; for medium-rare remove at 130°F (54°C) when meat is deep pink near the bone.
  3. Step 3: Transfer roast to a carving board and let rest, tented loosely with aluminum foil, for 10–12 minutes before serving.
  4. Step 4: Whisk ½ cup horseradish and ½ cup sour cream together in a small bowl. Carve roast (left) into thick or thin slices as desired, transfer to individual plates, and serve with horseradish sauce on top.
Sidebar "Carving Rib Roasts" (paraphrased): Carving prime rib, bone-in pork loin, and racks of lamb is easier when the butcher removes the chine bone that runs along the bottom. To carve, place roast on a carving board holding the knife parallel to the ribs, slice along the edge of the ribs under the rib-eye (the meaty portion) to separate it from the bones, then slice the rib-eye as thinly or thickly as liked; or cut between the bones for bone-in slices. Variation Tip (paraphrased): Rib roast can also be cooked on a grill — prepare a charcoal or gas grill for indirect grilling over medium-high heat (p. 106), place prepared roast fat side up over the cooler portion with a drip pan underneath, cover, and roast for 1 hour; check doneness as directed above.

Servings: 4–6 · Oven: 450°F (230°C)

Adapted from Poole's.

Why it’s healthy

Lamb brings the red-meat strengths in a controlled package: 50 g of protein in a serving and iron at 31% of a day's worth, in the form your body absorbs best, plus vitamin B12 for red blood cells and nerves. The crust earns its place — Dijon mustard, rosemary, garlic and olive-oil crumbs give a seared, savory shell for very little, and the olive oil's fat is mostly monounsaturated, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance. Sodium stays low for a restaurant-style main: 272 mg in a serving.

The honest cost

The lamb's own fat: 10 g of saturated fat in a serving — 52% of a day's 20 g limit — in 588 calories. Rack is a rich cut, though a leaner one than its reputation suggests once the crust, not a sauce, carries the flavor. There is no butter and no cream anywhere in this recipe; the cost is the cut itself, portioned by the chop.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Serve the two chops the recipe assigns. Carved into chops and served two to a diner, the portion is built into the dish — that is the honest size for a cut this rich, next to vegetables.
  • Rest the racks 5 to 10 minutes before carving. The juices stay in the meat, so each chop tastes complete on its own — no pan sauce needs inventing to rescue dryness.
  • Sear properly — hot pan, no crowding. A deep golden crust on every side is flavor the plate doesn't have to buy back with fat or salt later. What the lamb itself delivers is worth the sear's care: its iron is heme iron, absorbed at roughly 15–35% against 2–20% for plant iron. The crust's olive oil plays a supporting role — its monounsaturated fat improves cholesterol mainly by replacing saturated fat, and its bitter polyphenol, oleocanthal, calms inflammation; refined oil has little of that bite.
Ingredients
  • 2 racks of lamb, about 1 1/2 lb (750 g) each, frenched by the butcher
  • Salt and freshly ground pepper
  • 1 tablespoon olive oil
  • For the crust:
  • 1/2 cup (2 oz/60 g) dried bread crumbs
  • 2 teaspoons finely chopped fresh rosemary
  • 2 teaspoons garlic powder or granulated garlic
  • 1/4 cup (2 fl oz/60 ml) olive oil, or as needed
  • 2 tablespoons Dijon mustard
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Season the 2 racks of lamb generously with salt and pepper. Let meat stand at room temperature at least 15 minutes or up to 1 hour before cooking.
  2. Step 2: Preheat oven to 450°F (230°C).
  3. Step 3: In a large ovenproof frying pan over medium-high heat, heat 1 tablespoon olive oil. When oil starts to smoke, add racks fat side down. Sear until golden brown on all sides, about 2 minutes on each side; do not crowd the pan (use 2 frying pans if necessary). When browned, transfer to a platter and set aside to cool. Reserve the pan(s).
  4. Step 4: Crust: In a bowl, combine ½ cup dried bread crumbs, 2 teaspoons rosemary, and 2 teaspoons garlic powder and mix well. Add olive oil until bread crumbs have the feel of wet sand; you may need more or less than ¼ cup olive oil. Using a spatula, spread 2 tablespoons Dijon mustard over the meat of each rack, excluding the bones. Pack bread crumb mixture over the mustard to help it adhere.
  5. Step 5: Return racks to the pan(s) and roast in the oven until an instant-read thermometer inserted away from the bone registers 130°F (54°C) and meat is quite pink when cut into near the bone for medium-rare, 12–15 minutes.
  6. Step 6: Transfer to a carving board and let rest, loosely tented with aluminum foil, for 5–10 minutes before serving.
  7. Step 7: Carve into chops and serve 2 to each diner.
Sidebar "Pan-Roasting" (paraphrased): Pan-roasting involves browning meat on the stovetop then finishing it by roasting in a hot oven. In a restaurant this allows the chef to precook the meat then finish it quickly with a brief final roasting. For home cooks it offers partially cooking the roast ahead of time while ensuring a browned surface and perfectly cooked interior. For more on roasting, see p. 109.

Yield: 2 quarts

Adapted from Poole's.

Why it’s healthy

Popcorn is a true whole grain: real fiber that fills you up, in a snack that stays light as long as it isn't drowned in butter and salt — and this one isn't. The corn brings lutein, a pigment that collects in your eyes and helps protect vision as you age. The olive oil is never cooked; it's whisked raw with Dijon and black pepper and used as the coating, so everything good in the oil reaches the bowl intact.

The honest cost

Very little, by snack standards. A serving carries 1.5 g of saturated fat — 7% of a day's limit — and 150 mg of sodium, in about 99 calories. The quarter cup of olive oil is the only real fat, and it's spread across eight servings and a lot of popcorn. This is the rare crunchy snack whose cost is mostly about how much of it you eat.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Use extra virgin olive oil for the coating. Since the oil is never heated, its bitter compounds survive whole — this is exactly the dish where the best bottle earns its place. The bite in good olive oil is oleocanthal, a polyphenol that calms inflammation and shields blood-vessel walls; cheap, refined oil has little of it. Heat and time wear it down, but here the oil goes from bottle to bowl to popcorn without cooking — full strength, and you can taste that it is.
  • Add the Parmesan in three batches, by hand. The recipe's method coats every handful evenly, so a quarter cup of cheese flavors two quarts of popcorn — seasoning coverage instead of cheese volume.
  • Serve it right away. Fresh, it's crisp and loud with pepper; that's the satisfying version, the one that doesn't send you back for a second bowl out of habit.
Ingredients
  • 1/4 cup popcorn kernels, preferably an heirloom variety
  • 1/4 cup olive oil
  • 1 tablespoon Dijon mustard
  • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt
  • Black pepper in a mill
  • 1/4 cup finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Place ¼ cup popcorn kernels in a paper lunch bag and fold over the top three times in 1-inch folds. Place upright in the microwave for 1 minute 45 seconds, or until popping slows to 3 to 5 seconds between each pop.
  2. Step 2: In a large bowl, combine ¼ cup olive oil, 1 tablespoon Dijon mustard, ¼ teaspoon sea salt, and about 40 cranks of the pepper mill. Whisk together (it will not entirely emulsify), then use a rubber spatula to spread the mixture around the sides of the bowl (it will thicken into a paste as spread).
  3. Step 3: Add popcorn to the bowl and use a spatula to fold popcorn against the coated walls; make sure popcorn is well coated.
  4. Step 4: Add the ¼ cup grated Parmigiano-Reggiano in three batches, using hands to incorporate each addition before adding more. Serve immediately.
Intro (paraphrased): Popcorn described as an all-occasion food; author prefers heirloom varieties such as Indigo or Yellow Flint from Geechie Boy Mill for distinctive flavor; recipe has few ingredients so use best quality available but can be adapted to what is on hand; as a snack it feeds 2 really hungry skiers or 4 to 6 people with normal appetites.

Yield: 48 oysters · Oven: 400°F convection (425°F regular oven)

Adapted from Poole's.

Why it’s healthy

The oyster is one of the most nutrient-dense bites there is: more zinc per bite than almost any food — zinc is what your immune cells are built with — plus B12 for red blood cells, a little omega-3, and iron at 42% of a day's worth in a serving. Around it, turnip greens and their root, a raw tomato relish in olive oil, and vitamin C at 30% of a day.

The honest cost

The creamed greens. Half a cup of heavy cream is puréed into the turnip topping, and a serving carries 5.2 g of saturated fat — 26% of a day's limit. Pasture-raised cream shrinks that a little: dairy from grass-fed cows carries more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) and more of the fat-soluble vitamins A, E and K2 than conventional dairy. Still cream — just better built, and portioned by the teaspoon.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Keep the topping at a teaspoon per oyster. That's the recipe's measure — the cream becomes a seasoning on a lean oyster instead of a sauce the oyster swims in.
  • Squeeze the greens dry. The recipe wrings out the cooked greens before they meet the cream — less water in the purée means the topping stays rich-tasting without needing more cream to carry it.
  • Leave the relish raw, and use your best olive oil in it. The roasted tomatoes go on uncooked at the end, in oil that never sees heat — where its bitter, vessel-protecting compounds survive intact. Two different tomato-and-oil stories meet on this oyster. Roasting already did the lycopene work: heat bursts tomato cell walls and reshapes the red pigment into the form your gut absorbs best, and oil ferries it across. The raw relish oil does the other job — its bite is oleocanthal, a polyphenol that calms inflammation and shields blood-vessel walls, and refined oil has little of it.
Ingredients
  • 1/2 cup Roasted Tomatoes (page 162), minced
  • 1/2 teaspoon minced shallot
  • 2 tablespoons olive oil
  • Black pepper in a mill
  • Sea salt
  • 2 tablespoons neutral vegetable oil
  • 1/2 cup minced yellow onion
  • 10 ounces turnip greens (about 1 bunch), roughly chopped
  • 1/2 cup heavy cream
  • 1 cup finely diced turnip root
  • 4 dozen chubby East Coast oysters, on the half shell
  • 1/4 cup cornbread crumbs (see page 100)
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Tomato relish: In a small bowl, combine ½ cup roasted tomatoes, ½ teaspoon minced shallot, 2 tablespoons olive oil, 10 cranks of the pepper mill, and ¼ teaspoon salt. Set aside.
  2. Step 2: In a large, heavy-bottomed skillet, heat 2 tablespoons vegetable oil over medium heat. Add ½ cup minced yellow onion and cook until softened, about 3 minutes. Add 10 ounces turnip greens and cook, stirring occasionally, until greens are tender, about 4 minutes. Season with salt and remove from heat. When greens are cool enough to handle, squeeze out excess moisture; set aside.
  3. Step 3: In a small saucepan over medium heat, combine ½ cup heavy cream, ¼ teaspoon salt, 1 cup diced turnip root, and 1/2 cup water and bring to a simmer. Reduce heat to low and simmer until turnip is tender, about 12 minutes. Transfer cream and turnip mixture to a food processor and pulse until it forms a paste. Add reserved turnip greens and puree for 60 to 90 seconds. Taste and season to the salt level of the oysters (see Note). Set aside.
  4. Step 4: Preheat a convection oven to 400°F (or a regular oven to 425°F). Cover two rimmed baking sheets with a layer of rock salt to serve as a bed for the oysters. Arrange the 4 dozen oysters in their half shells on the rock salt. Season oysters lightly with salt, then top each with 1 teaspoon of the creamed turnip greens.
  5. Step 5: Transfer oysters to the oven and bake for 6 to 8 minutes, until oysters just start to bubble around the edges.
  6. Step 6: Top each oyster with 1/2 teaspoon of the tomato relish and a pinch of cornbread crumbs (¼ cup cornbread crumbs in total). Serve immediately.
Note printed with ingredients: If oysters are super briny, avoid adding extra salt. Method note: Creamed turnip greens can be made up to 3 days in advance and stored in the refrigerator until ready to use. Intro (paraphrased): Inspired by oysters Rockefeller and Carolina coast oyster bars; best enjoyed straight from the oven with a can of ice-cold beer-flavored beer.

Servings: 8

Adapted from Poole's.

Why it’s healthy

Four pounds of vegetables are the dish: oyster mushrooms with their savory depth and B vitamins, and asparagus bringing folate for making new cells plus inulin, the prebiotic fiber your good gut bacteria feed on. A serving still lands 5 g of fiber and a quarter of a day’s iron, and the lemon squeezed in at the end keeps its vitamin C — and helps that iron absorb — because no heat touches it.

The honest cost

The cream sauce the vegetables wear: three-quarters of a cup of heavy cream plus two butters bring a serving to 9.7 g of saturated fat — 48% of a day’s limit — and the sherry, though reduced hard, is still alcohol added to a pan. Grass-fed cream and butter shrink the dairy’s cost a little, carrying more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) and more fat-soluble vitamins A, E and K2 than conventional dairy.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Sear the mushrooms until their edges crisp. Cook off the moisture they release, as written — caramelised mushrooms taste so complete that the cream reads as a gloss instead of the main event.
  • Reduce the sherry by three-quarters. That reduction, before the cream goes in, concentrates flavor and cooks down much of the alcohol — patience here is what lets less sauce satisfy.
  • Keep the lemon last and raw. Stirred in off the heat, its vitamin C survives whole and goes to work on the asparagus’s iron in the same bites. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, which is why a finish squeeze outperforms juice cooked into a sauce. Its strongest trick is pairing: eaten in the same meal, it can multiply the absorption of plant iron severalfold — here, the iron in the asparagus and mushrooms themselves.
Ingredients
  • 3 tablespoons neutral vegetable oil
  • 2 pounds oyster mushrooms, tough stems removed, torn into bite-size pieces
  • Sea salt
  • 1/4 cup minced shallots
  • 4 thyme sprigs
  • 2 pounds asparagus, ends trimmed and cut into 2-inch pieces
  • 1 cup amontillado sherry (I like Lustau)
  • 3/4 cup heavy cream
  • 2 tablespoons cold unsalted butter, cut into cubes
  • 2 tablespoons Porcini Butter (page 20)
  • Juice of 1/2 lemon
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a large skillet, heat 3 tablespoons vegetable oil over medium heat. Add 2 pounds oyster mushrooms and let sear, stirring a few times, until moisture they release has evaporated and edges begin to crisp and caramelize. Season lightly with salt.
  2. Step 2: Add ¼ cup minced shallots and 4 thyme sprigs and cook for 1 minute, stirring to combine and coat everything. Stir in 2 pounds asparagus, then add 1 cup amontillado sherry and deglaze the pan by swirling and scraping the bottom to release browned bits. Cook until liquid is reduced by three-quarters, stirring occasionally, about 3 minutes.
  3. Step 3: Add ¾ cup heavy cream and let it reduce until slightly thickened and coating the asparagus and mushrooms, about another 2 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in the cold butters (2 tablespoons unsalted butter and 2 tablespoons Porcini Butter).
  4. Step 4: Stir in the juice of ½ lemon, season with salt to taste, and serve immediately.
Intro (paraphrased): Oyster mushrooms described as meaty, mild, buttery; mushrooms hold moisture so season with salt after searing to let liquid evaporate, ensuring caramelization before tossing with sherry and cream.

Servings: 6 to 8

Why it’s healthy

Under the richness, the potatoes themselves deliver: potassium — 1,273 mg in a serving — that helps keep blood pressure in check, vitamin C at 60% of a day’s worth, and nearly 6 g of fiber across Yukon golds and russets. The cream is scented, not just poured: garlic, shallot, bay and thyme steep into it, so flavor arrives before fat does.

The honest cost

The cream is the dish: 49 g of saturated fat in a serving — about two and a half days’ 20 g limit — inside 925 calories, 46% of a 2,000-calorie day. Grass-fed cream and butter shrink the cost a little: dairy from grass-fed cows carries more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) and more of the fat-soluble vitamins A, E and K2 than conventional dairy. Still an occasion portion, made knowingly.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Stop when it turns silky. The recipe itself says you may not need all the cream and butter — add them bit by bit and quit at smooth; every spoon left in the pan is saturated fat nobody tastes missing.
  • Let the steep do the seasoning. Fifteen minutes of garlic, shallot, bay and thyme in the warm cream means the potatoes taste deeply seasoned before extra salt or fat enters the argument.
  • Serve it next to lean and green. A modest mound beside a lean main and a green vegetable is the plate this dish belongs on — its potassium and fiber count, its cream is shared.
Ingredients
  • 4 cups heavy cream
  • 1 1/2 teaspoons black peppercorns
  • 1/2 shallot
  • 1 head garlic, halved across the equator
  • 1 fresh bay leaf
  • 4 thyme sprigs
  • 2 pounds Yukon gold potatoes
  • 2 pounds russet potatoes
  • Kosher salt
  • 1 cup unsalted butter, cut into cubes, at room temperature
  • Sea salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a large saucepan over medium heat, bring 4 cups heavy cream, 1 1/2 teaspoons black peppercorns, ½ shallot, 1 head garlic, and 1 fresh bay leaf to a boil. Remove from heat and add 4 thyme sprigs. Let steep for 15 minutes. Strain cream through a fine-mesh sieve, discarding solids and reserving cream.
  2. Step 2: Peel the 2 pounds Yukon gold potatoes and 2 pounds russet potatoes and cut into 1-inch cubes. Place potatoes in a pot with 10 cups water and season with 2 tablespoons kosher salt. Place pot over high heat and bring to a boil. Reduce to a simmer and cook for 18 to 20 minutes, until potatoes are fork-tender. Drain potatoes well and return to the pot.
  3. Step 3: In a large saucepan, warm cream but do not boil. Place pot of potatoes over low heat just to warm through. Using an electric mixer, whip potatoes on medium speed until smooth. Add half of warm cream to potatoes, followed by half of the 1 cup unsalted butter. Continue to beat with mixer, and when both are fully incorporated, continue to add remaining cream and butter bit by bit until a silky-smooth consistency is reached; you may not need all cream and butter, depending on starchiness of potatoes.
  4. Step 4: Season potatoes with 1 teaspoon sea salt or to taste and serve immediately.
Intro (paraphrased): Cream is scented with aromatics so mashed potatoes move from canvas to foreground; gravy is welcome but author suggests these potatoes do not need it.

Servings: 6 to 8 · Oven: 350°F (oil temperature)

Adapted from Poole's.

Why it’s healthy

Under the crunch is a genuinely useful vegetable: onions bring fibers that feed the good bacteria in your gut — that's what "prebiotic" means — and help calm everyday inflammation. The rings are cut fat, a quarter inch to an inch thick, so a serving is mostly onion, not mostly coating. And they're made from scratch, from ingredients you can name, with no preservatives and nothing hidden.

The honest cost

Fried is fried. The rings drink up the pot's oil as they cook — a serving lands at 216 calories with 14.5 g of total fat — and the flour-and-cornstarch dredge is refined starch, while the seasoned coating and the finishing salt bring 502 mg of sodium, 22% of a day's ceiling. The onion is the virtue; the fry is the price.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Bake or air-fry a batch. The pack's own advice: the same seasoned rings, crisped with a fraction of the oil — you keep the onions and lose most of the fat.
  • Drain them well. The recipe lands the rings on two or three layers of paper towels — give them a minute there. Oil that wicks into the towel is oil nobody eats.
  • Keep the rings fat. Thick rings mean more onion and less coating per bite — the ratio is the health move, and it's already how the recipe cuts them. Your gut bacteria ferment those onion fibers into short-chain fatty acids, and those acids are the payoff: they feed the cells lining your colon and signal inflammation down. Onions are a steady, modest source — the benefit builds from eating them often, across many dishes, not from one basket of rings.
Ingredients
  • 4 Vidalia or other sweet onions
  • 3 cups all-purpose flour
  • 1 cup cornstarch
  • 2 tablespoons sea salt
  • 1 tablespoon freshly ground black pepper
  • Neutral vegetable oil, for frying
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Trim tip and tail of each onion, then cut the 4 sweet onions into fat 1/4- to 1-inch-thick rings crosswise (across the equator). Break onion slices into their natural rings, discarding centers.
  2. Step 2: Mix 3 cups all-purpose flour, 1 cup cornstarch, 2 tablespoons sea salt, and 1 tablespoon black pepper in a large bowl. Line a baking sheet with two or three layers of paper towels.
  3. Step 3: Fill a heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven with 3 to 4 inches of oil and set over high heat until oil reaches 350°F on a deep-fry thermometer.
  4. Step 4: Dredge onion rings in flour mixture, coating well. Transfer in batches to the pot and fry until golden brown, flipping occasionally, 5 to 6 minutes.
  5. Step 5: Transfer to prepared baking sheet and season with sea salt. Serve with choice of condiment (author notes a preference for Basic Malt Mayo on p. 21).
Intro (paraphrased): Best onion rings are imperfect, barely holding a simple batter of seasoned flour and cornstarch bound by a splash of buttermilk; mismatched ring size allows varied thickness/crunch; suggested as a starter at a gathering or served on the table as a side dish.

Servings: 4

Why it’s healthy

What is genuinely here is substance from real cheese: 27 g of protein and 637 mg of calcium — about half a day’s worth — in a serving, over macaroni cooked barely al dente, made entirely from scratch from ingredients you can name. Three cheeses — grana padano, Jarlsberg and white cheddar — mean a small portion tastes complete, not diluted.

The honest cost

The cream and cheese, at full strength: 41 g of saturated fat in a serving — about twice a day’s 20 g limit — inside 862 calories. Grass-fed dairy shrinks that cost a little: cream and cheese from grass-fed cows carry more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) and more of the fat-soluble vitamins A, E and K2 than conventional dairy. Better built — still an occasion dish, knowingly made.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Keep the reserved cheese on top. Sixty percent of the cheese goes over the surface, as written, where the broiler turns it into a golden crust — the strongest cheese flavor in every bite, from the same total amount.
  • Serve a scoop, beside something green. The gratin brings protein and calcium but almost no fiber — 1.4 g in a serving — so a salad or green vegetable completes the plate it cannot complete itself.
  • Rest it the full five minutes. The sauce settles and thickens off the heat, so a smaller serving holds together and satisfies instead of running thin.
Ingredients
  • Kosher salt
  • 6 ounces dry elbow macaroni (about 1 1/4 cups)
  • 1 teaspoon neutral vegetable oil
  • 2 ounces grana padano, shredded
  • 2 ounces Jarlsberg, shredded
  • 6 ounces white cheddar, shredded
  • 2 cups heavy cream
  • Sea salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a medium saucepan, bring 2 quarts water and 1 1/2 tablespoons kosher salt to a boil. Add the 6 ounces elbow macaroni and return to a boil; once boiling, cook until barely al dente (about 5 minutes), then drain pasta well. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet and mix in 1 teaspoon vegetable oil to keep noodles from sticking. Let cool completely; yield should be about 3 cups.
  2. Step 2: Set a rack in the oven about 4 inches from the broiler and preheat broiler. Combine 2 ounces grana padano, 2 ounces Jarlsberg, and 6 ounces white cheddar in a large bowl; reserve 60 percent of cheese for the top.
  3. Step 3: In a large deep saucepan, bring 2 cups heavy cream and 1 teaspoon sea salt to a boil. Let simmer for about 2 minutes; cream will foam up then subside into a simmer. Add noodles and cook, stirring occasionally, about 90 seconds; cream will start to thicken slightly and coat noodles.
  4. Step 4: Start adding 40 percent of cheese in small handfuls, stirring and waiting for each addition to melt and incorporate before adding more.
  5. Step 5: Transfer contents of pan to a 2 1/2-quart skillet or baking dish, mound reserved cheese over top, and place dish on a baking sheet to catch drips. Place baking sheet under broiler for 3 to 5 minutes, rotating throughout, until cheese melts and caramelizes into a golden-brown crust; watch carefully as broilers differ.
  6. Step 6: Remove gratin from oven and let rest 5 minutes. Serve immediately.
Intro (paraphrased, long): Macaroni au Gratin is Poole's mac and cheese, made to order with reduced cream, slightly al dente elbows, three cheeses (Jarlsberg, grana padano, sharp white Vermont cheddar), and sea salt; topped cheese is broiled to a caramelized crisp. Described as a signature, most-ordered dish and a representation of the restaurant's cooking goals.

Servings: 4 · Oven: 300°F convection (325°F regular) to start, then raised to 450°F convection (475°F regular)

Why it’s healthy

The bird itself is lean, complete protein — 45 g in a serving, every building block for keeping muscle. The brine is discarded and the pieces patted dry, so a serving lands at only 170 mg of sodium, remarkably low for roast chicken. The finish is the other smart move: pan drippings simmered, then taken off the heat and whisked with lemon juice and olive oil, so the lemon's vitamin C never cooks and the oil keeps the bitter compounds that protect blood vessels. Rosemary and thyme season the pan the whole way through.

The honest cost

Skin-on chicken roasted in its own fat, with a piece of butter melting over each quarter: 15 g of saturated fat in a serving — 77% of a day's 20 g limit — in 708 calories. Grass-fed butter improves its small share a little, with more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than conventional butter. Most of the cost, though, is the skin and the drippings the sauce is built from — which is also where much of the pleasure is. Know the trade; it is a fair one at the table.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Eat your piece skin-off when you want the lighter plate. The skin crisped in the pan has already flavored the meat beneath it; the chicken under it is the lean protein the dish promises.
  • Rest the chicken the full 10 minutes before the sauce is made. The recipe builds the sauce while the meat rests — juices stay in the chicken, so a drizzle of sauce finishes it instead of a flood.
  • Keep the lemon and olive oil off the heat, as written. Whisked in after the pan comes off the simmer, both arrive at full strength. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more of it — and in the same meal it can multiply the absorption of plant iron severalfold, which is work for whatever greens sit beside the chicken. The oil's oleocanthal, the polyphenol behind its bitter bite, is spared the same way; refined oil has little of it to begin with.
  • Take the garlic for flavor, honestly. The halved head roasts in the pan and comes out sweet and mellow — long cooking spends its allicin, so enjoy it as the garnish it makes, not as the health ingredient.
Ingredients
  • Kosher salt
  • 3 tablespoons sugar
  • 1 (3½-pound) whole chicken, quartered, backbones and wingtips removed (reserve these for making stock later)
  • 2 tablespoons neutral vegetable oil
  • 1 head garlic, halved across the equator
  • 2 rosemary sprigs
  • 4 thyme sprigs
  • 2 tablespoons unsalted butter
  • Juice of ½ lemon
  • 1 tablespoon olive oil
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Make brine: in a large pot stir 6 tablespoons salt, the 3 tablespoons sugar, and 4 cups water until dissolved; add 4 more cups cold water, add the chicken pieces (the 1 (3½-pound) whole chicken, quartered), cover and refrigerate 8 to 12 hours. Lift chicken out, discard brine, pat pieces dry.
  2. Step 2: Put a rack in the bottom third of the oven and preheat to 300°F convection (325°F regular). Heat the 2 tablespoons vegetable oil in a large cast-iron skillet over medium heat until it shimmers.
  3. Step 3: Season chicken lightly with salt, lay pieces skin-side down in the skillet with as much skin touching the pan as possible; cook 1 minute, then add the 1 head garlic, halved, cut-side down plus the 2 rosemary sprigs and 4 thyme sprigs. Sear until herbs and garlic are very aromatic, about 4 to 5 minutes, then move the herbs and garlic on top of the chicken pieces so they do not burn but still flavour the chicken. Keep cooking until the skin is very crisp — lifting a piece to peek — about 3 more minutes .
  4. Step 4: Cut the 2 tablespoons unsalted butter into four equal pieces and put one piece on top of each chicken piece.
  5. Step 5: Move the pan to the oven and cook 30 minutes. Flip the chicken and raise the oven to 450°F convection (475°F regular); cook about 10 minutes more, watching closely so it does not brown too fast. Take the skillet out and move the chicken, skin-side up, to a wire rack; rest at least 10 minutes.
  6. Step 6: Take the herbs and garlic out of the skillet (the roasted garlic cloves can be used as a garnish) and pour the pan drippings into a small saucepan. After the chicken has rested 10 minutes, bring the saucepan to a simmer over medium heat, turn off the heat, and whisk in the juice of ½ lemon and 1 tablespoon olive oil.
  7. Step 7: Put the chicken on a platter, drizzle with the pan sauce, garnish with the garlic cloves if liked, and serve.
Intro (paraphrased): author presents simple roast chicken as a favourite last-meal dish, inspired by the roast chicken for two at Zuni Café in San Francisco; roast chicken is also a regular at Poole's, where a longer, slower roast is used at home to get crisp skin and tender flesh.

Servings: 6 · Oven: 450°F convection (475°F regular) to start, then reduced to 250°F convection (275°F regular)

Why it’s healthy

Same generous cut as any short rib — 47 g of protein, iron in the form your body absorbs best, B12 for blood and nerves — but cooked with unusual restraint: salt, pepper, wine, garlic, thyme and rosemary, and nothing else. That plainness shows in the numbers: a serving carries just 211 mg of sodium, 9% of a day's ceiling, where a sauced braise runs several times higher. The herbs bring big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the meat needs little salt to taste seasoned.

The honest cost

Plainer cooking, same cut, same math: 21 g of saturated fat in a serving — 106% of a day's 20 g limit — on the meat alone, in a 705-calorie portion. The wine and herbs add flavor, not offset. This is two ingredients' worth of honesty: rich meat, simply cooked. The simplicity is the virtue; the richness is the price, paid knowingly.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Give it the full vented rest. Twenty minutes with the foil corners turned up lets the heat escape gradually and keeps the juices in the meat — juicier slices satisfy in a smaller portion, which is the only real lever this dish has.
  • Slice between the bones to portion. The bone-in slab divides naturally into servings; cutting it that way, as the recipe offers, keeps the occasion portion an actual portion.
  • Stir fresh garlic in at the end, if you want the health side. Four hours of roasting takes out most of the garlic head's protective compound — it stays as deep, mellow flavor. A little fresh crushed garlic over the slices is where that benefit lives. The herbs work mostly by indirection. Their compounds are polyphenols, dense per gram — but a serving is grams, so the direct dose stays small. The bigger mechanism: food that tastes seasoned needs less salt, and sodium is the heavier lever. Here the method already proves it, at 211 mg a serving.
Ingredients
  • 5 pounds bone-in beef short rib slab
  • Sea salt
  • Black pepper in a mill
  • 2 cups red wine
  • 1 head garlic, halved across the equator
  • 8 thyme sprigs
  • 4 rosemary sprigs
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Preheat convection oven to 450°F (regular oven to 475°F).
  2. Step 2: Coat the 5 pounds short ribs well on all sides with salt and pepper. Put them in a large roasting pan and roast 20 minutes, until a caramelized crust forms. Take the pan out and lower the oven to 250°F convection (275°F regular).
  3. Step 3: Let the ribs rest 10 minutes, then pour the 2 cups red wine and 2 cups water into the bottom of the pan. Add the 1 head garlic, halved, 8 thyme sprigs, and 4 rosemary sprigs to the pan. Cover the pan tightly with foil and return to the oven.
  4. Step 4: Roast 4 hours, until the ribs are very tender but not falling apart. Remove from the oven and turn up the corners of the foil while keeping the pan mostly covered, so residual heat escapes gradually and the ribs keep most of their juices. Rest 20 minutes.
  5. Step 5: To serve: either slice between the bones and divide among plates, or cut the whole slab off the bone and cut it into 1-inch-thick slices.
Intro (paraphrased): a dead-simple method the authors settled on after trying searing/braising and grilling; the meat is versatile — suggested uses include putting it in a potpie (see page 196), tossing with dumplings, serving over potato salad, or glazing with pepper jelly. Printed note (paraphrased): if making the ribs to use the meat in the Short Rib Pot Pie (page 196) or the Short Rib Hash (page 215), let the meat cool completely, cut it off the bone, dice into ¾-inch cubes, and refrigerate until ready to use.

Yield: about 20 cookies · Oven: 375°F convection (400°F regular)

Why it’s healthy

Keep this honest: these are cookies, and their health story is small but real. The eggs bring complete protein and choline, which your brain uses to make a key memory-and-focus chemical and which most people don't get enough of. The chocolate chips bring cocoa flavanols, which help blood vessels relax so blood flows more easily. And everything in the bowl is an ingredient you can name — a treat made properly, not a health food in disguise.

The honest cost

The sugar and the butter, counted plainly: 27 g of sugar and 11.4 g of saturated fat in a serving — 53% of a day's added-sugar limit and 57% of a day's saturated-fat limit — in 338 calories. Butter from grass-fed cows softens that a little — its fat carries more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than the conventional kind. None of that changes the category: an occasion food, in an occasion portion.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Freeze the scooped dough, bake what you'll eat. The recipe already chills the rounds overnight and freezes them for up to six months — portioned dough means fresh cookies without a full tray calling from the counter. Sugar is the mechanism, not just the calories: a dose this size floods the liver, which stores the overflow as fat, and repeated spikes wear on insulin sensitivity. Saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol — the particle count that tracks artery disease — more reliably than anything else in food. Making the cookies knowingly is the whole ask.
  • Go darker with the chips. Darker chocolate carries more flavanols and less sugar per handful, so the same 2½ cups work a little harder. The flavanols at work here coax blood vessels into releasing nitric oxide, their widen-and-relax signal; measured at chocolate-bar doses in trials, the payoff is a few points of blood pressure. Processing spends them — heavily dutched cocoa has few left. A small, real effect, riding in a food eaten for pleasure.
  • One cookie, cold milk, sitting down. The recipe's own serving — a cookie still warm beside a glass of ice-cold milk — is the portion the dish was built around. Enjoyed that way, it's an event, not a habit.
Ingredients
  • 2¼ cups all-purpose flour
  • ¾ teaspoon sea salt
  • 1¼ teaspoons baking soda
  • 1¼ cups unsalted butter
  • 1 cup granulated sugar
  • ½ cup plus 2 tablespoons packed light brown sugar
  • 2 large eggs
  • 1½ teaspoons pure vanilla extract
  • 2½ cups chocolate chips
  • Milk, for serving
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Sift the 2¼ cups all-purpose flour, ¾ teaspoon sea salt, and 1¼ teaspoons baking soda into a medium bowl.
  2. Step 2: In a stand mixer with the paddle attachment, mix the 1¼ cups unsalted butter and both sugars (1 cup granulated sugar and ½ cup plus 2 tablespoons packed light brown sugar) on medium speed only until barely combined. Add the 2 large eggs and 1½ teaspoons vanilla and mix until only partly combined. Add the sifted dry ingredients and mix until the batter is lumpy but not fully combined. Add the 2½ cups chocolate chips and mix until just combined.
  3. Step 3: Using a 2-ounce scoop, scoop the cookies onto a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing them about 2 inches apart. Refrigerate overnight. Freezing option from the page: put the baking sheet in the freezer for 1 hour, then move the cookie rounds to a resealable plastic bag and store in the freezer for up to 6 months.
  4. Step 4: When ready to bake, preheat a convection oven to 375°F (regular oven to 400°F). Bake 12 to 18 minutes, until the edges are golden brown.
  5. Step 5: Cool slightly, then serve with a glass of ice-cold milk.
Intro (paraphrased): a regular dessert at Poole's — warm cookies with a glass of milk; this version aims for crunchy edges with a tender, chewy centre. Two technique points are stressed: mix the dough a bit less than you think you should at each stage (some unincorporated flour in the final dough is fine), and shape, refrigerate overnight, and bake straight from the refrigerator.

Why it’s healthy

Be straight about it: this is a drink, not a food, and its health story is small. What's real in the glass is the fresh fruit — pineapple and orange juices bring vitamin C at 44% of a day's worth, and fresh pineapple carries bromelain, an enzyme that helps break down protein and sits well after a heavy meal. The nutmeg is grated fresh over the top. That's the bright spot, and it's enough.

The honest cost

The coconut cream and the rum, together. Two ounces of coconut cream put 13 g of saturated fat in the glass — 65% of a day's 20 g limit — and on top of that sit two rums, including an overproof float. Alcohol's risks scale with the dose and start low; there is no amount where it turns helpful. A dessert in a glass, made knowingly.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Keep the juices fresh. The orange is squeezed fresh and the pineapple should be too — fresh pineapple keeps its bromelain, which heat and processing destroy. Bromelain's proven stage is the plate: it dismantles protein, which is why pineapple tenderizes meat and can start digesting a meal alongside you. Claims beyond digestion outrun the evidence — most of the enzyme is itself digested. The vitamin C is the dependable half.
  • Measure the rums, don't free-pour. The recipe's 1½ ounces of dark rum and ¾ ounce of 151 is already a strong drink; the float on top is a small amount by design — keep it that way.
  • Make it an occasion. One, with food, at the end of something — the fresh fruit is the pleasure, and the portion is the whole health strategy. Two separate prices. Nothing else in food pushes LDL cholesterol — the particle count tied to artery disease — up as dependably as saturated fat does. Alcohol's breakdown products damage DNA and liver tissue, and the risk rises from the first drink. Neither argues with making it; both argue for an occasion, not a habit.
Ingredients
  • 2 ounces coconut cream
  • 2 ounces pineapple juice
  • ½ ounce fresh orange juice
  • 1 ½ ounces your favorite dark rum
  • ¾ ounce 151 rum
  • Fresh nutmeg
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a pint glass, combine 2 ounces coconut cream, 2 ounces pineapple juice, ½ ounce fresh orange juice, and the rums (1 ½ ounces dark rum and ¾ ounce 151 rum).
  2. Step 2: Add ice to the mixing glass and shake well.
  3. Step 3: Strain into a highball glass over fresh ice, float a small amount of dark rum on top, and finish with several gratings of fresh nutmeg.

Why it’s healthy

Keep this honest: it is a drink, not a food. Its bright spots are the fresh parts — lemon and lime juice bring vitamin C, about a third of a day’s worth in the glass, the ginger syrup carries ginger’s stomach-settling bite, and the muddled mint adds real herb flavor instead of a bottled substitute. Nothing here turns rum and syrup into health food.

The honest cost

The sugar and the rum, together. A serving carries 44 g of sugar — 89% of a day’s 50 g added-sugar limit — before anything else is eaten, and alcohol’s risks rise with the dose from the first drink; there is no healthy amount underneath it.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Let the soda water do more. Top the glass generously, as written — the fizz stretches the same muddled citrus, mint and ginger across a longer, colder drink without another spoon of syrup.
  • Don’t strain out the good parts. The recipe keeps the muddled mint and citrus in the glass; that pulp and leaf are the freshest thing in it.
  • Keep it to the occasion. One, with food, is the portion this cost section describes — a second spends the sugar limit the first one nearly used up. A dose of sugar this size goes straight to the liver, which banks the overflow as fat; spike after spike, insulin sensitivity pays for it. Alcohol adds its own separate price through breakdown products that damage DNA and liver tissue. Making it knowingly — an occasion drink, in an occasion portion — is the whole point.
Ingredients
  • Half a handful of fresh mint
  • 2 lemon wedges
  • 3 lime wedges
  • 2 ½ ounces ginger infused simple syrup
  • 1 ½ ounces rum
  • 1 ounce fresh lemon juice
  • 1 ounce fresh lime juice
  • Soda water
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a pint glass, muddle mint with 2 lemon wedges and 3 lime wedges to crush the mint and release citrus juice.
  2. Step 2: Add the 2 ½ ounces ginger infused simple syrup and muddle a little more; do not strain.
  3. Step 3: Fill the glass with ice.
  4. Step 4: Add 1 ½ ounces rum, 1 ounce fresh lemon juice, and 1 ounce fresh lime juice.
  5. Step 5: Top with soda water, stir, and garnish with extra lemon and lime.

Adapted from Soulful Harvest.

Why it’s healthy

An accompaniment with a real aromatic spine: garlic, ginger and jalapeño do the flavor work, fresh orange juice brings brightness and a little vitamin C, and the chile heat makes rich food satisfying in smaller portions — the peppers' quiet gift. There's almost no fat in the pot, a tenth of a gram in a serving, so a spoonful delivers the flavor of a dish without delivering the dish.

The honest cost

The soy sauce and the brown sugar. A serving carries 828 mg of sodium — 36% of a day's ceiling — and about 15 g of sugar, nearly a third of a day's added-sugar limit. Spooned on as a glaze, the dose keeps both in check; poured like a gravy, this sauce spends the meal's salt and sugar budget by itself.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Rest the mince before the pot. Everything is minced and simmered together, so give the garlic its 10 minutes after mincing — its protective compound forms in that window, before the simmer can stop it. A whole clove contains no allicin: a building block and the enzyme that uses it wait in separate compartments until mincing mixes them, and the compound builds over about ten minutes. In a sauce that simmers everything at once, the rest on the cutting board is the only chance it gets — and in this dish, garlic carries more health weight than any other seasoning.
  • Keep the simmer at the short end. Eight minutes, not ten: vitamin C fades with long cooking, and the orange juice and peppers keep more of theirs in a shorter simmer.
  • Glaze, don't pour. The sauce is built loud on purpose — a brushed-on coat gives the full boom for a fraction of the sodium and sugar a poured serving carries.
Ingredients
  • 1 cup soy sauce
  • 1 cup brown sugar
  • 2 tablespoons Sriracha
  • 1 cup fresh orange juice
  • 2 jalapeños, minced
  • 4 cloves garlic, minced
  • 1 3-inch knob ginger, minced
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Put all ingredients together: 1 cup soy sauce, 1 cup brown sugar, 2 tablespoons Sriracha, 1 cup fresh orange juice, 2 jalapeños, 4 cloves garlic, 1 3-inch knob ginger. Bring to a strong simmer.
  2. Step 2: Cook 8–10 minutes.
  3. Step 3: If needed, thicken with a corn starch slurry.
