Adapted from Soulful Harvest.

Why it’s healthy

A spoonful of seasoning, not a serving of food — and the seasoning is doing real work. Fresh parsley, chives and dill bring concentrated flavor from protective plant compounds, lemon juice brings vitamin C, and black pepper keeps the whole thing loud enough that a thin spread satisfies. The garlic is powder here, so expect its flavor rather than fresh garlic’s full protective punch.

The honest cost

The mayonnaise and sour cream base. A serving carries 2.4 g of saturated fat and 247 mg of sodium in 113 calories — modest numbers that grow fast if this is poured instead of spread. There is no lighter ingredient hiding in it; the dose is what keeps the cost small.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Spread it, don’t spoon it. The herbs, lemon and pepper are concentrated on purpose — a thin layer over a sandwich or vegetables delivers the full flavor for a fraction of a dollop.
  • Put it on beans or greens. That pairing is where the lemon earns more than flavor: its vitamin C, eaten in the same bites, helps your body take up the iron in plant foods. Honest sizing: vitamin C will not prevent an ordinary cold, and its collagen work is upkeep, not transformation. The iron effect is the dependable one — alongside beans or greens, it can raise plant-iron absorption severalfold. Because this aioli is never cooked, none of that vitamin C is spent to heat.
  • Keep it cold and use it within three days. The recipe’s own limit — the herbs stay bright, the lemon stays sharp, and nothing in the bowl has been dulled by heat.
Ingredients
  • ¼ cup buttermilk
  • ¼ cup sour cream
  • ½ cup mayonnaise
  • ½ teaspoon fresh parsley, finely chopped
  • 1 ¼ teaspoon fresh chives, finely chopped
  • 1 teaspoon fresh dill, finely chopped
  • 2 tablespoons lemon juice
  • ½ teaspoon onion powder
  • ¼ teaspoon garlic powder
  • ½ teaspoon salt
  • ¾ teaspoon black pepper
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Mix all ingredients together until smooth: ¼ cup buttermilk, ¼ cup sour cream, ½ cup mayonnaise, ½ teaspoon fresh parsley, 1 ¼ teaspoon fresh chives, 1 teaspoon fresh dill, 2 tablespoons lemon juice, ½ teaspoon onion powder, ¼ teaspoon garlic powder, ½ teaspoon salt, ¾ teaspoon black pepper.
  2. Step 2: Refrigerate; keeps up to three days.

Adapted from Soulful Harvest.

Why it’s healthy

Mushrooms are the rare ingredient that tastes rich and isn't: deep savory flavor for very few calories, plus B vitamins your body uses to turn food into energy. The onions cooked down with them bring fibers that feed the good bacteria in your gut — that's what “prebiotic” means. And it's made from scratch, from whole ingredients you can name, so nothing hides in the bowl.

The honest cost

The cream, with a tablespoon of butter at the start. Half a cup of heavy cream across the pot puts 6.8 g of saturated fat in a serving — about a third of a day's limit — over an otherwise lean soup. Pasture-raised cream and butter shrink that cost a little: dairy from grass-fed cows carries more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) and more of the fat-soluble vitamins A, E and K2 than conventional dairy. Still a cream soup — just better built.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Cook the mushrooms until their liquid is gone. The recipe waits for every drop to evaporate before the sherry goes in — that concentration is free flavor, depth the cream doesn't have to fake. The B vitamins are cofactors — the tools your cells use to run energy chemistry, not energy itself. Mushrooms also carry ergothioneine, an antioxidant almost no other food has in quantity, and they make vitamin D if they see sunlight before cooking. The savory-for-almost-no-calories trade is still their headline gift.
  • Blend half, as written. Pureeing half the soup and recombining gives the body of a fully creamed soup — the mushrooms themselves do the thickening, so the half cup of cream reads as more than it is.
  • Keep the chives raw and last. Scattered on at serving, they stay bright and sharp against the richness — the contrast is what makes a modest bowl feel finished. The onion family's gut benefit runs through fermentation: bacteria turn those fibers into short-chain fatty acids, which feed the cells lining your colon and signal inflammation down. One soup is a modest dose — the effect builds from eating alliums often, across many dishes.
Ingredients
  • ¾ lb. mushrooms
  • A couple onions, chopped
  • 1 tablespoon unsalted butter
  • 3 tablespoons EVOO
  • 2 tablespoons sherry
  • 1 ½ cups chicken stock
  • ½ cup heavy cream
  • 2 tablespoons chives, chopped
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Quarter the ¾ lb mushrooms and chop the onion.
  2. Step 2: In a saucepan over moderate heat, cook mushrooms and onion in 1 tablespoon unsalted butter and 3 tablespoons olive oil, stirring occasionally, until softened and any liquid given off has evaporated.
  3. Step 3: Add 2 tablespoons sherry and reduce by half; add 1 ½ cups chicken stock and ½ cup heavy cream and simmer 16–18 minutes.
  4. Step 4: Blend half the mixture, then recombine; season with salt and pepper to taste and add more sherry if wanted.
  5. Step 5: Serve garnished with 2 tablespoons chopped chives.
Garnish with chopped chives.

Why it’s healthy

The cut is the start: tenderloin is the leanest cut of pork — closer to chicken breast than to ribs — bringing complete protein and thiamine (vitamin B1) at 36 g of protein in a serving. Around it, the broth works hard for few calories: shiitake mushrooms bring deep savory flavor plus B vitamins, the ginger's gingerol helps calm nausea and eases everyday inflammation, the jalapeño brings heat and vitamin C, and the peanut crust adds plant protein and monounsaturated fat, the heart-friendly kind, that keeps you full.

The honest cost

The broth and the crust carry the cost: 1,514 mg of sodium in a serving — two-thirds of a day's 2,300 mg ceiling — and 14 g of saturated fat, 71% of a day's limit, much of it from the butter that binds the miso-peanut crust. Grass-fed butter improves that butter a little, with more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than conventional butter. The lean meat was never the problem; what coats it and surrounds it is.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Keep the oven finish brief — 8 to 9 minutes, as written. Tenderloin dries fast; a rested, juicy slice satisfies in a way dry lean meat never does, and satisfaction is what keeps the portion where it belongs.
  • Serve the broth as a sauce, not a soup. Spoon it under and over the slices rather than ladling a bowlful — the flavor is concentrated, and the sodium lives in the liquid.
  • Finish with the fresh herbs, every time. Basil, mint and cilantro go on raw at the end, so their brightness survives — a plate that tastes vivid needs less salt to feel seasoned. The jalapeño works the same trick from the heat side: its capsaicin trips the nerve receptors that sense heat — the burn is a signal, not damage — and the body answers with widened blood vessels and a small rise in calorie burn. Honest size: the metabolic effect is minor; the way heat makes a rich plate satisfying in smaller portions is the bigger gift.
Ingredients
  • 1 pork tenderloin
  • ¼ cup red miso
  • 4 tablespoons scallions
  • ⅔ tablespoon fresh ginger, minced
  • ½ cup peanuts, finely chopped
  • ⅓ cup panko
  • 3 ounces butter, melted
  • ⅔ tablespoon grapeseed oil
  • Salt and pepper, to your taste
  • Fresh basil, chopped
  • Fresh mint, chopped
  • Fresh cilantro, chopped
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a mixing bowl, combine ¼ cup red miso, 4 tablespoons scallions, ⅔ tablespoon fresh ginger, ½ cup peanuts, and ⅓ cup panko with the 3 ounces melted butter.
  2. Step 2: Season the 1 pork tenderloin with salt and pepper, then press the mixture onto it as a crust and refrigerate briefly to set.
  3. Step 3: Heat ⅔ tablespoon grapeseed oil in a sauté pan and sear the pork until browned on all sides.
  4. Step 4: Move to a baking sheet and finish in a 375 F oven for 8–9 minutes.
  5. Step 5: Rest, slice on the bias, and garnish with cilantro, basil, and mint. Serve with the Shiitake Scallion Jalapeno Broth below.

Adapted from Soulful Harvest.

Why it’s healthy

A broth that earns its place at 40 calories a serving: the shiitakes bring deep savory flavor for almost nothing, plus B vitamins your body uses to turn food into energy, and the jalapeño's capsaicin warms you and opens blood flow a little while the pepper adds vitamin C. It's made from scratch — water, miso, mushrooms, pepper, scallions — so the flavor is built, not poured from a carton of hidden extras.

The honest cost

Count it with the dish it seasons, not alone. A cup of this broth is otherwise nearly free — mushroom depth in seasoned water — and its one real entry is the miso's salt, stated plainly: a quarter cup of red miso seasons the whole pot, and a serving still carries 642 mg of sodium, 28% of a day's ceiling, with just 88 mg of potassium to answer it. Drunk as a sauce over the pork it was built for, that salt rides along with the main dish's own seasoning, so count the two together.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Heat the miso gently, as written. The broth warms rather than boils hard at the start — gentle heat keeps the miso's flavor round, so the salt you do use tastes like more.
  • Finish with the scallions fresh. They go on raw at the end, never simmered — the bright, sharp top note is what makes a light broth read as complete. Capsaicin's burn is borrowed: it trips the receptors that report heat, the body answers with widened vessels and a small lift in calorie burn, and no tissue is harmed in the process. Honest size: the effect on metabolism is slight. The pepper's vitamin C and the way heat makes a light broth satisfying are the bigger gifts, and vitamin C fades with long cooking — another reason the scallions stay raw.
  • Spoon it on, don't soak in it. This is a broth for moistening slices of tenderloin — a ladle over the meat gives the full shiitake-jalapeño effect while most of the salt stays in the pot. Shiitakes share the mushroom family's quiet extra: ergothioneine, an antioxidant almost no other food carries in quantity, alongside the B vitamins. At two ounces across the pot the dose is small — the savory depth per calorie remains the real reason this broth works.
Ingredients
  • 1 cup water
  • ¼ cup red miso
  • 2 ounces shiitake mushrooms, stemmed and sliced
  • 1 jalapeño pepper, seeded and sliced thinly
  • Fresh scallions, fresh-cut, for finishing
Preparation
  1. Step 1: This is the sub-recipe / broth for Pork Tenderloin with Shiitake Jalapeno Broth (same page).
  2. Step 2: In a saucepan, combine 1 cup water and ¼ cup red miso and heat gently.
  3. Step 3: Add 2 ounces shiitake mushrooms and 1 jalapeño pepper and let the broth simmer.
  4. Step 4: Finish with a sprinkle of fresh-cut scallions.

Servings: 4–6 · Oven: 400°F

Nutrition couldn’t be verified for this one — treat the numbers as a rough estimate.

Adapted from Flavors from the Farm.

Why it’s healthy

The garlic is the plate, and roasting transforms it: three or four whole heads come out soft, golden and sweet enough to spread like butter — richness of texture with almost nothing behind it. Around it, small things with real value: the figs in the preserves bring fiber for digestion and potassium for blood pressure, and the blue cheese brings protein and calcium in the seasoning-sized amounts a board like this uses. A little of each, in combination, is the whole idea.

The honest cost

The cheese and the sweetness. Blue cheese is rich and salty even in a mild, creamy style like Saint Agur or Gorgonzola dolce, and fig preserves — like the honey offered as the alternative — are sugar to your body, however natural the source. The baguette underneath is the vehicle, not a virtue. None of it is hidden; the board is honest about being a treat built around a nearly free centerpiece.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Let the garlic be the spread. Squeeze a whole roasted clove over the torn baguette first, then a thin smear of cheese — the clove carries the bulk and the sweetness, so the cheese can stay a seasoning. Roasting trades away garlic's allicin — the protective compound that forms on crushing and dies in heat — for caramelized sweetness and depth. That trade is this dish's whole point, and it is a good one; just don't credit the board with raw garlic's health effects.
  • Keep the preserves at the recipe's small spoonful. A little fig on top of the cheese and garlic reads as a full flavor; the spoon is the difference between an accent and a dessert.
  • Drizzle the olive oil on the garlic, not the board. The oil belongs to the roasting packet, where a little keeps the heads moist and carries their flavor — the cheese needs no help being rich.
Ingredients
  • 3–4 heads garlic
  • Extra-virgin olive oil
  • Maldon salt
  • Soft, creamy blue cheese with not too much bite, such as Saint Agur or Gorgonzola dolce
  • Fig preserves or runny honey
  • Chewy sourdough baguette
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Preheat oven to 400°F.
  2. Step 2: Remove loose papery outer skins from the 3–4 heads garlic while keeping heads intact; cut tips off each head to expose clove ends.
  3. Step 3: Place foil on a sheet pan, set garlic heads root-side down in the centre, drizzle with oil, sprinkle with salt, and fold foil edges over to form a sealed packet.
  4. Step 4: Bake 40–60 minutes until soft and golden/caramelised.
  5. Step 5: Arrange garlic on a platter/board with the blue cheese and a pot of fig preserves alongside.
  6. Step 6: To eat: spread torn baguette pieces with cheese, squeeze a roasted clove over, and add a small spoonful of preserves; suggested drink pairing is a lightly chilled red or sparkling Lambrusco.
Hot tip (paraphrased): foil-wrapped garlic can instead be cooked over hot coals. Headnote is a short prose passage about favourite autumn smells including roasting garlic.

Servings: 4–6

Adapted from Flavors from the Farm.

Why it’s healthy

The base is exactly what it should be: leafy greens bringing folate for new cells, vitamin K for clotting and bones, and natural nitrates for blood flow, all for almost no calories. The Gruyère works as a seasoning — protein and calcium in a flavorful layer, not a cheese course — and the dressing is made from scratch, so nothing hides in it. The radishes and shallot keep it sharp and alive.

The honest cost

The dressing. A full cup of oil goes into it, and a serving of this salad lands at 565 calories with 10 g of saturated fat — half a day's limit — most of it poured from the cruet, not grown in the garden. The greens are nearly free; the dressing is the meal. Swapping the grapeseed oil for extra virgin olive oil improves the fat itself — its bitter compounds protect blood vessels — without touching the mustard-sharp flavor.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Drizzle, then toss by hand. The recipe's method is the portion control: dressing tossed through by hand coats every leaf with a film instead of pooling — you taste all of it and use less of it.
  • Keep the cheese split. Half tossed in, half over the top, the way it's written — the same 4 to 6 ounces reads as more cheese, in more bites, than one addition would.
Ingredients
  • For the dressing
  • 1 cup grapeseed oil
  • 1/3 cup red wine vinegar
  • 3 tablespoons Dijon mustard
  • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
  • 1–2 heads frilly red leaf and/or green leaf lettuce
  • 6–8 petite radishes, thinly shaved and immersed in ice water
  • 4–6 oz Gruyère cheese, grated on the medium holes of a box grater
  • 1 shallot, thinly shaved
  • 1–2 handfuls of herb croutons
  • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Make the dressing: blend the 1 cup grapeseed oil, ⅓ cup red wine vinegar, 3 tablespoons Dijon mustard, 2 pinches of salt and several cracks of pepper until smooth and emulsified, with a creamy, shiny look similar to thick heavy cream. Thin with a little water if needed, taste and adjust; it should be pungent, salty and mustard-forward. Set aside.
  2. Step 2: Trim the 1–2 heads of lettuce and tear the leaves into manageable pieces; place in a large bowl. Drain the 6–8 petite radishes, pat dry, and add to the lettuce with 2–3 oz Gruyère (half of the total), the 1 shallot and the 1–2 handfuls of herb croutons. Drizzle dressing over the top and toss gently by hand. Season with salt and plenty of pepper and toss again.
  3. Step 3: Mound the salad high on plates using two hands, finish with the remaining 2–3 oz Gruyère and more cracked pepper, and serve immediately.
Headnote (paraphrased) describes a piquant, tangy, rich salad; Batavia lettuce varieties are recommended as the best choice because the loose, frilly leaves have enough body for the emulsified dressing and cheese; use plenty of cheese and black pepper, pile the salad high and dress it with care. Suggested pairing: a floral white or light red wine and a crisp baguette with cold butter. Footer: Soup & Salad Time, page 121.

Servings: 4–6

Why it’s healthy

The asparagus is genuinely good for you: folate for making new cells, and inulin — a fiber your good gut bacteria feed on, which is what "prebiotic" means. The Parmesan works as a seasoning here, adding protein and calcium in a thin, flavorful layer rather than a cheese course. And the whole thing is made from scratch, from whole ingredients you can name.

The honest cost

The brown butter. Eight to ten tablespoons go over the platter, and a serving carries 16 g of saturated fat — 80% of a day's limit — over a lean vegetable. Grass-fed butter improves that fat a little, with more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than conventional butter, but it doesn't change the math: an occasion sauce, in an occasion portion.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Blanch tender-crisp, then shock. The ice bath stops the cooking cold, so the stalks stay bright and firm — the vegetable stays the main event under the butter, not a soft bed for it.
  • Pour, don't drown. The brown butter is there to melt the cheese and gloss the stalks; a coating does the whole job. What stays in the pan is saturated fat nobody misses.
Ingredients
  • 2 bunches asparagus, trimmed of woody ends
  • Wedge of Parmesan cheese (3–4 oz)
  • 8–10 tablespoons butter
  • Maldon salt and freshly ground black pepper
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Blanch the 2 bunches asparagus following the directions on page 18 until tender but still crisp, then shock in an ice bath until cool and drain well.
  2. Step 2: Arrange the asparagus on a serving platter. Grate a generous amount of Parmesan, about 1 cup grated Parmesan, over it and let it sit at room temperature while the butter is prepared.
  3. Step 3: Melt the 8–10 tablespoons butter in a sauté pan over medium heat. Let it foam, then watch as the milk solids settle and begin to brown; stir occasionally and continue heating until the solids are deep chocolate brown and smell nutty, then take off the heat.
  4. Step 4: Pour the hot brown butter over the platter so it melts the cheese covering the stalks. Sprinkle with salt and several twists of pepper and serve at once with tongs.
Headnote (paraphrased) says the dish was passed down from Uncle Fredo via his mother, in Fredo style, with juicy asparagus coated in Parmesan and brown butter. Hot Tip (paraphrased): Manchego is suggested as an excellent alternative to the Parmesan. Footer: Flavors from the Farm.

Servings: 6–8 · Oven: 450°F

Adapted from Flavors from the Farm.

Why it’s healthy

Four pounds of potatoes are the substance: potassium at a quarter of a day’s worth in a serving, vitamin C past half a day’s, and 5.5 g of fiber, seared in olive oil and braised in broth until they melt. Garlic and a handful of thyme, oregano or rosemary sprigs do the aromatic work, and the broth — not cream — carries the sauce.

The honest cost

The butter that foams over the sear: eight to ten tablespoons across the pan, bringing a serving to 10 g of saturated fat — half a day’s limit — in 418 calories. Butter from grass-fed cows improves the profile of its share — more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than the conventional stick. Rich for a potato side, and worth knowing before the sauce goes over.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Sear in the olive oil option. The recipe offers extra-virgin olive oil or rendered animal fat — the oil keeps the crust and swaps saturated fat for the monounsaturated kind, which is where its cholesterol benefit actually comes from. Swapping is the mechanism: monounsaturated fat improves cholesterol mainly by replacing saturated fat, not by being added alongside it. Extra-virgin oil brings one thing rendered fat cannot — oleocanthal, the bitter polyphenol that calms inflammation and shields blood-vessel walls, which cheap refined oil has little of.
  • Rest the garlic before the foam. The cloves meet foaming butter late and cook briefly — crush them about 10 minutes ahead so their protective compound forms before the heat arrives. That compound, allicin, is absent from a whole clove: a building block and its enzyme sit apart until crushing mixes them, and the build takes about 10 minutes. Hard heat destroys it quickly, so in a dish where garlic lands in hot butter, the rest on the board is its only protected window.
  • Spoon the sauce, don’t flood the platter. The reduced broth-and-butter sauce is glossy and concentrated — spooned over, as written, it coats each round; pooled, it is just more butter.
Ingredients
  • 4 lb potatoes (see headnote)
  • 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil or rendered animal fat
  • Kosher salt
  • 8–10 tablespoons (4–5 oz) butter
  • 6–8 cloves garlic
  • Several fresh thyme, oregano, marjoram, or rosemary sprigs, plus chopped herbs for garnish
  • Splash of dry white wine
  • 3–4 cups bone broth or stock (the best you can find)
  • Maldon salt and freshly ground black pepper
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat the oven to 450°F.
  2. Step 2: Peel the 4 lb potatoes and cut them into thick, scallop-like rounds with flattened sides; pat dry. Heat a large, heavy sauté pan over medium heat, add the ¼ cup oil/fat and heat until very hot and slightly smoking; brown in batches if the pan is not large enough.
  3. Step 3: Season the potatoes liberally with kosher salt and place them directly in the hot oil. Leave undisturbed about 5 minutes so a deep sear forms, gently rotating/swirling the pan instead of moving the pieces. When the underside is dark golden brown, flip with a spatula and cook undisturbed until the second side is also dark golden brown.
  4. Step 4: Once both sides are seared, add the 8–10 tablespoons butter, 6–8 cloves garlic and herb sprigs. When the butter melts and foams, cook 1–2 minutes longer. Add the wine to deglaze, stirring to loosen browned bits. Pour in the 3–4 cups bone broth, bring to a boil, transfer the pan to the oven and cook 35–40 minutes, until the potatoes give no resistance when pierced with a knife and the liquid has thickened.
  5. Step 5: Return the pan to the stovetop, move the potatoes to a platter, and reduce the sauce further over medium heat until shiny and emulsified. If it separates, add a little water or oil and bring it back together, then cook 1 more minute.
  6. Step 6: Spoon the sauce over the potatoes, finish with Maldon salt, pepper and chopped herbs, and serve immediately.
Headnote (paraphrased) identifies these as pommes de terre fondantes, described as an easy classic French preparation suitable for a weeknight with roast chicken or displayed around a standing rib roast at New Year's Eve. Butter alone works, but rendered animal fats such as beef tallow, bacon drippings, duck fat or schmaltz are suggested for extra flavour; a gelatinous bone broth or stock is key to the creamy melted texture and emulsified sauce. Waxy potato varieties are said to hold their shape better than starchy russets, though russets can be used; a cast-iron sauté pan is preferred, stainless steel also works; cut sides should be straight rather than sloping to contain liquid and steam. Safety caution (paraphrased): hot fat pops and splatters, so confidence and caution and kitchen goggles or glasses are recommended. Footer: Friends & Family, page 173.

Servings: 12

Why it’s healthy

The build is smarter than most mousses: there is no cream — a cup of extra-virgin olive oil, mostly monounsaturated fat, does the rich work, melted gently into a full pound of dark chocolate whose cocoa flavanols help blood vessels relax. Ten eggs bring complete protein and choline, the nutrient your brain uses to build its memory-and-focus messenger. The honey sweetens with trace protective compounds alongside — though your body still counts it as sugar.

The honest cost

Rich in both directions: 27.5 g of sugar and 12.1 g of saturated fat in a serving — 55% of a day's added-sugar limit and 60% of a day's saturated-fat limit — inside 487 calories for a small bowl. Pasture-raised eggs improve their share a little: hens that forage pick up more omega-3 fat and vitamin D than grain-only hens. Better built — still an occasion dessert, in an occasion portion.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Keep the chocolate darkest. The recipe's blend reaches for 99% cacao alongside the 68% — darker chocolate means more flavanols and less sugar in every spoonful. Flavanols are the cocoa's gift to blood vessels — they prompt the release of nitric oxide, which relaxes and widens them; at chocolate-bar doses, trials put the effect at a few points of blood pressure. How the cocoa was processed decides how much survives — heavy dutching spends most of the flavanols before the bag is opened. In this mousse the dark blend is doing quiet work under the pleasure.
  • Use your fruity, buttery olive oil. The recipe asks for exactly that — a good extra-virgin oil's bitter compounds protect blood vessels, and refined oil has little of them. The oil improves cholesterol mainly by replacing saturated fat — swapping is the mechanism, not adding — and here the swap is structural: oil standing where cream would. Its bitter bite is oleocanthal, a polyphenol that calms inflammation and shields blood-vessel walls, and the chocolate is melted over low heat, gently enough to keep it.
  • Portion it into glasses, not a bowl. The recipe offers serving glasses as an option — a set glass is a finished portion, and the overnight chill firms the mousse so a small one feels dense and complete.
Ingredients
  • 1 lb dark chocolate or blend of dark chocolates, such as TCHO 68% and 99% cacao, chopped
  • 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil, preferably with fruity, buttery notes, plus more for garnish
  • 10 large eggs, chilled
  • 1/4 cup runny honey, for the egg yolks
  • 1/3 cup runny honey, for the egg whites
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a heavy saucepan over low heat, warm the 1 lb dark chocolate and 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil together, stirring often, until melted and smooth. Set aside to cool slightly.
  2. Step 2: Prepare 2 medium bowls. Separate the 10 large eggs one at a time, whites in one bowl and yolks in the other. Add the ¼ cup honey to the yolks and beat with a handheld electric mixer on medium speed about 10 minutes, until lighter, more buttery in colour and doubled in volume.
  3. Step 3: Clean the beaters very thoroughly so no fatty yolk residue remains. Beat the whites on medium speed until bubbly with a bit of froth.
  4. Step 4: Heat the ⅓ cup honey in a small, heavy pan over medium heat just until it starts to simmer, then remove from the heat. With the mixer on medium speed, stream the hot honey into the whites and beat until they form soft peaks; stiffer whites give a firmer mousse.
  5. Step 5: Stir the yolk mixture briefly to check it has kept its character, then gently stir it into the chocolate–olive oil mixture until evenly coloured.
  6. Step 6: Fold the whipped whites into the chocolate mixture in a few batches, as gently as possible so as not to deflate them, folding just until no white swirls remain.
  7. Step 7: Spoon or pour the mousse into a larger vessel for later portioning, or directly into serving glasses or bowls. Cover the surface tightly with plastic wrap to prevent a skin forming and chill at least overnight or up to 1 day.
Headnote (paraphrased) describes a dairy-free, dense, rich mousse made from farm eggs and honey; portion size can be reduced to make more than twelve servings; it benefits from being made in advance and can be portioned ahead. Because the eggs are raw, the quality of the eggs, chocolate and olive oil is emphasised. Serving suggestions (paraphrased): a glass of Champagne or Château d'Yquem, or a small dollop of crème fraîche or vanilla whipped cream, or fresh raspberries or whole cherries over ice. Hot Tip (paraphrased): just before serving, garnish with a drizzle of the extra-virgin olive oil and a few crystals of Maldon salt. Page 198, footer: Flavors from the Farm.

Yield: One 9-inch cake · Oven: 325°F if using the convection setting or 400°F if using a conventional oven

Why it’s healthy

Call it what it is — a treat — and then credit its one real upgrade: a full cup of extra-virgin olive oil stands where butter would, trading saturated fat for the monounsaturated kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, and keeping the crumb moist for days. The eggs bring complete protein and choline, and fresh orange juice and zest do the brightening a frosting usually does.

The honest cost

The sugar: a slice carries 32 g — 64% of a day’s 50 g added-sugar limit — in 486 calories. The olive oil is a better fat than butter; it does not change the sugar.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Use your best extra-virgin oil, including the brush-on finish. The oil brushed over the warm cake, as written, is uncooked — its bitter protective compounds arrive whole, where a sugary glaze would only add sugar. That bitter bite is oleocanthal, a polyphenol that calms inflammation and shields blood-vessel walls; cheap, refined oil has little of it, and gentle treatment keeps the most. In a cake the swap is the story — monounsaturated fat improving cholesterol by replacing saturated fat, bite by bite.
  • Choose pasture-raised eggs. Same three eggs, same batter — hens that forage pick up a little more omega-3 fat and vitamin D than grain-only ones, a small upgrade to the cake’s best nutrient. The eggs’ headline is choline, which your brain uses to make acetylcholine, its memory-and-focus messenger, and which also keeps fat from building up in the liver. Eggs are among the richest sources there are — two cover roughly half a day’s need — so this ingredient carries real weight even inside a treat.
  • Cut a modest slice and serve it plain. Ten servings are written into the pan, and the orange and oil already finish it — no frosting, no syrup, nothing the cake is missing. The calories are only half the story — sugar this concentrated floods the liver, the overflow is stored as fat, and repeated spikes dull insulin sensitivity over time. That is the whole argument for a modest slice, enjoyed on purpose — none of it argues against baking the cake.
Ingredients
  • Butter and all-purpose flour, for the pan
  • 2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
  • 2 1/4 teaspoons kosher salt
  • 1 1/4 teaspoons baking powder
  • 1 teaspoon baking soda
  • 1 1/2 cups sugar
  • 3 large eggs
  • 1 cup plus 2 tablespoons whole milk
  • 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for brushing after baking
  • 1/2 cup fresh orange juice
  • 1 1/4 teaspoon grated orange zest
  • Dash of pure vanilla extract or vanilla bean paste
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat the oven to 325°F on convection or 400°F in a conventional oven. Generously grease a 9-inch Bundt pan with butter, getting into every nook, then dust with flour and tap out the excess.
  2. Step 2: In a medium bowl, whisk together the 2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour, 2 1/4 teaspoons kosher salt, 1 1/4 teaspoons baking powder and 1 teaspoon baking soda. In a large bowl, combine the 1 1/2 cups sugar, 3 large eggs, 1 cup plus 2 tablespoons whole milk, 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil, 1/2 cup fresh orange juice and 1 1/4 teaspoon grated orange zest, and vanilla and stir to mix well. Fold the flour mixture into the oil mixture just until the batter is evenly moistened and homogeneous.
  3. Step 3: Pour the batter into the prepared pan. Bake 45–60 minutes, until a toothpick inserted into the centre comes out moderately clean.
  4. Step 4: Let the cake cool in the pan on a wire rack for 15 minutes. Brush the top with a good amount of olive oil, unmould the cake onto the rack, lift off the pan, and brush the sides with more oil. Let cool completely before serving.
Headnote (paraphrased) discusses olive oil in sweets in Italy versus newer familiarity in the United States, and says a more intensely flavoured olive oil is better and a fruitier oil is preferred over a peppery one. Serving suggestions (paraphrased): serve plain alongside an afternoon espresso, or dress it up for lunch with softly whipped cream, sugared blueberries, a bit of citrus zest and a dash of Maldon salt, finishing with a drizzle of more olive oil. The cake can be made in advance and is said to taste even better the next day. Footer: Sweets & Treats, page 201.

Servings: 6

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why it’s healthy

The scallop at the center is lean protein with B12 for red blood cells and magnesium, a mineral muscles and nerves need to work and relax properly. The pineapple wrapped in with it brings real vitamin C — 31% of a day's worth in a serving — plus bromelain, an enzyme that helps break down protein. Grilled fast and served at once, the seafood stays the point of the skewer.

The honest cost

The wrap and the glaze. Every scallop wears a bacon slice, and the honey mustard and orange marmalade brush on as sugar: a serving carries 15.2 g of sugars, 4 g of saturated fat — about a fifth of a day's limit — and 436 mg of sodium. The honey is a natural sweetener with trace protective compounds, but your body still treats it as sugar. A party skewer, priced like one.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Keep the bacon thin, as written. The recipe warns against thick-cut for a reason — the thin slice crisps and seasons the scallop; a thick one turns the skewer into bacon with a scallop garnish.
  • Serve the reserved sauce at the table, not on the grill. Half the mustard mixture is already held back for serving — a dip at the table lets each eater spend the sweet glaze by the bite instead of baking a full coat onto every skewer.
  • Pull them at opaque. About six minutes, turning often, is the whole cook — scallops taken off the moment they turn opaque stay sweet and tender, so the lean center needs no extra glaze to be satisfying. Bromelain's proven stage is the plate: it dismantles protein, which is why pineapple tenderizes meat and can start digesting your meal alongside you. Claims beyond digestion outrun the evidence — most of the enzyme is itself digested, and heat destroys it — so the vitamin C is the dependable half of the pineapple's contribution here.
Ingredients
  • 1/2 cup honey mustard
  • 1/4 cup orange marmalade
  • Pinch red pepper flakes (optional)
  • 12 slices bacon,* cut in half crosswise
  • 12 medium sea scallops (8 ounces), cut in half crosswise
  • 1 can pineapple chunks, drained (24 pieces)
  • *Do not use thick-cut bacon.
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Oil the grill grate and prepare the grill for direct cooking over medium heat. Soak 12 (6-inch) bamboo skewers in water for 20 minutes to prevent burning.
  2. Step 2: Stir the ½ cup honey mustard, ¼ cup orange marmalade and red pepper flakes, if using, together in a small bowl. Reserve ½ cup of the mustard mixture in a separate small bowl for serving.
  3. Step 3: Wrap one bacon slice around one scallop half and one pineapple chunk and thread onto a skewer. Repeat with the remaining bacon (12 slices bacon), scallops (12 medium sea scallops) and pineapple (1 can pineapple chunks), putting two bacon-wrapped scallops on each skewer.
  4. Step 4: Grill the skewers about 6 minutes, or until the scallops are opaque, turning frequently and brushing with the remaining (non-reserved) mustard mixture. Serve immediately with the reserved mustard mixture.
Section header: Appetizers. Footnote on the bacon: do not use thick-cut bacon.

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why it’s healthy

Two ingredients — corn flour and water — and the corn itself has already been improved by one of the oldest food-processing tricks there is. Masa flour comes from nixtamalized corn, soaked in lime water in the traditional step that frees the corn's niacin so your body can use it and adds calcium in the bargain. Made from scratch, a tortilla brings a little fiber and iron, no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.

The honest cost

Almost none, and it's worth saying plainly: a tortilla carries 0.15 g of saturated fat, barely a gram of total fat and essentially no sodium — 1.4 mg. The only honest line is that it is a starch: 21.8 g of carbohydrate doing a carrier's job, so what it carries to the table matters more than the tortilla itself.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Rest the dough its 15 minutes. Covered, as written — hydrated masa presses thin and even, so the tortillas cook through in the comal's dry heat instead of needing more grease to behave.
  • Keep the comal lightly greased, and finish on the “face.” The recipe's light greasing is all it takes; flipped back to its first side at the end, the tortilla puffs slightly — the sign it's cooked through, tender, and ready without a drop more fat.
Ingredients
  • 2 cups corn flour
  • 1 cup water
  • A tortilla press
  • 2 circles of plastic paper
Preparation
  1. Step 1: English "Preparation" text, paraphrased: Put the 2 cups corn flour in a bowl, add the 1 cup water, and mix softly and quickly to combine. Cover the dough and let it rest 15 minutes.
  2. Step 2: Lightly grease a skillet or comal and heat over medium heat. Place a ball of dough in the tortilla press between the two plastic discs so it does not stick, close the press and press firmly.
  3. Step 3: Open the press, remove the top plastic, and carefully flip the tortilla onto one hand. Remove the remaining plastic and place the tortilla in the skillet/comal. Cook until it begins to lightly brown, then flip it to the first side (called the "face" of the tortilla) and finish cooking; it should puff up slightly. The page also gives the same preparation in Spanish under "Preparación".
English subtitle printed: "Handmade Tortillas". Introductory text in Spanish and English (paraphrased) explains the tortilla as food, plate and utensil, dating to the beginnings of agriculture in the Americas, ground/mixed/rolled with stone implements, and describes cooks shaping tortillas with their palms over ceramic or metal comales at feasts and celebrations. Page number 27. The photo at top right shows blocks of a pale solid (masa/cheese-like) — no caption transcribed.

Servings: 6

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why it’s healthy

The fish is the whole story: dorado is lean, complete protein — nearly 46 g in a serving with under 2 g of fat — plus potassium for blood pressure. Nothing is cooked, so the citrus juice's vitamin C and the fish's delicate fats reach the plate exactly as they started. The onion feeds your good gut bacteria, and the cilantro and chile make the bowl taste seasoned without leaning on salt.

The honest cost

Almost nothing pulls this one down. A serving carries 0.2 g of saturated fat and 137 mg of sodium — 6% of a day's ceiling — because there is no cooking fat, no sauce and no cheese anywhere in it. The only real dial is the salt and chili you add to taste, and both are in your hands at the bowl.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Squeeze the citrus by hand, gently. The recipe's own tip: press the peel too hard and bitter resins sour the fish — a clean squeeze keeps the juice bright, so the bowl needs less salt to taste alive.
  • Respect the two-hour marinade. Acid firms the fish the way heat does, but left too long it dries the cubes out; two hours at room temperature, then the fridge, keeps the texture — and the protein — at its best.
  • Put beans or greens on the same plate. The lime and bitter-orange juice does double duty at the table: its vitamin C is the key that unlocks plant iron in the foods beside it. Honest weighting: vitamin C's collagen role is upkeep, not transformation, and it does not stop colds in ordinary life. The iron effect is the strong claim — eaten in the same meal, vitamin C can multiply how much iron you absorb from beans and greens several times over. In a ceviche, the juice is already pooled around the fish, so the pairing costs nothing.
  • Let the chile work for you. Heat makes a lean bowl feel generous, which is how a modest portion satisfies. The burn is capsaicin tripping the nerves that sense heat — a signal, not an injury — and the body answers with slightly widened blood vessels and a small rise in calorie burn. Keep the size honest: that metabolic nudge is minor. The chile's real gifts here are its vitamin C, which no cooking ever gets to fade, and the satisfaction.
Ingredients
  • 1 1/2 kg. dorado (mahi mahi or other white fish)
  • 3 large onions, minced
  • 15 limes
  • 15 bitter oranges
  • salt
  • hot chili to taste
  • 3 Tbsp. minced cilantro
  • chili hot sauce (optional)
Preparation
  1. Step 1: English "Preparation" text, paraphrased: Cut the 1 1/2 kg dorado into small cubes and place in a glass dish. Add the 3 large onions, finely chopped, and the juice of 15 limes and 15 bitter oranges. The page's tip is to squeeze the limes and oranges carefully by hand without pressing the peel too hard, so resins that would sour the fish are not released.
  2. Step 2: Add salt and chili to taste, mix with a wooden spoon and cover the bowl. Leave at room temperature for two hours, then refrigerate. Do not marinate too long or the fish will dry out.
  3. Step 3: Just before serving, sprinkle with the 3 Tbsp minced cilantro. The page also gives the same preparation in Spanish under "Preparación".
English subtitle printed: "Fish Ceviche". A sub-recipe for chili hot sauce appears on the same page (see separate entry below). Page number 55.

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why it’s healthy

This is a seasoning, not a serving — and a clean one. Onion, carrot, peppercorns and a chili pepper steeped in vinegar: the carrot brings beta-carotene, the pigment your body turns into vitamin A for eyes and immune system; the chili brings capsaicin and a little vitamin C; and the onion's fibers feed your good gut bacteria. At about 10 calories a serving, flavor is nearly all it adds.

The honest cost

There is barely one to name. No fat, no added sugar and about 4 mg of sodium in a serving — the vinegar base sees to that. The honest limit is different: a spoonful is a condiment's dose of everything, so the vegetables in the jar season a meal rather than counting as a vegetable serving in themselves.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Give the jar its full three days. The recipe rests it sealed so the flavors blend completely — a sauce that tastes finished gets used by the spoonful, not poured on chasing flavor that isn't there yet.
  • Spend it on rich food. Heat is this sauce's lever: a sharp, hot spoonful makes a heavy plate feel complete in a smaller portion, which is where a 10-calorie condiment earns its keep. The heat is a false alarm: capsaicin switches on the same nerve receptors that report real heat, so the body responds as if cooling itself — blood vessels widen and calorie burn ticks up slightly. Honest size: that metabolic effect is minor. What matters at the table is simpler — food that tastes intense satisfies sooner.
  • Serve it where there's a little fat. The carrot's beta-carotene absorbs far better alongside fat than alone, so the sauce does its best nutritional work on the plate, not in the jar. One honest limit: the conversion is inefficient — roughly twelve molecules of beta-carotene in for one of vitamin A out — so carrots support vitamin A rather than cover it alone. Fat at the same meal is what closes the gap, multiplying what you absorb several times over. Raw and pickled, as here, the pairing at serving is the whole trick.
Ingredients
  • 1 onion, finely minced
  • 1 carrot peeled and minced
  • 12 whole black peppercorns
  • 1 minced Panamanian or jalapeño chili pepper
  • white vinegar
Preparation
  1. Step 1: English "Preparation" text, paraphrased: Put the 1 onion, 1 carrot, 12 whole black peppercorns and 1 chili pepper in a glass jar and cover all the ingredients with enough vinegar. Seal the jar tightly and store for three days so the flavours blend completely. Refrigerate after opening. The Spanish version says to refrigerate once it begins to be used.
none beyond the method above; this is the "salsa picante (opcional)" listed in the ceviche ingredients.

Servings: 4

Adapted from The Whole Fish Cookbook.

Why it’s healthy

Small fish, outsized return. Sardines and anchovies are the richest easy source of EPA and DHA, the omega-3 fats that help keep heart rhythm steady, calm inflammation and build brain cells — and because these fish are small and short-lived, they carry far less mercury than the big predators. Eat the soft bones and you get calcium with the protein. The lemon thyme oil is mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance.

The honest cost

The oil itself, in quantity. The fish are lean and the sodium is low, but the plates are covered generously, and a serving lands at 18.7 g of total fat and 219 calories for 12 g of protein. Using the good-quality extra-virgin oil the recipe calls for shrinks that cost a little — its oleocanthal polyphenols are what refined oil lacks. Still oil: the pour is the portion.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Eat the soft bones. No pin-boning is needed and the rib bones come out, but the fine, soft bones that stay are where the calcium lives — leaving them on the plate leaves the mineral behind too.
  • Use the optional lemon juice. The recipe offers it to offset the oiliness — a squeeze brightens each bite, so the fish satisfies with less oil clinging to it.
  • Mop, don't flood. Crusty bread is served for the oil; a mop of the plate gives you the thyme-scented best of it without drinking the pool the fillets swam in. Olive oil works two ways at once. Its monounsaturated fat improves cholesterol mainly when it replaces saturated fat — the swap is the mechanism. And the bitter bite in a good oil is oleocanthal, a polyphenol that calms inflammation and shields blood-vessel walls; cheap, refined oil has little of it, which is why this recipe specifies good-quality extra-virgin oil heated only gently, to 85°C.
Ingredients
  • 10 fresh whole sardines
  • 10 fresh whole anchovies
  • sea salt flakes and freshly cracked black pepper
  • Lemon thyme oil
  • 500 ml (17 fl oz/2 cups) good-quality extra-virgin olive oil
  • 2 tablespoons lemon thyme leaves or native thyme leaves
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Fillet the sardines: for a right-handed cook, place a sardine with its head to the left off the board, tail to the right and backbone facing you; the fish are filleted with the gut in because removing it beforehand is too time-consuming. Make a small cut behind the head to separate the collar from the rest of the fillet, then cut cleanly down the frame from head to tail to remove the first fillet intact in one movement, letting the bottom fillet rest on the board for support. The second fillet is trickier; use the board for support. No pin-boning is needed, but cut the rib bones out with a small knife.
  2. Step 2: Fillet the remaining sardines and anchovies the same way (10 fresh whole sardines and 10 fresh whole anchovies in total). Keep the bones, heads and gut, which can be made into garum (see page 73).
  3. Step 3: Make the oil (see also separate Lemon thyme oil entry): preferably in a Thermomix set to 85°C (185°F), blending on high for 10 minutes until fragrant; otherwise bring the 500 ml olive oil and 2 tablespoons lemon thyme leaves to 85°C (185°F) in a small saucepan, then blitz in a blender until fragrant. Strain through a sieve lined with muslin (cheesecloth).
  4. Step 4: To serve, arrange five anchovies on a warmed serving plate and place the sardines on top; repeat with a second plate. Season to taste and pour over enough oil to cover the plates generously. Optional lemon juice can offset the oiliness, but serve with plenty of crusty bread.
Introductory text (paraphrased) stresses using ultra-fresh sardines and anchovies, served warm — not cold — and still raw, not cooked, for texture and flavour, and pairs having both fish on one plate favourably against truffle and foie gras. Alternative Fish list at bottom left: Herring; Mackerel. Page 88, section "The Recipes".

Oven: 85°C (185°F)

Adapted from The Whole Fish Cookbook.

Why it’s healthy

This is olive oil made louder, so less of it is needed. Extra-virgin olive oil is mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus the bitter compounds that protect blood vessels — and two tablespoons of lemon thyme leaves perfume the whole two cups, so a drizzle tastes like a deliberate finish, not plain fat.

The honest cost

It is still pure fat: an assumed serving runs 246 calories with 3.8 g of saturated fat, and a free pour can double that before you notice. Choosing good extra-virgin oil over cheap refined oil shrinks the cost a little — the bitter polyphenols that protect blood vessels are in the extra-virgin oil and largely missing from refined. Concentrated either way; measure by the drizzle.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Hold the heat at 85°C. The recipe’s gentle temperature is the point — hot enough to pull the thyme’s flavor into the oil, gentle enough to spare the oil’s own protective compounds. Two things make extra-virgin oil worth this care. Its monounsaturated fat improves cholesterol mainly when it replaces saturated fat, not when it is simply added on top. And its bitter bite is oleocanthal, a polyphenol that calms inflammation and shields vessel walls — the compound harsh heat and refining spend first.
  • Finish with it, don’t cook in it. Save this oil for the end of a dish, where the thyme and lemon notes land whole and a teaspoon perfumes a plate.
  • Strain it clean. The muslin-lined sieve in the recipe leaves clear, leaf-free oil that keeps its flavor instead of turning on stray leaves.
Ingredients
  • 500 ml (17 fl oz/2 cups) good-quality extra-virgin olive oil
  • 2 tablespoons lemon thyme leaves or native thyme leaves
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Combine the 500 ml olive oil and 2 tablespoons lemon thyme leaves and heat to 85°C (185°F): in a Thermomix at 85°C (185°F) blend on high for 10 minutes until fragrant, or bring the oil and leaves to that temperature in a small saucepan and then blitz in a blender until fragrant.
  2. Step 2: Strain through a sieve lined with muslin (cheesecloth).

Yield: a 3-pound chicken with sauce left over

Why it’s healthy

The bird is the substance: lean, complete protein — 43 g in a serving — with all the building blocks for keeping muscle. The sauce, for all its sweetness, starts from real fruit: three cups of blueberries whose anthocyanins are linked to healthier blood vessels, and whose tartness does work that bottled sauces give to extra sugar and dye. Grilling keeps the cooking honest — smoke, heat, and a rested bird.

The honest cost

The sauce is the cost: 36 g of sugar and 2,099 mg of sodium in a serving — 91% of a day's sodium ceiling and nearly three-quarters of a day's added-sugar limit on one plate — plus 10 g of saturated fat from the skin and dark meat.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Baste in the recipe's rhythm, then stop. Thin coats every five minutes caramelize into real flavor; the final douse is where the sugar piles up — a toss through the sauce, as written, is plenty. Sodium holds water in the blood, and blood pressure follows the volume — and most of this serving's 2,099 mg is invisible: the dish tastes seasoned, not salty. The sugar works the same quiet way, flooding the liver, which stores the overflow as fat. None of this argues with making it; it argues for making it knowingly.
  • Eat yours skin-off. The grill and the glaze have already done the flavor work; the skin is where much of the fat rides, and the chicken underneath is lean.
  • Rest it the full 10 minutes. The juices stay in the meat instead of on the board — a juicier bite needs less sauce to feel complete.
Ingredients
  • 1 3-pound chicken
  • 3 teaspoons salt
  • 1 1/2 teaspoons black pepper
  • Blue Q Sauce
  • 3 cups blueberries
  • 2 cups apple cider vinegar
  • 2 cups granulated sugar
  • 1 3-inch cinnamon stick
  • 1 bay leaf
  • 1 teaspoon salt
  • 1/4 teaspoon chili flakes
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Cook the chicken: Light the grill and heat it to roughly 350°F. If using charcoal, add some water-soaked cherry-, pecan- or apple-wood chips to the charcoal for a smoke effect.
  2. Step 2: Have the butcher butterfly/spatchcock the chicken by cutting out the backbone and sternum and flattening it. About 10 minutes before cooking, bring the 1 3-pound chicken to room temperature and season it thoroughly with 3 teaspoons salt and 1 1/2 teaspoons black pepper.
  3. Step 3: Place the chicken skin-side up on the grill and close the lid. Cook covered for 20 minutes, then begin basting with the blueberry sauce (see Blue Q Sauce entry) every 5 minutes for an additional 20 minutes, keeping the grill lid closed between bastings.
  4. Step 4: After 40 minutes in total, turn the chicken over to caramelise the skin and baste the other side for 10 more minutes. Using a thermometer, check the temperature of a meaty part of the leg; if it is at 165°F, remove it from the grill, otherwise cook until it reaches the proper temperature, skin-side up.
  5. Step 5: Off the grill, douse the chicken in blueberry sauce and let it rest for 10 minutes. Once well rested, cut the chicken into 6 or 8 pieces and toss once more in sauce. Serve warm or at room temperature. The sauce method itself is in the separate Blue Q Sauce entry below.
Introductory text (paraphrased) explains the sauce, called Blue Q, is unlike a traditional Eastern Carolina-style barbecue sauce, is useful on items beyond meat, and works like a shrub — a fruit syrup punctuated by vinegar — mixed with club soda or alcohol, and as a fruity vinaigrette; it is used heavily on the author's own grill menu. Caution (paraphrased): whether using it on chicken or pork, it is not a marinade — brush it on toward the end of cooking and let it soak for a bit before serving, and the final soak is key.

Adapted from Deep Run Roots.

Why it’s healthy

The color is the real thing: three cups of blueberries, whose deep blue is anthocyanins — protective compounds linked in studies to slower memory decline and healthier blood vessels. It's a vinegar-based sauce with essentially no fat, and its tartness and color do work that bottled sauces hand over to extra dye. A small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.

The honest cost

The sugar. Two cups of it simmer into the batch, and a serving of the finished sauce carries about 28 g of sugar — over half a day's added-sugar limit — before it ever touches the chicken. The blueberries are real; so is the sugar. This is a glaze to be spent in coats, not a sauce to be poured.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Use it as a glaze, in coats. Brushed on in thin layers — the way the chicken recipe bastes with it — the sauce caramelizes and reads as intense; poured, it's just sweet.
  • Give it the overnight rest. The recipe rests it a night for the flavors to mellow — a mellower sauce satisfies in a thinner coat, which is where the sugar saving lives.
Ingredients
  • Blue Q Sauce
  • 3 cups blueberries
  • 2 cups apple cider vinegar
  • 2 cups granulated sugar
  • 1 3-inch cinnamon stick
  • 1 bay leaf
  • 1 teaspoon salt
  • 1/4 teaspoon chili flakes
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Combine the 3 cups blueberries with a little of the vinegar in a food processor and pulse just to break the berries up and get the blue juice flowing, not to make them smooth.
  2. Step 2: In a 4-quart saucepan, combine all the sauce ingredients (2 cups granulated sugar, 1 3-inch cinnamon stick, 1 bay leaf, 1 teaspoon salt, 1/4 teaspoon chili flakes and the remaining vinegar), bring to a simmer over medium heat and cook, covered, for 1 hour, stirring from time to time because it can burn.
  3. Step 3: Transfer the sauce carefully to a blender, remove the small knob on top of the lid and cover with a dish towel to prevent an explosion, and blend until as smooth as possible. Strain through a fine-mesh strainer back into the saucepan, bring back to a boil and reduce the sauce by a third. It should coat the back of a spoon, with a viscosity more like maple syrup than honey.
  4. Step 4: Refrigerate overnight to let the flavours mellow. The sauce keeps for months, covered, in the refrigerator.
See the Blueberry BBQ Chicken entry above for the headnote uses of this sauce (grilling, shrub-style drink, vinaigrette) and the caution that it is not a marinade.

Servings: 4 · Oven: 400°F

Why it’s healthy

The plate is substantial in the right places: a chicken-leg quarter brings 38 g of complete protein, and four cups of fresh corn bring fiber for digestion, potassium, and lutein, the yellow pigment that collects in your eyes and protects your vision as you age. The corn roasts two ways at once — dry and caramelised at the edges, juicy under the chicken — and everything is made from scratch, from whole ingredients you can name.

The honest cost

The salt and the skin: 1,938 mg of sodium in a serving — 84% of a day's ceiling — and 10.4 g of saturated fat, 52% of a day's limit, in 628 calories. Most of the sodium is invisible; the dish tastes seasoned, not salty.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Let the skin crisp, then leave it. The skin does its work in the pan — browning, rendering, flavoring the corn beneath — and eating yours skin-off keeps the roast's flavor while handing back a good share of its fat. Sodium holds water in the blood, and blood pressure follows the volume — which is why a number this size matters even when the plate doesn't taste salty. The saturated fat works the other familiar way, raising LDL cholesterol, the particle count that tracks artery disease. None of this argues with making it; it argues for making it knowingly — an occasion plate, in an occasion portion.
  • Stir all the corn together, as written. Mixing the caramelised edges through the juicy corn under the chicken spreads the most flavorful kernels across every serving, so no plate needs extra drippings spooned over it.
  • Taste before the corn's salt goes on. The corn is seasoned separately with its own teaspoon — the chicken was salted first and its drippings carry seasoning with them, so the full measure may be more than the pan needs. The corn's own contribution is worth the salt it does get: lutein is one of two pigments your eye concentrates in the macula, the high-definition center of the retina, where it filters harsh blue light and absorbs oxidative damage. Your body cannot make it — every bit arrives by plate, and a roasted ear's worth is a steady contributor.
Ingredients
  • 4 chicken-leg quarters, about 10 ounces each (this means drumettes and thighs attached)
  • 3 teaspoons salt, divided
  • 30 turns of the pepper mill or scant 1 teaspoon black pepper, divided
  • 2 tablespoons vegetable oil
  • 4 cups fresh corn
  • 1 teaspoon granulated sugar
  • 4 thyme sprigs
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat the oven to 400°F. Season both sides of the chicken with 2 teaspoons salt of the salt and 10 turns of the pepper mill.
  2. Step 2: In a 12-inch skillet, heat the 2 tablespoons vegetable oil over medium heat until it shimmers. Add the 4 chicken-leg quarters skin-side down and let it begin to brown slowly, without the oil smoking — the sound should be a gentle rendering of fat and caramelising of skin.
  3. Step 3: As the legs brown, toss the 4 cups fresh corn with the remaining 1 teaspoon salt, 20 turns of the pepper mill and the 1 teaspoon granulated sugar. Spread it on a 13x18-inch baking sheet with no more than a 1-inch lip, reaching to the edges in a 1/2-inch layer. Lay the 4 thyme sprigs on top of the corn to mark where the chicken will be placed.
  4. Step 4: Once the skin side of the legs is golden brown, lay the chicken skin-side up on top of each thyme sprig, with an inch or two between the legs. Slide the sheet pan onto the middle rack of the oven and roast for 45 minutes.
  5. Step 5: On removing it from the oven, the corn should be cooked unevenly across the pan: the edges dry and caramelised and the corn under the chicken juicy and fragrant. Remove the leg quarters, set them aside and discard the thyme. Stir all the corn together with a spoon or spatula and serve it under the chicken.
Headnote (paraphrased) recounts that the dish recreates corn roasted under a chicken as made by the author's grandmother Iris, as described by his aunt Currie — savoury, caramelised, chewy in places, creamy in others and spicy with black pepper — and notes the method goes against what the author considers "correct" cooking technique. The pan, temperature and size of the chicken legs are said to matter very much. Running heads: page 222, Deep Run Roots; page 223, Sweet Corn.

Servings: 6

Adapted from Deep Run Roots.

Why it’s healthy

The dip is built on genuinely good things: a pound of crab brings lean protein — 17 g in a serving — plus zinc for your immune system and B12 for red blood cells. The cucumber is mostly water, so it hydrates and fills with almost no calories, plus a little vitamin K. The lemon juice goes in uncooked, so its vitamin C arrives intact, and horseradish, hot sauce, scallion and mint deliver big flavor for nearly nothing.

The honest cost

The cream cheese base. A cup of it carries the dip to 8 g of saturated fat in a serving — 40% of a day's limit — with 667 mg of sodium, 29% of a day's ceiling, in 220 calories before a single cracker is counted. The crab and cucumber are light; the base is the bill, and what you dip decides how fast it grows.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Take the Greek yogurt option. The recipe lists yogurt, sour cream or crème fraîche for the tablespoon that loosens the base — yogurt is the lightest of the three, and the cucumber water does the rest of the loosening for free.
  • Drain the cucumber properly. The salted slices sit over a colander while the dip is made — that step keeps the dip thick on its own, so it never needs extra cream cheese to hold together.
  • Serve it with crudités. The recipe offers crackers, crudités or chips; vegetables keep the dip the event, while crackers and chips quietly stack their own salt and fat under every scoop. The mint and scallion pull indirect weight here: herbs are dense in polyphenols per gram, though a serving is grams, so the direct dose stays small. The bigger mechanism is flavor — a dip that tastes bright and seasoned needs less salt to land, and sodium is the heavier lever. Fresh herbs, added at the end and never cooked, keep both the flavor and the benefit at full strength.
Ingredients
  • 2 medium cucumbers or 1 large English cucumber
  • 1 1/2 teaspoons salt, divided
  • 1 cup cream cheese, at room temperature
  • 1 tablespoon Greek yogurt, sour cream, or crème fraîche
  • 1 pound picked crabmeat (anything but claw will work fine)
  • 1/4 cup lemon juice
  • 2 tablespoons prepared horseradish
  • 1/2 teaspoon hot sauce
  • 1/4 cup finely chopped scallion
  • 3 tablespoons chopped mint
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Peel, halve and seed 1 1/2 medium cucumbers or 2/3 of a large English cucumber. Using a mandoline, slice the halves into 1/16-inch half-moons. Toss the slices with 1/2 teaspoon salt and set them over a colander to drain while the rest of the dip is made; this should yield roughly 1 cup of limp cucumber slices.
  2. Step 2: Using a Microplane, grate the remaining cucumber; this leaves cucumber pulp and the water that leaches from it. Strain the pulp from the water and discard the pulp. Set aside up to 1/3 cup of the water for the dip (the text jokes the remainder can be drunk as-is or with tequila).
  3. Step 3: In the bowl of a mixer fitted with the paddle attachment, beat the 1 cup cream cheese, 1 tablespoon Greek yogurt and cucumber water until lightened and smooth. Add the 1 pound crabmeat, the remaining 1 teaspoon salt, 1/4 cup lemon juice, 2 tablespoons prepared horseradish, 1/2 teaspoon hot sauce, 1/4 cup scallion and 3 tablespoons chopped mint, and paddle until it looks like dip.
  4. Step 4: Stir in the cucumber slices by hand and serve chilled with crackers, crudités or chips.
Headnote (paraphrased) credits the author's friend Eleanor Johnston and family gatherings built around dips, notes the author's family dislikes mayonnaise, and explains the cucumber was paired with crab (inspired by a note in Gray Kunz's The Elements of Taste that hands smell like cucumber after handling crab) to add freshness and texture, giving a lighter, "wetter" crab dip. Serving suggestion (paraphrased): plain Jane salt-seasoned crackers and a crisp cool glass of white wine. Running head: page 251, Cucumbers.

Servings: 2

Why it’s healthy

The toppings carry this bowl. The fried egg brings complete protein and choline, which your brain uses to make a key memory-and-focus chemical and which most people don't get enough of. The shiitakes give deep savory flavor for very few calories, plus B vitamins. And the ginger and garlic are working seasonings, not garnish: gingerol eases everyday inflammation, and garlic's protective compound supports blood vessels and the immune system.

The honest cost

The butter and the salt, at fried-rice scale: 13.7 g of saturated fat in a serving — 68% of a day's 20 g limit — and 1,390 mg of sodium, 60% of a day's ceiling, in a 510-calorie bowl. Grass-fed butter is the better-built version of the same ingredient — more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than conventional butter. Rich, and worth making knowingly.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Rest the garlic before it meets the pan. Mince it about 10 minutes ahead; here it lands on top of the rice mid-cook rather than in the first hot fat, which already helps — the rest beforehand is what lets its compound form. Allicin doesn't exist in a whole clove: a building block and the enzyme that uses it sit in separate compartments, and mincing mixes them — the compound builds over about 10 minutes, then hard heat destroys it fast. In this dish the garlic steams on top of the rice before being stirred in, so a rested mince arrives with its work already done.
  • Leave the shiitakes alone to caramelize. Two undisturbed minutes, as written, builds the deep flavor that makes a buttered bowl taste complete — flavor earned by patience instead of by another spoonful of fat.
  • Keep the yolk runny. The egg goes on top still flowing, and that yolk sauces the whole bowl — richness you can spread across every bite instead of cooking more fat into the rice. The choline in that yolk feeds acetylcholine, the messenger your brain uses for memory and focus, and also keeps fat from building up in the liver. Eggs are one of the richest sources there are — two cover roughly half a day's need — so the egg on this bowl is substance, not decoration.
Ingredients
  • ½ cup long-grain rice
  • 3 tablespoons butter, divided
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil
  • 1 cup diced shiitake mushrooms (you can substitute any mushroom you like)
  • 1 heaping tablespoon minced ginger
  • 1 teaspoon minced garlic
  • 1 cup leeks, white part only, sliced ¼ inch thick
  • ¼ teaspoon chili flakes
  • 1 teaspoon salt, divided
  • 2 large eggs
  • 2 tablespoons picked cilantro
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Cook the ½ cup rice following the instructions on page 292, then let it sit uncovered in the refrigerator a minimum of 1 hour and up to overnight, so it dries slightly and will crisp better.
  2. Step 2: In a 10- to 12-inch sauté pan heat 1 tablespoon butter and the 1 tablespoon vegetable oil over medium heat until foaming. Add the 1 cup shiitakes, shake pan once, leave undisturbed and let caramelize 2 minutes.
  3. Step 3: Add 1 tablespoon butter, then the cooked rice. Press rice into a thin layer covering the whole pan surface. Once pressed, leave it alone and resist stirring. Add 1 heaping tablespoon ginger, 1 teaspoon garlic, 1 cup leeks, ¼ teaspoon chili flakes and ½ teaspoon salt on top.
  4. Step 4: After about 3 minutes, lift a little rice at the edge with a spatula to check: once it has started to take on slight golden colour and crisp texture, stir in the ingredients that were sitting on top, press rice down again into an even layer, and cook another 2 minutes before removing from heat.
  5. Step 5: Cook the eggs and serve: In a 10-inch cast-iron skillet (or preferred egg pan) heat the remaining 1 tablespoon butter over medium heat until foaming. Crack the 2 large eggs onto opposite sides of the pan and cook gently about 2 minutes, until whites are set. Sprinkle eggs with remaining ½ teaspoon salt.
  6. Step 6: Fluff the rice and serve it topped with a runny fried egg; garnish with 2 tablespoons cilantro.
Intro frames this as a way to turn leftover rice into a new dish; almost any ingredients on hand can be used, but success depends on letting the rice sit undisturbed in the hot fat and not stirring it.

Servings: 2

Nutrition couldn’t be verified for this one — treat the numbers as a rough estimate.

Adapted from Deep Run Roots.

Why it’s healthy

Fried, and still carrying something most fried food doesn’t: okra’s slippery soluble fiber survives the pan, slowing how fast sugar from the meal reaches your blood and giving gut bacteria something to feed on. The cornmeal crust brings fiber of its own plus lutein, the pigment that protects vision, and the finished plate is light — 158 calories with 4.5 g of fiber and a quarter of a day’s vitamin C.

The honest cost

The frying and the salt. The okra cooks in a skillet of vegetable oil, so the crust drinks some of it no matter how well it drains, and the two half-teaspoons of salt bring a serving to 976 mg of sodium — 42% of a day’s ceiling — on a two-serving side. Honest numbers for a hash; the fiber is what sets it apart from its fried peers.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Keep it a single layer, undisturbed. Four minutes untouched on the first side, as written, builds a real crust in the oil that’s already there — crowding steams the pieces and tempts a second pour.
  • Drain it properly. Out with a slotted spoon onto the paper-towel plate, as written — the oil left on the towel is oil nobody eats, and the crust stays crisp instead of greasy.
  • Let the cayenne work. A quarter teaspoon in the cornmeal plus the okra’s own character means the final half-teaspoon of salt seasons a dish that already tastes awake. The cornmeal’s lutein is one of two pigments your eye concentrates in the macula, the high-definition centre of the retina, where it filters harsh blue light and absorbs oxidative damage. Your body cannot make it, so every bit arrives by plate — here, a modest, steady contribution riding in a crust.
Ingredients
  • ½ cup cornmeal
  • 1 teaspoon salt, divided
  • ¼ teaspoon cayenne
  • 2 cups of okra sliced ⅓ inch thick (about 15 medium okra)
  • cup vegetable oil
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Stir ½ cup cornmeal, ½ teaspoon salt and ¼ teaspoon cayenne together in a medium bowl. Rinse okra well, toss the 2 cups okra with the cornmeal mixture, and set aside.
  2. Step 2: In a 12-inch cast-iron skillet heat the oil over medium-high heat. When oil shimmers, test with one piece of okra; if it sizzles right away, add all the remaining okra, spreading it in a single layer so every piece touches oil.
  3. Step 3: Lower heat slightly and cook undisturbed on one side 4 minutes.
  4. Step 4: Toss okra with a spatula and cook a further 3 to 4 minutes, until pieces range from honey-brown to chestnut to blond.
  5. Step 5: Lift out with a slotted spoon onto a paper-towel-lined plate to drain. Season with remaining ½ teaspoon salt and serve warm.
Intro explains the dish combines different fried-okra styles the author encountered; despite the name given, it is served draining on a paper-towel-lined plate.
Incomplete as photographed: oil quantity fraction is partly cropped/blurred at the right edge of the ingredient column; best reading is ⅓ cup. All other ingredients and the full method are legible.

Servings: 6–8 · Oven: 400°F

Why it’s healthy

Under the sweetness there is a real bread: two eggs and two cups of buttermilk bring complete protein and 182 mg of calcium, and the heirloom yellow cornmeal brings fiber for digestion plus lutein, a yellow pigment that collects in your eyes and helps protect your vision as you age. It is made from scratch in a cast-iron skillet, from ingredients you can name — the base is sound, even if the build is rich.

The honest cost

This is sweet bread, not plain bread: 25 g of sugar and 11.3 g of saturated fat in a serving — half a day's limit of each — plus 789 mg of sodium, a third of a day's ceiling, in 456 calories, before anything is spread on it. Grass-fed butter improves its share a little: dairy from grass-fed cows carries more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) and more of the fat-soluble vitamins A, E and K2. Still sweet bread — made knowingly.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Give it the full 30-minute rest. The recipe rests the skillet before cutting — the crumb sets, slices cut clean and even, and an even slice is a portion you chose rather than a wedge that chose you.
  • Eat it plain, warm from the skillet. The crust and the butter already in the batter do the work; what gets spread on top at the table is pure addition to a serving that has already spent half a day's saturated fat.
  • Serve it beside the lean and the green. Corn bread is a side — next to beans, greens or grilled fish, a slice is the rich note on a balanced plate instead of the meal itself. Your macula — the retina's high-definition center — stocks lutein on purpose: it screens harsh blue light and soaks up oxidative damage there. None of it is made in the body; the eye's supply is whatever the plate delivered. Cornmeal is a modest, steady contributor rather than a headline source, which suits a food eaten by the slice.
Ingredients
  • 1/2 cup (4 oz) salted butter, melted, plus 1 tablespoon for the skillet
  • 1/4 cup avocado or canola oil
  • 2 large eggs
  • 2 cups buttermilk
  • 1 cup fine-grind heirloom yellow cornmeal
  • 1 cup all-purpose flour
  • 3/4 cup organic sugar
  • 1 tablespoon baking powder
  • 1 teaspoon kosher salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Preheat oven to 400°F.
  2. Step 2: In a liquid measuring cup, combine 1/2 cup melted butter and 1/4 cup oil. In a medium bowl, whisk 2 large eggs and 2 cups buttermilk until smooth. In a large bowl, whisk 1 cup cornmeal, 1 cup all-purpose flour, 3/4 cup organic sugar, 1 tablespoon baking powder, and 1 teaspoon kosher salt. Add buttermilk-egg mixture to cornmeal mixture and whisk together. Stream in butter-oil mixture while whisking constantly until smooth.
  3. Step 3: Preheat a 10- to 12-inch cast-iron skillet over medium heat for 2 minutes. Add the 1 tablespoon butter; when melted, pour in batter and cook 1 minute to create the crust.
  4. Step 4: Transfer skillet to oven and bake until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean, 25–30 minutes; timing can vary (as fast as 20 minutes and as slow as 40 minutes depending on skillet size and oven).
  5. Step 5: Place skillet on a trivet and let corn bread rest and relax at room temperature for 30 minutes before cutting.
Intro notes starting in a hot buttered cast-iron skillet creates a rich, crispy toffee-like crust; recipe is intentionally rich like yellow birthday cake in butter/eggs/sugar; suggested treats: with butter and honey, or with a scoop of vanilla ice cream and fresh-picked lavender.

Servings: 4

Why it’s healthy

What's genuinely here: a lot of protein and calcium — 43 g of protein and nearly a day's calcium in a serving — from the milk and Parmigiano-Reggiano, over coarse heirloom grits cooked from scratch. It's real food, made from ingredients you can name, with nothing hidden in it. The black pepper isn't decoration either; at a full tablespoon, it's a working ingredient, not a garnish.

The honest cost

The dairy, at full strength: 38 g of saturated fat in a serving — nearly two days' limit — in 963 calories, which is 48% of a 2,000-calorie day spent before the day's fiber and produce are accounted for. Grass-fed dairy shrinks the cost a little: milk, butter and cheese from grass-fed cows carry more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) and more of the fat-soluble vitamins A, E and K2 than conventional dairy. Better built — still an occasion bowl, in an occasion portion.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Serve it as the side it is. Four servings of something this rich work best shared at the table next to a lean main — a scoop, not a bowlful, delivers everything the dish promises.
  • Put something green beside it. The bowl has almost no fiber or produce; a bitter-green salad or grilled vegetables balance the plate in the places the grits can't.
Ingredients
  • 4–6 cups organic whole milk
  • 1 1/2 cups coarse-ground heirloom grits
  • 4 tablespoons salted butter, cut into cubes and kept cold
  • 2 cups grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese
  • 1 tablespoon freshly ground black pepper
  • Kosher salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: First determine the grain-to-liquid ratio and total cook time for the grits being used from the package / mill / farm instructions, noting some coarse grits need overnight soaking before cooking tender.
  2. Step 2: General method: In a large saucepan over medium heat, bring 4 cups milk of the milk to a gentle simmer. Slowly stream in 1 1/2 cups grits while whisking constantly.
  3. Step 3: Cook grits for the time indicated on the package instructions, whisking frequently; if needed, continue adding milk 1/2 cup at a time until cooked to desired doneness.
  4. Step 4: Whisk in 4 tablespoons salted butter a few cubes at a time, then whisk in 2 cups grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and finally 1 tablespoon black pepper.
  5. Step 5: Season with salt to liking and serve immediately.
Intro explains cacio e pepe is a Roman pasta dish of grated aged hard cheese and freshly ground black pepper, originally shepherds' food; applied to grits it makes a bold, creamy bowl. Recommendation to follow the suggested method of the mill or farm the grits are sourced from; instructions often available online if not on package.
