Servings: 6

Why it’s healthy

The base is a real vegetable soup: potatoes bring potassium, which helps keep blood pressure in check by balancing salt, plus filling starch, and the leeks and onion cook down into the pot with them. The garnishes do genuine work — avocado brings creaminess from monounsaturated fat, the kind that supports a healthier cholesterol balance, plus more potassium; capers, dill and chives add brightness for almost nothing; and a serving carries 6 g of fiber and nearly a third of a day's vitamin C.

The honest cost

The cream — twice. Three-quarters of a cup blends into the soup and another three-quarters is chilled and spooned over the top, and a serving lands at 17 g of saturated fat, 83% of a day's 20 g limit. Pasture-raised cream shrinks that cost a little: dairy from grass-fed cows carries more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) and more of the fat-soluble vitamins A, E and K2 than conventional dairy. Still rich — just better built.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Rest the crushed garlic before it meets the pot. The cloves are crushed and peeled in this recipe — give them about 10 minutes before the leeks go in, so garlic's protective compound can form. Allicin doesn't exist in a whole clove: a building block (alliin) and the enzyme that uses it (alliinase) sit in separate compartments, and crushing mixes them — it builds over about 10 minutes, then relaxes blood-vessel walls and fights bacteria and fungi. In a soup where the garlic cooks gently from the start, that rest beforehand is the only window the compound gets.
  • Leave the potato skins on before dicing. Much of the fiber is in the skin and right under it; since the soup is blended smooth, the skins disappear into the body of it and the fiber stays.
  • Spoon the garnish cream, don't pour it. A chilled dollop per bowl gives the contrast the dish is built on; the soup underneath is already creamy from the blended potato itself.
  • Finish with the olive oil drizzle and the lemon halves. Both go on at serving, uncooked — the oil keeps the bitter compounds that protect blood vessels, and the lemon's vitamin C arrives intact. The oil's bitter bite is oleocanthal, a polyphenol that calms inflammation and shields blood-vessel walls; cheap, refined oil has little of it. Its monounsaturated fat improves cholesterol mainly by replacing saturated fat — which is exactly the trade a finishing drizzle makes against another spoonful of cream.
Ingredients
  • 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil
  • 1 cup sliced leeks (split the leeks lengthwise first and cut into ¼-inch-thick slices)
  • ½ cup finely chopped Spanish onion
  • 3 garlic cloves, crushed and peeled
  • Sea or kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
  • 4 cups ½-inch-dice russet (baking) potatoes
  • 2 cups chicken stock or canned low-sodium broth
  • 2 cups water
  • 1 tablespoon fresh thyme leaves
  • 2 teaspoons dried oregano
  • ¾ cup heavy cream
  • Garnishes
  • ¾ cup heavy cream
  • 2 ripe avocados
  • Generous splash of lemon juice
  • Sea or kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
  • 3 tablespoons drained capers
  • 2 tablespoons fresh dill
  • 2 tablespoons chopped fresh chives
  • 2 teaspoons fresh lemon thyme leaves
  • 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil
  • 3 lemons, cut in half
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat the 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil in a pot. Add the 1 cup sliced leeks, ½ cup finely chopped Spanish onion, and 3 garlic cloves and cook until translucent.
  2. Step 2: Season with salt and pepper, then add the 4 cups russet potatoes.
  3. Step 3: Pour in the 2 cups chicken stock and 2 cups water, add the 1 tablespoon fresh thyme leaves and 2 teaspoons dried oregano, and cook the potatoes until tender.
  4. Step 4: Meanwhile, put the ¾ cup heavy cream (the garnish cream) in the refrigerator to chill. Slice the 2 ripe avocados and toss them with the lemon juice.
  5. Step 5: Blend the soup with an immersion blender (or a regular blender) until smooth and creamy — the potato cream. Thin with a little water or stock if needed.
  6. Step 6: Ladle the potato cream into serving bowls. Top with the chilled cream, the avocado slices, 3 tablespoons drained capers, and the herbs (2 tablespoons fresh dill, 2 tablespoons chopped fresh chives, and 2 teaspoons fresh lemon thyme leaves), drizzle with the 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, and serve with the 3 lemons, halved.
Intro (paraphrased): inspired by ajiaco, a Colombian potato and chicken stew with herbs and avocado served in Queens, New York; this version leaves out the chicken to make a side dish that goes with many entrées, such as chicken or lightly smoked cod.
Method note: the method is on the facing page (page 30), which appears only as cut-off line beginnings at the right edge of the dish photo. The steps above are rebuilt from every legible fragment of that page — the start of each printed line — together with the ingredient list on page 29. The ends of the lines are cut off in the photo and could not be read, so any exact cooking times in the original are not stated here.

Servings: 2 · Oven: 375°F [190°C]

Why it’s healthy

The fruit and tomato genuinely lighten this sandwich. The roasted tomato brings lycopene, the red pigment that helps protect the heart and blood vessels — and roasting is the rare case where cooking helps, since heat and a little fat make lycopene far easier to absorb. The pineapple brings serious vitamin C, over half a day's worth in a sandwich, and the two cheeses and ham deliver 37 g of protein and a third of a day's calcium.

The honest cost

A grilled cheese with the volume up: 18.3 g of saturated fat in one sandwich — 92% of a day's 20 g limit — with 1,418 mg of sodium, 62% of a day's ceiling, and about 14 g of sugar from the sweet bread and pineapple. The tomato and pineapple add real nutrients; they do not cancel the cheese and ham. An occasion sandwich, made knowingly.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Keep the roast on the pineapple and tomato. Twelve minutes until the surfaces look dry concentrates their flavor and readies the tomato's lycopene — the fillings arrive loud enough that the cheese can stay a layer, not a pile. Lycopene lodges in cell membranes and neutralizes the oxidative damage linked to vessel aging. Heat bursts the tomato's cell walls and reshapes lycopene into the form your gut absorbs best, and the sandwich's fat ferries it across — cooked tomato is one of the few cases where processing clearly helps.
  • Serve a fresh pineapple bite alongside. The roasted rings keep their vitamin C, but roasting costs the fruit its bromelain — a fresh piece on the side keeps the enzyme the oven took. Bromelain dismantles protein, which is why fresh pineapple tenderizes meat and can start digesting your meal alongside you — but heat destroys the enzyme, and claims beyond digestion outrun the evidence anyway. The vitamin C is the dependable half, and it survives the roast.
  • Cut it in half and plate half. The recipe already halves the sandwiches — half, with something fresh beside it, delivers the whole experience at half the saturated fat and sodium.
Ingredients
  • 4 slices fresh pineapple (about ¼ in [6 mm] thick), cored, or ½ of a small can of pineapple rings in juice, drained
  • 6 to 8 slices ripe plum tomato (about ¼ in [6 mm] thick)
  • 1 Tbsp salted butter, at room temperature
  • 4 slices Hawaiian bread (slightly sweet white bread) or artisan white bread
  • 4 slices [85 g] fontina cheese
  • 4 oz [115 g] sliced ham
  • 3 oz [85 g] fresh mozzarella cheese, thinly sliced
  • Pinch of red pepper flakes (optional)
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Preheat the oven to 375°F [190°C] and line a baking sheet with parchment paper or aluminium foil.
  2. Step 2: Lay the 4 slices fresh pineapple and 6 to 8 slices ripe plum tomato on the prepared sheet and bake 12 minutes, until the surfaces look dry but not yet browned, turning the pieces over halfway through. Remove from the oven and set aside.
  3. Step 3: Heat a cast-iron or nonstick skillet over medium-low heat.
  4. Step 4: Butter one side of each bread slice with the 1 Tbsp salted butter, dividing the butter evenly. Put two slices buttered-side down on a clean cutting board. On each, layer two slices of the fontina (4 slices fontina cheese in total), half of the 4 oz sliced ham, three or four slices of the roasted tomato, two rings of the roasted pineapple, and half of the 3 oz fresh mozzarella cheese. Sprinkle with the red pepper flakes if using. Top with the remaining bread slices (4 slices Hawaiian bread in total), buttered-side up.
  5. Step 5: With a wide spatula, put both sandwiches in the pan, cover, and cook until the bottoms are nicely browned, about 4 minutes. Turn and cook until the second sides are browned, the cheese is melted, and the fillings are heated through, about 4 minutes longer.
  6. Step 6: Cut the sandwiches in half if desired and serve immediately.
Intro (paraphrased): based on the authors' fondness for Hawaiian pizza — mozzarella, sweet-tart pineapple, savoury ham, and spicy tomato sauce — turned into a grilled cheese sandwich using fresh, high-quality ingredients.

Servings: 6 as a side dish

Adapted from Grilled Cheese Kitchen.

Why it’s healthy

The bowl is built on vegetables — corn, potatoes and onion bring fiber for digestion, potassium that helps keep blood pressure in check, and lutein from the corn, which protects your vision as you age. The garlic is the quiet heavyweight: no other seasoning in the dish does as much for your blood vessels and immune system. And the chile's heat makes a rich bowl satisfying in a smaller portion.

The honest cost

The cream and butter. Three-quarters of a cup of heavy cream and a tablespoon of butter are where nearly all the saturated fat lives — everything else in the pot is lean. Pasture-raised cream and butter shrink that cost a little: dairy from grass-fed cows carries more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) and more of the fat-soluble vitamins A, E and K2 than conventional dairy — still rich, just better built. This is a rich dish built on a healthy base.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Rest the garlic. Crush or mince it and let it sit about 10 minutes before it hits the pot — that's when its protective compound forms. The recipe already treats it gently: one minute, at the end of the onion. Its compound, allicin, doesn't exist in a whole clove: a building block (alliin) and the enzyme that uses it (alliinase) sit in separate compartments, and crushing mixes them — allicin builds over about 10 minutes, relaxes blood-vessel walls, and fights bacteria and fungi. Hard heat destroys it fast, which is why the rest and the gentle finish matter.
  • Leave the potato skins on. The recipe peels them; much of the fiber is in the skin. Lutein is one of two pigments your eye concentrates in the macula, the high-definition center of the retina, where it filters harsh blue light and absorbs oxidative damage. Your body cannot make it — every bit arrives by plate.
  • Swap half the cream for stock. The corn and potato carry the body of the soup — you keep the chowder and lose much of the saturated fat. Capsaicin trips the nerve receptors that sense heat — the burn is a signal, not damage — and the body answers with widened blood vessels and a small rise in calorie burn. Honest size: the metabolic effect is minor; the peppers' vitamin C is the bigger gift, and it fades with long cooking.
  • Finish with your best olive oil. A drizzle on each bowl, instead of cooking it all at the start — gentle treatment keeps the compounds that protect blood vessels, and the flavor lands harder. Mostly monounsaturated fat — it improves cholesterol mainly by replacing saturated fat; swapping is the mechanism, not adding. The bitter bite is oleocanthal, a polyphenol that calms inflammation and shields blood-vessel walls; cheap, refined oil has little of it.
Ingredients
  • 1 Tbsp salted butter
  • 1½ tsp olive oil
  • 1 medium yellow onion, cut into ¼-in [6-mm] dice
  • 1 large garlic clove, minced
  • 1 tsp minced fresh thyme or ½ tsp dried thyme
  • 1 Tbsp plus 2 tsp all-purpose flour
  • 3 cups [720 ml] vegetable stock
  • ¾ cup [180 ml] heavy cream
  • 2 medium Yukon gold potatoes, peeled and cut into ¼-in [6-mm] dice
  • Kernels from 3 ears fresh corn or 2 cups [340 g] frozen corn kernels, drained
  • ¾ tsp piment d'Espelette chile powder or cayenne pepper
  • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
  • 1 Tbsp minced fresh flat-leaf parsley
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a medium soup pot over medium heat, melt the 1 Tbsp salted butter in the 1½ tsp olive oil. Add the 1 medium yellow onion and cook, stirring often, until translucent, about 8 minutes. Add the 1 large garlic clove and 1 tsp minced fresh thyme and cook 1 minute longer.
  2. Step 2: Sprinkle the 1 Tbsp plus 2 tsp all-purpose flour into the onion mixture gradually, whisking constantly to avoid lumps. Stir in the 3 cups vegetable stock and raise the heat to bring it to a low boil. Add the ¾ cup heavy cream and 2 medium Yukon gold potatoes and return to a boil. Lower the heat to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the potatoes can be easily pierced with a fork, about 7 minutes.
  3. Step 3: Stir in the kernels from 3 ears fresh corn (or 2 cups frozen corn kernels) and the ¾ tsp piment d'Espelette, and season with salt and pepper. Simmer, stirring occasionally, until the corn is tender, about 10 minutes longer. Take off the heat and stir in the 1 Tbsp minced fresh flat-leaf parsley.
  4. Step 4: Ladle the chowder into bowls and serve immediately.
Intro (paraphrased): a popular summer special — the kitchen goes through about fifty ears of just-picked corn a day; the sweet corn comes through the cream and herbs, the potatoes add body, and a pinch of chile powder cuts the richness. Serving suggestion: serve with a salad made with ripe, fresh heirloom tomatoes. Technique note (paraphrased): to cut kernels from a fresh cob, cut the cob in half crosswise, stand each half up on its thicker end on a clean cutting board, and carefully run a sharp knife down all sides of the standing cob.

Why it’s healthy

The chicken is real substance: complete protein for keeping muscle, and dark thigh meat carries more iron and zinc than breast meat does. The jalapeño and garlic are more than heat and perfume — the pepper's capsaicin nudges blood flow open, and the garlic is sautéed for just two to three minutes before the caramel goes in, a short cook that keeps some of its protective compound alive while the braise mellows the rest into flavor.

The honest cost

The caramel is the cost: 17 g of sugar in a serving — 34% of a day's 50 g added-sugar limit — and 568 mg of sodium, a quarter of a day's ceiling, before the salt you add to taste, plus 8.6 g of saturated fat from the skin-on thighs and the oil marinade.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Press the garlic and let it sit while the chicken fries. Crushing builds its protective compound over about 10 minutes, and the recipe's short sauté then keeps some of it — a rested press arrives at the pan with more to give.
  • Glaze by flipping, not by ladling. The chicken braises in the caramel and gets flipped a couple of times as it reduces — a shiny coat on every piece, instead of extra sauce pooled at the table. The sugar works quietly: a dose this size floods the liver, which stores the overflow as fat, and repeated spikes wear on insulin sensitivity. The sodium is quieter still — it holds water in the blood, and blood pressure follows the volume, while the dish tastes glazed and savory rather than salty. Making it knowingly is the whole ask.
  • Eat yours skin-off at the table. The skin did its work crisping in the pan and flavoring the braise; leaving it on the plate keeps the dark meat's protein, iron and zinc and drops a share of the fat.
  • Let the heat do portion work. Jalapeño heat makes a rich, sweet dish satisfying in a smaller serving. Capsaicin works by deception — it triggers the nerves that sense heat, and the body, fooled, widens its blood vessels and burns a few extra calories answering. Honest size: expect a nudge, not a burn-off. The pepper's real gift here is satiety — heat makes glazed chicken feel complete sooner.
Ingredients
  • Marinade:
  • ½ cup vegetable oil
  • ¼ cup sugar
  • 1 tablespoon fish sauce
  • Caramel sauce:
  • 1 tablespoon fish sauce
  • ¼ cup water
  • ¼ cup sugar
  • 2 tablespoons rice wine vinegar
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil
  • 6 chicken thighs
  • Garlic, several cloves, pressed, to taste
  • Jalapeño, several slices, sliced, to taste
  • Salt and black pepper, to your taste
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Marinate the 6 chicken thighs with the ½ cup vegetable oil, ¼ cup sugar, and 1 tablespoon fish sauce.
  2. Step 2: Stir the caramel sauce together in a bowl — the 1 tablespoon fish sauce, ¼ cup water, ¼ cup sugar, and 2 tablespoons rice wine vinegar — and set aside.
  3. Step 3: Heat a skillet over medium to medium-high heat. Add the 1 tablespoon vegetable oil and pan fry the chicken thighs skin-side down for 4–5 minutes, then flip and cook 4 minutes more. Transfer the chicken to a platter.
  4. Step 4: Add the garlic and jalapeno and sauté 2–3 minutes. Add the caramel mixture and bring it to a strong simmer. Return the chicken thighs to the skillet and braise 8–10 minutes.
  5. Step 5: Lower the heat and cook until the caramel reduces a bit, flipping the chicken a couple of times for even cooking and a glaze.
  6. Step 6: Season to taste with salt and black pepper.

Servings: 1

Why it’s healthy

The oats are a proven lever, not a vague one: their soluble fiber, beta-glucan, lowers LDL cholesterol by about 10 points at roughly 3 grams a day, and a cup of dry oats covers that dose — alongside 10 g of total fiber in the bowl. Hemp seeds add about 6 g of protein plus potassium and iron, and cinnamon brings warmth that reads as sweetness.

The honest cost

The salt, surprisingly: a full teaspoon in a single bowl puts the serving at 2,379 mg of sodium — 103% of a day’s ceiling — in a breakfast that tastes of maple and cinnamon, not salt. The maple syrup adds most of the 13 g of sugar, and the butter a little saturated fat; grass-fed butter improves that half-tablespoon, with more omega-3s and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) than conventional.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Season it like a single bowl, because it is one. The teaspoon of salt is written for the pot — tasting before the full amount goes in keeps the bowl’s sodium somewhere a breakfast should be.
  • Pull it off the heat early. The recipe’s own cue: the oats keep cooking in the bowl, so stopping soft keeps the texture distinct instead of gluey — and a bowl you enjoy is a bowl you keep making. Beta-glucan works by binding bile acids in the gut; the liver then pulls cholesterol from the blood to replace them, which is the whole mechanism behind the roughly 10-point LDL drop. The gluey texture people notice in oatmeal is that same soluble fiber, doing its work in the bowl first.
  • Stir the hemp seeds in at the end. As written, they go in off the boil — their protein, potassium and iron land in the bowl intact, with a nutty texture that survives.
Ingredients
  • 2 cups filtered water
  • 1 cup oats
  • ½ tablespoon butter
  • 2 tablespoons hemp seeds
  • 1 tablespoon maple syrup
  • 1 teaspoon cinnamon
  • 1 teaspoon salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Bring the 2 cups of filtered water to a boil.
  2. Step 2: Add the 1 cup of oats and turn the heat down to low.
  3. Step 3: Stir for about four minutes, off and on.
  4. Step 4: You know the oatmeal's done when most of the water is absorbed and it's just about the right consistency. It will keep cooking a little bit, so take it off the heat before you think it's done.
  5. Step 5: Add the ½ tablespoon butter, 2 tablespoons hemp seeds, 1 tablespoon maple syrup, 1 teaspoon cinnamon, and 1 teaspoon salt, and stir them in.

Yield: 4 servings · Total time: 20 minutes

Adapted from NYT Cooking.

Why it’s healthy

The brussels sprouts do the heavy lifting. A pound of them brings nearly all of the dish’s vitamin C — about 98 mg a serving, more than a full day’s worth — and most of its potassium, and the vitamin C sits in the same pan as the sprouts’ own iron, which is the pairing that helps your body absorb iron from plants. The sprouts and the gnocchi split the fiber, about 9 g a serving, and the cooking fat is extra-virgin olive oil.

The honest cost

The brown butter, and it isn’t close. Six tablespoons over four servings is a tablespoon and a half each, and the butter alone accounts for about 11 of the 13 g of saturated fat in a serving — 63% of a day’s limit. The packaged gnocchi brings most of the sodium, 625 mg a serving in all. Pasture-raised butter improves the fat itself — grass-fed dairy fat carries more omega-3s and CLA, plus more vitamins A, E and K2 — but the amount is the amount. Still rich, just better built.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Leave the sprouts alone in the pan. The undisturbed, cut-side-down sear is where the flavor comes from — deep browning is what lets a vegetable dish taste this rich on a tablespoon of oil a serving. The short, hot cooking is also what the sprouts’ own chemistry wants. The sprouts’ protective compounds form through an enzyme that heat destroys, and long boiling leaches what is left into the water. A fast sear threads the needle the tips describe for crucifers: cooked briefly, nothing poured away. Halving the sprouts and letting them sit a few minutes before the pan gives the enzyme a head start.
  • Keep the honey at a whisper. Half a teaspoon across the whole pan is a glaze note, there to balance the sprouts’ bitter edge and help the butter brown — it adds under a gram of sugar a serving, so the dish stays savory.
  • Grate the Parmesan at the table, as written. It is the one ingredient nobody measured. Kept as a finish each person adds for themselves, it stays a finish, not a layer.
Ingredients
  • 1 pound brussels sprouts (or cruciferous vegetables like broccoli, cauliflower or even cabbage)
  • 1 lemon
  • 4 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil
  • Kosher salt (such as Diamond Crystal) and black pepper
  • ½ teaspoon red-pepper flakes
  • 1 (18-ounce) package shelf-stable or refrigerated potato gnocchi
  • 6 tablespoons unsalted butter, sliced into 6 pieces
  • ½ teaspoon honey
  • Freshly grated Parmesan, for serving
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Trim and halve the brussels sprouts. Using a vegetable peeler, peel thick strips of zest from the 1 lemon, then coarsely chop. (You should have about 2 teaspoons chopped zest.)
  2. Step 2: In a large (preferably 12-inch) skillet, heat 3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil over medium-high. Add the 1 pound brussels sprouts, season with ½ teaspoon salt and a few grinds of pepper, then arrange the sprouts in an even layer, cut side down. Scatter the lemon zest over the top and cook, undisturbed, until the sprouts are well browned underneath, 3 to 5 minutes. Add the ½ teaspoon red-pepper flakes, stir and cook until the sprouts are crisp-tender, 2 to 3 minutes. Transfer to a medium bowl.
  3. Step 3: In the same skillet, heat the remaining 1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil over medium-high. Break up any gnocchi that are stuck together, add the 1 (18-ounce) package shelf-stable or refrigerated potato gnocchi to the pan and cook, covered and undisturbed, until golden brown on one side, 2 to 4 minutes. Add the 6 tablespoons unsalted butter and ½ teaspoon honey, season with salt and a generous amount of black pepper, and cook, stirring, until the butter is golden, nutty smelling and foaming, 1 to 2 minutes. Stir in the brussels sprouts until warmed through. Serve with grated Parmesan.

Servings: 14–16 · Prep: 15 minutes · Cook: 2–2½ hours, after an overnight soak · Quickcook: about 2 hours, no soak

Fifteen kinds of beans, peas and lentils from one bag, simmered in a Cajun-spiced tomato broth with Italian sausage and onion, and finished with lemon.

Why it’s healthy

Start with the beans — fifteen kinds in one pot, and the variety itself is a nutrient: different legumes carry different fibers, and a mix of fibers feeds a wider range of gut bacteria than any single bean can. A serving brings 7.5 g of fiber and 13.7 g of protein, and the lemon juice and tomatoes are not just flavor — their vitamin C is what unlocks the beans' plant iron, 16% of a day's worth in the bowl, so it can actually be absorbed. The sausage makes it dinner; the beans make it good for you.

The honest cost

The flavor packet is the price of admission, and the bowl mostly pays it back. The Cajun seasoning packet carries roughly 2,100 mg of sodium by itself — an estimate worked out from Hurst's own label — and the sausage links carry 540 mg each on theirs; together they put a serving at 356 mg of sodium, 15% of a day's ceiling, before any salt added at the end. But the beans and tomatoes answer in the same serving with 623 mg of potassium — nearly two milligrams of potassium for every milligram of sodium — and potassium is the mineral that blunts sodium’s effect on blood pressure. The swap already made in this kitchen did its work on the other side of the ledger: the chicken-and-kale sausage holds saturated fat to 0.5 g a serving, where the classic pork sausage would put it at 2.2 g. Its price is 2 g of sugar a link, 1 g of it added. Low-sodium diced tomatoes trim a little more — tasting before you salt trims the most.

Keep it healthy — and make it healthier

  • Rest the garlic before the skillet. The garlic is minced and goes into hot fat, where the enzyme that builds its protective compound dies fast — mincing it about 10 minutes ahead gives the compound its only window to form. Allicin doesn't exist in a whole clove: a building block and the enzyme that uses it sit in separate compartments, and crushing mixes them. In a sauté this short, the rest beforehand is the whole trick — heat stops the enzyme, but it cannot unmake allicin that has already formed.
  • Keep the lemon in the pot. It goes in with the tomatoes for the final simmer, and its vitamin C works the whole time on the beans' iron — plant iron absorbed severalfold better with vitamin C in the same meal. A fresh squeeze over the bowl doubles down on the same effect.
  • Taste before you reach for salt. The packet and the sausage have already seasoned the pot — the recipe's "salt to taste" is the one pile of sodium entirely in your hands.
Ingredients
  • 1 (20 oz) bag Hurst's HamBeens Cajun 15 Bean Soup mix, rinsed and picked over
  • 1 lb sweet Italian chicken sausage with kale, or mild or hot Italian sausage, Polish sausage, or ham
  • 1 large onion, chopped
  • 1 (14.5 oz) can diced tomatoes
  • Juice of 1 lemon
  • 1–2 garlic cloves, minced
  • The Cajun seasoning packet from the soup mix
  • 8 cups water, plus more for soaking
  • Salt and black pepper, to taste
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Soak the beans. Rinse the 20 oz bean soup mix and place the beans in a large pot. Cover with 8 cups water and let them soak overnight, or for 8 hours. After soaking, drain the water.
  2. Step 2: Simmer the beans. Place the beans in a large pot with 8 cups water. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer, covered, for 1½–2 hours, stirring occasionally.
  3. Step 3: Brown the sausage. While the beans are simmering, sauté the 1 large onion, 1–2 garlic cloves and 1 lb chicken sausage in a skillet until the sausage is browned. Drain the excess grease.
  4. Step 4: Combine. Add the sautéed ingredients to the beans, along with the 14.5 oz can diced tomatoes, the juice of 1 lemon and the contents of the Cajun seasoning packet.
  5. Step 5: Finish. Simmer for 30 minutes. Salt and pepper to taste.
Preparation — Quickcook (no soak)
  1. Step 1: Start the beans. Place the rinsed 20 oz bean soup mix in a large pot with 8 cups water.
  2. Step 2: Boil. Bring the beans to a boil. Reduce the heat, cover and continue at a medium boil for 60–70 minutes, stirring occasionally.
  3. Step 3: Brown the sausage. While the beans are boiling, sauté the 1 large onion, 1–2 garlic cloves and 1 lb chicken sausage in a skillet until the sausage is browned. Drain the excess grease.
  4. Step 4: Combine. Add the sautéed ingredients to the beans, along with the 14.5 oz can diced tomatoes, the juice of 1 lemon and the contents of the Cajun seasoning packet.
  5. Step 5: Finish. Reduce the heat, cover and lightly boil for 45 minutes. Salt and pepper to taste.

Your daily targets

By default, scores use FDA Daily Values (2,000 kcal). Enter your details for targets matched to you — saved only in your browser, never sent anywhere.

Height is needed for the most accurate calorie estimate (Mifflin-St Jeor). Leave it blank for a rougher weight-only estimate — the page will say so.

Using FDA Daily Values (2,000 kcal reference).

How your targets are calculated

Calories: basal metabolic rate (BMR) by Mifflin-St Jeor — men: 10 × weight (kg) + 6.25 × height (cm) − 5 × age + 5; women: the same, minus 161 (Mifflin et al., American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 1990) — multiplied by an activity factor: sedentary 1.2, lightly active 1.375, moderately active 1.55, very active 1.725, extra active 1.9. Without height, BMR is estimated from weight alone (24 kcal/kg/day (10.9 kcal/lb/day) for men, 22 (10.0 kcal/lb/day) for women) and labelled as a rough estimate. Protein: 1.2–1.6 g per kg of body weight per day (0.55–0.73 g/lb) (Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025–2030), scaled by activity from 1.2 (sedentary) to 1.6 (very/extra active). Fat: 20–35% of calories and carbohydrate: 45–65% (acceptable ranges, Dietary Guidelines); the targets use the middle of each range. Fiber: about 14 g per 1,000 kcal. Iron, calcium, vitamin D, vitamin C, vitamin A and potassium use age- and sex-specific recommended intakes (NIH Office of Dietary Supplements); sodium (2,300 mg), saturated fat (under 10% of calories) and cholesterol (300 mg) are daily limits. Total sugars has no daily value. Targets are estimates for a generally healthy adult, not medical advice.

Pick the dishes you're eating — the meal describes itself here first, in plain words, then the numbers.

Builds on Pairs well with: one tap drafts a full day of eating from the archive — recipes and portion sizes chosen to make a full day of eating, scored with the same daily targets as the combiner above. Sauces and cocktails are never meal components; a dessert appears only as a small treat, if at all. Plans keep to two or three dishes: a real breakfast, then one main dish cooked once and eaten for both lunch and dinner, with portion sizes — not extra cooking — doing the rest of the work. Nothing is applied until you say so, and the manual combiner stays exactly as it is.

Nutrition data source▶

All values are estimates from USDA FoodData Central data — not laboratory analysis. Where an ingredient has no USDA entry it is left out and noted on the recipe; where a recipe doesn't state a quantity, standard amounts are assumed and noted. Salt to taste is not counted, so sodium may be higher.

Core Framework & Principles

Issued January 7, 2026 by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). The 10-page guidelines bring back the food pyramid — flipped upside down, replacing MyPlate as the federal nutrition icon — with protein, dairy, and healthy fats at the top.

Protein, Dairy & Healthy Fats

Top tier: red meat, eggs, whole milk, yogurt, butter.

1.2–1.6 g/kg/day (0.55–0.73 g/lb/day)
Vegetables & Fruits

Middle tier: whole vegetables and fruit every day.

3 veg · 2 fruit / day
Whole Grains

Bottom tier: whole wheat bread, rice, oats.

2–4 servings / day

Also emphasized: whole foods first, a sharp cut in ultra-processed foods, and stricter limits on added sugars.
