Evidence-Informed Cooking & Nutrition Tips

93 evidence-informed tips — click to browse them all. The same tips are also linked from inside the recipes where they apply.

From the Evidence-Informed Nutrition and Cooking Guide — themes drawn from the work of Rhonda Patrick, Peter Attia, Andrew Huberman, and Jo Robinson (Eating on the Wild Side), plus mainstream dietary research. Not medical advice.

How to read the evidence tags: [Strong] Supported by large trials or consistent long-term evidence. [Moderate] Reasonable human evidence, but smaller or less consistent. [Limited] Mostly lab, mechanistic, or small-study evidence. Low risk, uncertain payoff.

Two things to keep in mind: changes in nutrient absorption or biomarkers don’t automatically mean fewer diseases or a longer life — and overall dietary pattern matters far more than any single food or trick.

Top 10: Start Here (10 tips)
  1. Eat plenty of fiber, aiming for 30 g or more per day from vegetables, legumes, fruit, whole grains, nuts, and seeds. [Strong] Fiber is the single highest-yield habit on this page. It feeds gut bacteria, which repay you in compounds that calm inflammation, and it slows sugar and cholesterol absorption. Most adults get about half of 30 g; closing that gap beats any supplement.
  2. Make extra virgin olive oil your main everyday fat — as a swap, not an addition: its fat improves cholesterol balance when it replaces saturated fat, and its bitter compounds protect blood vessels. [Strong] This is a swap, not an addition: olive oil's monounsaturated fat replaces saturated fat, which is what improves cholesterol balance. Its bitter polyphenols also protect blood vessels. A foundational habit — small at any one meal, large across years.
  3. Eat legumes (lentils, beans, chickpeas) several times a week: their fiber, plant protein, and resistant starch — the starch that reaches the colon undigested — steady blood sugar and feed gut bacteria at once. [Strong] Legumes pair fiber with plant protein and resistant starch, so they steady blood sugar and feed gut bacteria at once. Cheap, filling, and hard to overeat — one of the strongest patterns in nutrition research, not a garnish-level tip.
  4. Eat fatty fish (salmon, sardines, trout, herring) twice a week. [Strong] Fatty fish is the only meaningful food source of EPA and DHA, the omega-3s tied to heart rhythm, lower triglycerides, and brain structure. Twice a week is the dose the evidence is built on; plant omega-3s convert too poorly to substitute.
  5. Get enough protein (roughly 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg (0.55 to 0.73 g/lb) body weight for most active adults), spread across 3 to 4 meals. [Moderate to Strong] Protein is what muscle is rebuilt from, and the rebuilding signal fades with age, so the daily total matters more as you get older. Spreading it out keeps the signal on. For an active adult this is a top-three lever, alongside fiber and sleep.
  6. Minimize ultra-processed foods, added sugar, and excess sodium. [Strong] This is the subtraction half of the Top 10, and it carries as much weight as the additions: added sugar, sodium, and ultra-processing drive most of the modern disease burden. No single swap matters more than what quietly leaves the cart.
  7. Eat cruciferous vegetables regularly, and chop them ahead of cooking. [Moderate] Crucifers carry the sulforaphane system (detailed in tip 1-1): a genuine cellular-defense switch, but a supporting player next to fiber, fish, and total diet quality. Regularly, not religiously — a few servings a week captures it.
  8. Eat a variety of colorful fruits and vegetables, fresh or frozen. [Strong] Variety is a coverage strategy: different colors mean different protective compounds, and no single vegetable covers them all. Frozen counts fully — it is picked ripe and frozen fast. A strong foundational habit, mostly because of what it crowds out.
  9. Walk 10 to 15 minutes after meals when you can. [Moderate] After a meal, working muscle pulls glucose straight out of the blood, no extra insulin needed. Ten minutes is enough to blunt the spike measurably. A modest lever per meal that compounds across three meals a day, every day.
  10. Limit alcohol. Less is better. [Strong] Alcohol's risks — cancer, liver, sleep, blood pressure — scale with dose and start low; there is no threshold where it turns helpful. Cutting down is one of the clearest wins on this page, and the benefit arrives within weeks.
1. Get More From Plant Compounds (5 tips)
  1. Chop and rest. Chop or crush broccoli, garlic, and onions, then wait about 10 minutes for garlic and onions and 30 to 40 minutes for broccoli before cooking. This lets enzymes (myrosinase in cruciferous vegetables, alliinase in garlic) form protective compounds such as sulforaphane and allicin before heat deactivates them. [Limited to Moderate] The compounds do not exist in the whole plant. Crushing mixes a stored precursor with an enzyme that builds them — alliinase makes allicin, myrosinase makes sulforaphane — and heat destroys the enzyme, not the product. So the rest must finish before cooking. A real effect, mid-weight: worth the wait, not worth skipping garlic over.
  2. Eat broccoli sprouts. Sprouts carry many times a mature head’s supply of the broccoli compound that switches on your cells’ own antioxidant defenses. Eat them raw in salads, eggs, sandwiches, and lentils. [Limited to Moderate] Sprouts concentrate the precursor: gram for gram they carry many times a mature head's glucoraphanin, and eating them raw keeps the enzyme alive to convert it. Sulforaphane switches on Nrf2, your cells' master antioxidant-response switch. Promising, still early evidence — a cheap add, not a core lever.
  3. Add mustard powder to cooked crucifers. Cooking destroys broccoli’s enzyme, so no protective compound forms; a little mustard powder lends its own enzyme and restarts the process. Raw broccoli doesn’t need it. [Limited] Mustard seed keeps its own myrosinase, and a little powder lends it to the cooked broccoli, restarting sulforaphane formation in the bowl. A rescue trick, small in the rankings — it recovers part of one compound in one vegetable family.
  4. Eat purple and deeply colored produce. The purple-blue pigment in red cabbage, blueberries, blackberries, purple carrots, and purple potatoes helps blood-vessel walls stay responsive and mops up oxidative stress — the deeper the color, the more you get. [Moderate] Anthocyanins are the pigment and the protection in one: they help blood-vessel walls stay responsive and mop up oxidative stress. Color is the label — the deeper the purple or blue, the more you get. Mid-weight: real compounds, ordinary doses.
  5. Include onions regularly. Onions’ protective compounds sit mostly in the outer layers, so don’t peel deep. Eat onions raw in salads or gently cooked in soups, beans, and lentils — gentle cooking keeps most of the compounds. [Limited to Moderate] Quercetin is an antioxidant concentrated in the outer layers, so peeling deep throws away the best part; the sulfur compounds are the onion family's milder cousins of garlic's allicin. Gentle cooking keeps most of both. A supporting player — onions earn their place mostly by making healthy food taste good.
2. Choose and Store Produce Well (9 tips)
  1. Favor darker, more colorful varieties. Plants concentrate protective compounds in skins and outer leaves, where sun and stress hit — so dark, small, deeply colored produce (red leaf lettuce, dark cherries, berries, small tomatoes) carries more than pale, large kinds. [Limited] Plants make more protective compounds where the sun and stress hit — skins and outer leaves — so dark, small, and deeply colored usually means denser. A shopping heuristic, not a law: it nudges choices at the margin, which is where shopping tips live.
  2. Tearing lettuce may help. Some research suggests that damaging leaves ahead of time can raise certain antioxidants. The evidence is thin, so treat it as optional. [Limited] A torn leaf reads the damage as an attack and raises its defensive compounds — that part is real plant biology. Whether the increase survives to matter in a person is unproven. Honestly optional: do it if you prep salad ahead anyway.
  3. Eat delicate produce sooner. Spinach, asparagus, and broccoli lose nutrients during storage, so buy smaller amounts more often. [Moderate] Picked produce is still alive and still spending its vitamin C and folate; delicate leaves and spears spend fastest. This is a freshness habit, modest in size — it protects what you already paid for rather than adding anything new.
  4. Store tomatoes at room temperature until ripe. Refrigeration dulls flavor and texture. Refrigerate once ripe if you need more time. Cold switches off the tomato's ripening machinery and breaks down its texture from inside; a ripe tomato moved to the fridge keeps acceptably. Pure quality, no health stakes — flavor is the whole point of this one.
  5. Store potatoes cool and dark, not refrigerated. Cold can convert starch to sugar, changing flavor and cooking behavior. Avoid sunlight, which causes greening. In the cold, potato starch converts to sugar, which browns too fast and tastes sweet; in light, the skin greens with solanine, a bitter natural toxin. Cool and dark keeps both problems away. Storage common sense, small stakes.
  6. Buy frozen produce freely. Frozen vegetables and berries are picked and frozen at peak ripeness and can be nutritionally equal or better than “fresh” that has traveled for days. [Strong] Freezing within hours of harvest locks nutrients at their peak, while 'fresh' produce can spend a week in transit spending them. On equal footing in study after study. One of the few tips here with no downside: cheaper, less waste, same nutrition.
  7. Wash produce under running water, before cutting. Running water and rubbing remove soil, microbes, and surface residues. Don’t use soap — soap leaves chemicals never meant for food and does not clean better. Running water plus friction removes soil, microbes, and surface residues; soap adds chemicals never meant for food and does not clean better. Wash before cutting, not before storing — wet produce spoils faster. Basic hygiene, quietly load-bearing.
  8. Steam asparagus instead of boiling it. Asparagus is one of the richest common sources of folate (a B vitamin your body uses to build new cells) — about 149 micrograms per 100 grams cooked, over a third of the day's target — and folate dissolves in water, so steaming or microwaving keeps more of it than boiling does. [Moderate] Folate is water-soluble and heat-sensitive: the USDA's nutrient retention tables show boiling vegetables in water drains more of it away than steaming or microwaving with little water. Four spears (about 60 grams) still give roughly 89 micrograms — about a fifth of the daily target — even after cooking.
  9. Let bell peppers ripen to red. A red bell pepper is simply a green one left to ripen, and ripening pays: per 100 grams, red peppers carry about 128 milligrams of vitamin C against green's 80, and nearly eight times the beta-carotene (the pigment your body turns into vitamin A). [Moderate] Green bell peppers are picked unripe; given time on the plant they turn red and keep building sugars, vitamin C, and carotenoids, the red-and-orange pigment family. The vitamin C number comes from the USDA's entries for raw red and green sweet peppers. Ripeness is the whole trick — the plant does the work.
3. Cook to Improve Nutrient Availability (13 tips)
  1. Cook tomatoes and carrots. Heat breaks open their tough cell walls, freeing far more of their protective pigments — cooked tomato gives several times the usable pigment of raw. Add a little fat: the pigments dissolve in fat, not water. [Moderate] Lycopene and beta-carotene sit locked inside tough cell walls and bound to protein; heat breaks the walls and frees them, which is why cooked tomato gives you several times the usable lycopene of raw. Add a little fat — both compounds dissolve in fat, not water.
  2. Pair fat with fat-soluble nutrients. Olive oil, avocado, nuts, eggs, or butter improve absorption of carotenoids and vitamins A, D, E, and K from tomatoes, carrots, and leafy greens. Finish vegetables with a drizzle of extra virgin olive oil. [Moderate] Carotenoids and vitamins A, D, E, and K cannot cross into your blood without fat to ride in — a fat-free salad quietly wastes much of its best content. A drizzle is enough; this is one of the highest-yield small moves in the guide.
  3. Cook spinach lightly. It cooks down so you can eat more. Boiling and then discarding the water reduces oxalates (relevant for people prone to kidney stones). Cooking alone doesn’t solve this. [Moderate] Spinach cooks down to a fraction of its volume, so a panful becomes a serving you can actually finish. The boiling step matters only for stone-prone readers: oxalates leave in the water, which is why the water has to go, not into the soup.
  4. Steam cruciferous vegetables briefly. A few minutes of steaming keeps most of broccoli’s protective compounds, which long boiling destroys or pours away with the water — and the vegetables stay soft enough to eat plenty. [Moderate] The sulforaphane enzyme system (tip 1-1) is heat-fragile, and boiling also leaches compounds into water you pour away. Brief steaming threads the needle: soft enough to eat plenty, gentle enough to keep most of the chemistry. Chop-and-rest first and the margin grows.
  5. Roast or steam beets. Beets supply nitrates your body turns into nitric oxide, the signal that relaxes blood-vessel walls. Roasting keeps the juice — and the nitrates — in the beet instead of the pot. Beet nitrates convert, via bacteria on your tongue, into nitric oxide, the signal that relaxes blood-vessel walls; cooking makes beets sweet and easy to eat in real amounts. Roasting keeps the juice — and the nitrates — in the beet instead of the pot.
  6. Cook, cool, and reheat potatoes. Cooling creates some resistant starch, which may modestly improve glucose responses and feed gut bacteria. The effect is real but modest, and reheating retains part of it. [Limited to Moderate] Cooling re-crystallizes some starch into a form your enzymes cannot open, so it reaches the colon and feeds bacteria instead of raising blood sugar. The honest size: a few percent of the starch, a small glucose effect. Worth it when potatoes are cooked ahead anyway — not a reason to cook extra.
  7. Soak and thoroughly cook beans and legumes. This reduces antinutritional factors, improves digestibility, and lowers gas-producing oligosaccharides. Dried kidney beans must be boiled thoroughly, as undercooked ones are toxic. [Moderate] Soaking and boiling leach out the sugars that ferment into gas and soften the compounds that block mineral absorption. The kidney-bean warning is the serious part: their toxin survives a slow cooker that never boils, and is destroyed by a real boil. Comfort for most beans; safety for that one.
  8. Use cooking liquids. Vitamin C, B vitamins, and potassium dissolve into cooking water — serve the water in soups, sauces, and stews, or the drained pot pours that nutrition down the sink. Vitamin C, B vitamins, and potassium dissolve in cooking water in proportion to time and volume. A soup keeps the whole exchange; a drained pot pours a share of the nutrition down the sink. A quiet, reliable saver — one reason soups punch above their ingredients.
  9. Vary your cooking methods. Rotate steaming, roasting, sautéing, pressure cooking, and raw preparation. Raw isn’t always healthier. Some nutrients are better preserved with minimal heat, others become more available with cooking. Every method trades something: heat frees carotenoids but spends vitamin C; raw keeps enzymes but locks pigments away. Rotating methods averages the trades instead of always losing the same nutrient. A portfolio rule — no single meal has to be perfect.
  10. Marinate beef in spices before grilling. An hour in a spice-rich marinade before the grill cuts heterocyclic amines, the suspect compounds that form on meat grilled at high heat, by 57 to 88 percent in tested steaks. [Moderate] Researchers grilled steaks at 400°F after an hour in commercial spice marinades and measured total heterocyclic amines down 57, 72, and 88 percent versus unmarinated steak; the spices' plant compounds did much of the work. One study, one grill temperature — treat the size as approximate, the direction as reliable.
  11. Kiwi tenderizes meat — and stops jelly setting. Kiwifruit carries actinidin, an enzyme that breaks down protein: it tenderizes meat in a marinade and digests gelatin, so raw kiwi keeps a gelatin dessert from ever setting. [Limited] In test-tube digestion models, actinidin measurably sped up the stomach breakdown of beef, soy, and dairy proteins beyond digestive enzymes alone; a rat feeding study found the same direction. Direct human evidence is still thin, so treat the digestion claim as promising — the tenderizing and the jelly effect are kitchen certainties.
  12. Lemon juice keeps cut fruit from browning. Rub or toss cut apples, pears, and avocado with lemon juice: its acid slows the enzyme that browns cut surfaces on contact with air. Browning is an enzyme, polyphenol oxidase, reacting with air; lemon's citric acid lowers the surface pH — makes the cut surface more acidic — out of the enzyme's comfort zone and its vitamin C mops up oxygen first. Pure quality, like the tomato tip — flavor and looks are the whole point of this one.
  13. Cook red cabbage with something acidic. Red cabbage's purple pigments are pH-sensitive — they change color with the acidity of the cooking water: cook it with vinegar, wine, or apple and it stays red; cook it plain and it drifts blue-grey, and a pinch of baking soda turns it blue outright. [Moderate] The pigments are the anthocyanins — the purple pigments — from tip 1-4, and their color is their chemical state: acid holds them in the red form, alkaline (non-acid) water shifts them blue. Acid also keeps them in their most stable form, so the color you preserve is the compound you bought the cabbage for.
4. Build a Healthier Gut Microbiome (4 tips)
  1. Eat a variety of fibers. Different bacteria use different fibers, so rotate oats, legumes, berries, vegetables, seeds, and whole grains. [Strong] Your gut bacteria are specialists: each fiber type feeds different strains, and the strains repay you with short-chain fatty acids that nourish the gut lining and calm inflammation. Variety is the mechanism, not a slogan. Together with tip-top-1, this is the gut-health core — most other microbiome tips are footnotes to it.
  2. Eat lentils, beans, and other resistant-starch foods often. Resistant starch (in legumes, green bananas, and cooled potatoes or rice) reaches the colon intact, where bacteria ferment it into butyrate, the preferred fuel of the colon’s own lining cells. [Moderate to Strong] Resistant starch survives to the colon intact, where bacteria ferment it into butyrate, the preferred fuel of the colon's own lining cells. Legumes deliver it inside a package of fiber, protein, and minerals. Strong, practical, cheap — a workhorse, not a hack.
  3. Include fermented foods. Plain kefir, plain yogurt, kimchi, and sauerkraut provide live microbes. Choose refrigerated, unpasteurized versions with live cultures. Early research links fermented food intake with greater microbiome diversity and lower inflammation markers. [Moderate] Fermented foods deliver living microbes that pass through and interact with your gut and immune system; in trials they raised microbiome diversity and lowered inflammation markers where fiber alone did less of the first. Pasteurized versions keep the flavor but lose the microbes — the label's 'live cultures' is the whole game. Solid mid-tier lever.
  4. Green bananas hold the resistant starch (the kind that reaches the colon undigested); ripe ones have spent it. The resistant starch credited to green bananas in tip 4-2 drains away as the fruit ripens — in tracked Cavendish bananas it fell from about 35 percent of dry weight to about 5 percent as starch turned to sugar. [Moderate] Ripening is the banana converting its starch reserve into sugar for the seed's benefit, not yours. The resistant starch that survives to feed colon bacteria belongs to the firm, green, cooked-as-a-vegetable stage. A yellow dessert banana is a different food nutritionally, even though it is the same fruit.
5. Cardiovascular and Metabolic Health (16 tips)
  1. Eat fatty fish at least twice a week. Sardines, salmon, trout, and herring supply EPA and DHA, the fats built into heart and brain cell membranes and into the signals that resolve inflammation. [Strong] EPA and DHA are built into heart and brain cell membranes and into the signals that resolve inflammation. The twice-a-week dose is where the trial evidence sits; capsules are a fallback, fish is the tested form. One of the few Strong tags in this guide that needs no hedging.
  2. Eat a variety of nuts and seeds. A daily handful of walnuts, almonds, pumpkin seeds, chia, or flax tracks with better heart outcomes in trials — but nuts are calorie-dense, so a handful is the serving, not the bag. [Strong] Nuts combine monounsaturated fat, fiber, magnesium, and plant compounds in a form people actually eat daily — and in trials, a daily handful tracks with better heart outcomes. The catch is density: a handful is the serving, not the bag. High value, easy dose control.
  3. Use extra virgin olive oil as your main cooking fat. Its structure and its own protective compounds shield the oil from heat better than commonly believed — but smoking spends those protectors, so don’t let the oil smoke. [Strong] Same swap as tip-top-2, stated for the stove: olive oil's stability comes from its monounsaturated structure and its polyphenols, which sacrifice themselves to protect the oil. Smoking it spends those protectors. As a default fat used daily, its cumulative weight is large.
  4. Use vinegar with carb-heavy meals. Acetic acid may modestly lower post-meal glucose. Put balsamic or red wine vinegar in dressings. Don’t drink concentrated vinegar. The evidence comes from small, short studies. [Limited] Vinegar's acetic acid briefly slows stomach emptying and starch digestion, trimming the glucose peak after a carb-heavy meal — in small studies, by a modest margin. It belongs on food, in dressing form. A garnish-level effect with a Strong-adjacent reputation it has not earned; keep it in its place.
  5. Eat vegetables and protein before starches. This sequence can reduce post-meal glucose spikes. Evidence is mostly from small trials, largely in people with diabetes or prediabetes. [Limited to Moderate] Vegetables and protein first means fiber and fat reach the gut ahead of the starch, slowing its arrival and blunting the spike — the same meal, resequenced, measurably different glucose curve in small trials. Zero cost to try, modest effect, mostly proven in metabolic patients so far.
  6. Walk 10 to 15 minutes after meals. Working muscles take up glucose, blunting post-meal spikes. [Moderate] Muscle is the body's largest glucose sink, and a short walk switches it on right when blood sugar peaks. Ten to fifteen minutes is the tested dose. Per meal it is a nudge; across years of meals it is one of the cheapest metabolic habits there is.
  7. Minimize ultra-processed foods. Ultra-processed foods are engineered to be eaten past fullness — soft, fast, energy-dense, low in fiber — and in feeding trials people ate about 500 extra calories a day on them. Build meals around whole foods instead. [Strong] Ultra-processed foods are engineered to be eaten past fullness — soft, fast, energy-dense, low in fiber — and in controlled feeding trials people ate about 500 extra calories a day on them. This is the population-level giant of the group; home cooking is the practical antidote.
  8. Avocado lowers LDL — the 'bad' cholesterol — when it replaces other fats. In a controlled feeding trial, one avocado a day inside a heart-healthy diet lowered LDL cholesterol by 13.5 points — more than the same diet without the avocado. [Moderate] Forty-five adults ate each diet for five weeks with all food provided; the avocado diet beat a matched moderate-fat diet (down 8.3 points) and a lower-fat diet (down 7.4). The avocado swapped in for other fats rather than piling on top. The trial was funded by the Hass Avocado Board.
  9. Berries track with slower memory decline. In a 16-year study of 16,010 women over 70, those who ate the most blueberries and strawberries showed slower memory decline — testing as if their brains were up to about two and a half years younger. [Moderate] The Nurses' Health Study tracked diet and repeated memory tests; women eating a serving of blueberries at least weekly, or strawberries twice weekly, declined slowest. It is observational — berry eaters differ from non-eaters in other ways — an association, not proof. The direction matches the anthocyanin (purple pigments) evidence in tip 1-4.
  10. Blueberries improved blood-vessel measures in a month-long trial. Forty healthy volunteers drank a 200-gram-blueberry drink daily for a month: systolic blood pressure (the top number) fell about 5 points and blood-vessel responsiveness improved, tracking the breakdown products of the berries' anthocyanins (the purple pigments) in the blood. [Moderate] This was a randomized, controlled trial — small and short, in healthy volunteers rather than patients — and the vessel effect rose and fell with measured anthocyanin metabolites (breakdown products), which strengthens the case it was the berries. The daily dose was 200 grams — about a cup and a third of fresh berries.
  11. Cherries are linked to fewer gout attacks. Among 633 people with gout — a painful form of arthritis — followed for a year, eating cherries in the prior two days came with about 35 percent lower risk of an attack; a serving was about 10 to 12 cherries. [Limited] The design compared each patient's own attack days with their quiet days, which controls for the person but not for everything else they ate or drank. It is observational — no trial has yet confirmed cherries prevent attacks — and the benefit leveled off after about three servings in two days.
  12. Oats lower LDL cholesterol (the 'bad' cholesterol) — the dose is about 3 grams of beta-glucan. Oat beta-glucan, the soluble fiber that makes oatmeal gluey, lowers LDL cholesterol by about 10 points at 3 grams a day — roughly 60 grams of dry oats, a generous bowl. [Strong] Across 28 randomized trials, LDL cholesterol fell 0.25 mmol/L (about 10 mg/dL) at 3 or more grams of oat beta-glucan daily, with no effect on HDL or triglycerides. The FDA has authorized a heart-health claim for it since 1997; the fiber binds bile acids in the gut, and the liver pulls cholesterol to replace them.
  13. Eat the orange; the juice leaves the fiber behind. A medium orange carries about 3 grams of fiber and 12 grams of sugar; a cup of its juice holds about 21 grams of sugar — roughly three oranges' worth — with almost none of the fiber. [Moderate] Juicing strips the membranes and pulp where the fiber lives, so the sugar arrives faster and fullness arrives weaker. The vitamin C mostly survives; the structure does not. Numbers are the USDA's entries for a raw orange and raw orange juice. If you drink juice, a small glass with food beats a tall glass alone.
  14. Purple potatoes lowered blood pressure in a small trial. Eighteen adults with high blood pressure ate 6 to 8 small microwaved purple potatoes twice a day for four weeks: systolic pressure (the top number) fell about 5 points, diastolic (the bottom number) about 4, with no weight gained. [Limited] It was one small crossover trial (everyone took both turns), and 14 of the 18 were already on blood-pressure medication — promising, not proven, and no basis for changing any prescription. The potatoes were microwaved with skins on, keeping the anthocyanins that make them purple. Ordinary potatoes were not tested head-to-head here.
  15. Walnuts are the one tree nut with real omega-3. An ounce of walnuts carries about 2.6 grams of ALA, the plant omega-3 — more than the full day's target — while almonds and other tree nuts carry almost none. [Moderate] ALA is not EPA or DHA (the omega-3 fats in fish): the body turns only a little into those forms, which is why tip-top-4 says plant omega-3s cannot substitute for fatty fish. Walnuts still earn their place — the ALA, the unsaturated fats, and the nut trial record. An ounce is about 14 halves.
  16. Intact grains digest slower than the same grains milled. Whole wheat eaten as intact kernels raises blood sugar less after a meal than the identical wheat finely milled into flour — structure, not just fiber, sets the speed. [Moderate] In a crossover trial (everyone took both turns) in adults with type 2 diabetes, nutrient-matched porridges of finely milled whole wheat raised glucose (blood sugar) more than intact-kernel versions. Small sample — treat the size cautiously. Wheat berries, oat groats (whole oats), and brown rice keep the structure; flour, even whole-grain flour, spends it.
6. Protein, Muscle, and Recovery (11 tips)
  1. Spread protein across the day. Muscle building plateaus at roughly 25 to 40 g of protein per meal, so three to four moderate meals build more than one loaded dinner — especially past 40, when the response dulls. [Moderate] Muscle building responds to each protein feeding with a rise that plateaus — roughly 25 to 40 g captures most of it — so four moderate servings beat one large one across a day. Especially true past 40, when the response dulls. A planning rule, cheap to follow.
  2. Include high-quality protein. Eggs, fish, poultry, dairy, beef, and legumes provide essential amino acids. Animal proteins are especially efficient for building and maintaining muscle. [Strong] Essential amino acids are the ones your body cannot make; animal proteins carry all of them in roughly the proportions muscle wants, with leucine — the trigger amino acid — in useful amounts. Plant eaters get there by combining sources. The foundation the rest of this group decorates.
  3. Use Greek yogurt and cottage cheese. Straining removes whey — the watery part of milk — and water, concentrating the protein to roughly double — an easy way to hit each meal’s protein target with no powders, and a calcium source besides. Straining removes whey and water, concentrating protein to roughly double — food engineering in your favor, no powder required. Also a calcium source. A convenience tip, honestly small: it just makes tip 6-1 easier to hit.
  4. Try wild game in moderation. Elk, venison, and bison are lean and rich in protein, iron, zinc, and B12. If the animal was harvested with lead ammunition, lead fragments can contaminate the meat. Ask about non-lead ammunition, trim generously around wound channels, and cook to safe internal temperatures. Wild game is what red meat looks like without grain finishing: leaner, with iron, zinc, and B12 in full. The lead warning is the load-bearing part — fragments travel beyond the wound channel, so trimming and ammunition questions are not fussiness. Niche, but the safety half matters absolutely.
  5. Rotate seafood. Sardines give omega-3s and calcium, oysters give zinc, and salmon gives EPA and DHA. Favor lower-mercury choices (sardines, salmon, trout, herring, mussels, oysters) and limit high-mercury fish such as swordfish, king mackerel, and bigeye tuna. Pregnant people and young children should follow official fish-consumption guidance. Species choice trades nutrients against mercury, which accumulates up the food chain: small, short-lived fish give omega-3s and minerals with almost none of it; apex predators concentrate it. Rotation keeps both sides of the ledger. The pregnancy guidance is official because the stakes are developmental, not theoretical.
  6. Consider creatine monohydrate. It has strong evidence for improving strength and resistance-training performance. A common dose is 3 to 5 g per day. People with kidney disease should check with a doctor first. [Strong] Creatine tops up the muscle's rapid-energy buffer, the one used in the first seconds of hard effort — that is why it helps strength training specifically and does little for endurance. Among supplements it is the rare one with deep evidence and a long safety record; the kidney caution is for existing disease.
  7. Lactose intolerance is a dose, not a ban. Most people who can't digest lactose (milk's sugar) can still handle about 12 grams at once — roughly the amount in a cup of milk, especially with food — and aged hard cheeses carry almost none. [Moderate] Lactose is milk's sugar, and tolerance depends on how much enzyme you still make. Federal guidance puts the usual tolerated single dose near 12 grams; cheddar and Parmesan are aged until their lactose is nearly gone, and yogurt's live cultures digest part of its lactose for you. Start small rather than quitting dairy outright.
  8. The choline is in the yolk. One large egg carries about 147 milligrams of choline — a membrane-building nutrient most adults fall short on — and essentially all of it sits in the yolk, not the white. [Strong] Choline builds cell membranes and acetylcholine, the messenger chemical nerves signal with; the daily target is 550 milligrams for men and 425 for women, and only about 8 percent of US adults reach it in national survey data. Two eggs supply about 294 milligrams. Egg-white omelets keep the protein and discard this entirely.
  9. "Fish" is not one food: white fish barely carry omega-3. Cod and other lean white fish give clean protein but only about 0.2 grams of EPA and DHA (the omega-3 fats) per 100 grams — roughly a tenth of salmon's — so a white-fish dinner does not fill the fatty-fish slot in tip 5-1. [Strong] The omega-3s concentrate in fat, and white fish store almost none in their flesh; their protein, B12, and selenium (a mineral) are real, the omega-3 dose is not. Numbers are the USDA's entries for Atlantic cod and farmed Atlantic salmon. Count white fish as protein, and let salmon, sardines, or trout carry the omega-3 assignment.
  10. Mussels are a B12 outlier. A 3-ounce serving of cooked mussels delivers about 20 micrograms of vitamin B12 — over eight times the daily target — plus about 6 milligrams of iron, with very little mercury. [Strong] B12 is the nutrient mussels concentrate beyond every common food on this page: the USDA entry for cooked blue mussels lists 24 micrograms per 100 grams, alongside 24 grams of protein and EPA and DHA, the omega-3 fats, about 780 milligrams per 100 grams. They are also among the lowest-mercury seafoods in federal monitoring.
  11. On the tuna shelf, "light" beats "white" on mercury. Canned light tuna averages about 0.13 parts per million of mercury; canned albacore ("white") averages about 0.35 — nearly three times as much — which is why federal advice allows light tuna two to three times a week and albacore once. [Moderate] Both are the same style of fish at different sizes and species: albacore grow larger and live longer, so they accumulate more mercury, the mechanism behind tip 6-5's rotation rule. The figures are the FDA's monitoring averages across commercial samples. For most adults this is a budgeting habit, not a ban on either can.
7. Meal Timing and Everyday Habits (4 tips)
  1. Keep most eating within daylight hours. The same meal eaten late produces a higher, longer blood-sugar spike than the meal eaten at noon, because insulin — the hormone that moves sugar out of the blood — works less well toward night. Avoid making late-night eating a habit. [Moderate] Your glucose tolerance runs on a clock: the same meal eaten late produces a higher, longer spike than eaten at noon, because insulin sensitivity falls toward night. Keeping eating mostly in daylight works with the rhythm instead of against it. A background habit — real, but smaller than what you eat.
  2. Finish dinner 2 to 3 hours before bed when practical. This may support sleep quality and glucose regulation. [Limited to Moderate] Lying down on a full stomach worsens reflux, and late glucose stays elevated into the night's first sleep cycles, fragmenting them. Two to three hours lets the stomach mostly empty. Modest and practical; shift workers do the best version available and lose nothing by trying.
  3. Drink green tea between meals. Tea’s tannins bind plant iron, so tea with a meal cuts the iron you absorb from the meal; between meals you keep both — and the tea’s own metabolic effects are modest anyway. [Limited] Tea catechins, EGCG chief among them, show small metabolic effects in trials that shrink under scrutiny — enjoy it for itself. The timing detail is the useful part: tea's tannins bind plant iron, so between meals keeps both the tea and the iron. Limited, and labelled so.
  4. Stay hydrated. Blood volume, temperature control, and kidney function all run on water, and thirst is a late signal when you sweat heavily — so drink ahead of thirst then. Plain water covers nearly every case. Hydration is plumbing, not optimization: blood volume, temperature control, and kidney function all run on it, and thirst is a late signal during heavy sweating. Plain water covers nearly every case; electrolytes matter when sweat runs for hours. Basic, non-negotiable, unglamorous.
8. What to Limit (8 tips)

Most of this guide is about eating more of good things. These limits often matter more.

  1. Added sugar and sugary drinks — cut these first. Liquid sugar arrives faster than your fullness system can register, and added sugar across the day tracks with fatty liver, diabetes, and heart disease, rising with the dose. [Strong] The dose is the story: liquid sugar arrives faster than the fullness system can register, and added sugar across the day tracks with fatty liver, diabetes, and heart disease in a dose-dependent way. Sugary drinks first, sweets second. Among limits, this is the heavyweight.
  2. Excess sodium, most of which comes from packaged and restaurant food. Cooking at home gives you control. [Strong] Sodium raises blood pressure by holding water in the blood; the dose from packaged and restaurant food dwarfs the salt shaker's. Home cooking flips the ratio — you season to taste, which self-limits. A Strong limit with a practical mechanism: control returns when the kitchen does. What blunts sodium most in a home-cooked meal is potassium, which packaged food is short on and vegetables, beans and potatoes are rich in; the scorecard now judges a dish's sodium against the potassium that arrives with it.
  3. Alcohol. Risk rises with intake, and no amount is clearly beneficial. [Strong] Alcohol is processed into compounds that damage DNA and liver tissue, and risk curves for cancer rise from the first drinks upward; earlier claims of benefit were mostly comparison artifacts. Less is simply better. Shares the top weight in this group with sugar and processed meat.
  4. Processed and cured meats such as bacon, sausage, and deli meats — keep them occasional, not daily. Curing and smoking load the meat with nitrites, salt, and smoke compounds, and processed meat is a classified carcinogen — a substance officially judged to cause cancer: roughly a fifth higher colorectal (bowel) cancer risk per daily 50 g. [Strong] Curing and smoking load meat with nitrites, salt, and smoke compounds; processed meat is a classified carcinogen with a dose-response for colorectal cancer — roughly a fifth higher risk per daily 50 g in the assessments. Occasional, not daily, is the honest reading of the data.
  5. Repeatedly reheated cooking oils at high temperatures, which accelerates oxidation and degradation. Each high-heat cycle breaks oil down further — oxidized compounds and off-flavors accumulate, which is why old fryer oil smells tired. Fresh oil for high heat, and retire oil that smokes early or smells stale. A quality-of-exposure limit, smaller than this group's headline items.
  6. Aluminum foil touching food — use parchment paper instead for lining and covering. Foil leaches small amounts of aluminum into food, more with acidic or salty foods and high heat; parchment avoids it. Parchment scorches above about 425°F, so keep foil for high-heat wrapping and grilling. [Moderate] Aluminum migrates into food in small amounts, fastest with acid, salt, and heat — tomato sauce on foil is the worst case. Ordinary exposure is well below safety limits; parchment simply removes the question where it can. The 425°F parchment ceiling is the practical half of the tip.
  7. Cook in cast iron, carbon steel, or stainless steel instead of non-stick (PTFE) pans. PTFE is safe at normal cooking temperatures, but it can release fumes when overheated above about 500°F (260°C), and the coating degrades with use — cast iron has no coating to degrade. [Moderate] PTFE's hazard is temperature, not normal use: past about 500°F the coating breaks down into fumes genuinely harmful to breathe (and lethal to pet birds). Cast iron and steel have no coating to fail and improve with use. A durability choice with a safety edge, honestly mid-weight.
  8. One tablespoon of butter is half a day's saturated fat. Butter packs about 7 grams of saturated fat into a single tablespoon; the American Heart Association's target is about 13 grams for the whole day at 2,000 calories. [Strong] That is the arithmetic behind butter's place in this group rather than in the fat-pairing tip, where a little butter on vegetables is a fair trade. The AHA target is under 6 percent of calories from saturated fat. Used by the tablespoon in cooking, butter spends the budget before the meal starts.
9. Nutrient-Absorption Tricks (6 tips)
  1. Pair vitamin C with plant-based iron. Lemon, kiwi, oranges, and bell peppers improve absorption of non-heme iron from lentils, beans, and vegetables. [Moderate to Strong] Plant iron arrives in a form your gut absorbs poorly — often under a tenth of what's eaten. Vitamin C chemically converts it to the absorbable form in the same meal, multiplying uptake severalfold. One of the best-evidenced tricks in this group, and it costs a squeeze of lemon.
  2. Combine turmeric with black pepper. Piperine can substantially raise curcumin levels in the body. This is an absorption effect, and increased absorption doesn’t automatically mean a health benefit. [Limited] Piperine blocks the liver and gut enzymes that clear curcumin, so blood levels rise sharply — that measurement is real. What curcumin then does at food doses is far less proven. Read this as an absorption trick, not a benefit promise; the guide's most honestly Limited entry.
  3. Grind flaxseed. Whole seeds can pass through undigested. Ground flax provides more accessible ALA omega-3, fiber, and lignans. [Moderate] The seed's shell is the barrier: intact flax transits whole, its omega-3 (ALA) and lignans locked inside. Grinding opens it — and starts the clock, since ground flax oxidizes faster (see tip 10-2). A small, complete mechanism: grind, refrigerate, use.
  4. Get vitamin C with collagen. Vitamin C is required for normal collagen synthesis. A normal diet usually provides enough, so mega-doses aren’t needed. [Limited] Collagen is assembled with vitamin C as a required cofactor — without it the fibers form weakly, which is literally what scurvy is. Ordinary diets clear the requirement easily, so this is a completeness note, not a supplement case. Limited weight, stated plainly.
  5. Get magnesium from food. Magnesium is a working part in hundreds of enzyme reactions — energy production, muscle relaxation, nerve signaling — and shortfalls are common. Pumpkin seeds, almonds, spinach, legumes, and whole grains are excellent sources. [Moderate] Magnesium is a cofactor in hundreds of enzyme reactions — energy production, muscle relaxation, nerve signaling — and food sources come packaged with fiber and potassium. Shortfalls are common and usually mild. Getting it from food is the reliable route; no trick to it, which is the point.
  6. Almond labels overstate the calories you absorb. Measured in people, an ounce of whole almonds delivers about 129 calories, not the roughly 170 the label's math gives — the nuts' rigid cell walls trap some fat and carry it through. [Strong] USDA researchers fed almonds to volunteers and measured the energy actually absorbed; whole roasted and chopped almonds gave progressively more, and almond butter the most, at about 6.5 calories per gram. The label is not lying — it counts what is in the nut, not what your gut can reach.
10. Food Safety and Storage (7 tips)
  1. Cool and refrigerate cooked rice promptly. Cooked rice left at room temperature can grow Bacillus cereus, which produces toxins that reheating doesn’t destroy. Refrigerate within about an hour and reheat until steaming hot. Don’t leave rice out to “develop resistant starch.” This is the most important safety tip in this guide. Bacillus cereus spores survive boiling, then germinate in warm rice and produce a toxin that reheating cannot destroy — the poisoning is in the rice before it is reheated. Refrigeration within the hour is the entire defense. The guide itself flags this as its most important safety tip; the ranking is earned.
  2. Refrigerate nuts and ground seeds. Their unsaturated fats oxidize, especially after grinding. Grinding multiplies surface area, and unsaturated fats oxidize on contact with air — rancid fats lose their value and add off-flavors. Cold storage slows the chemistry. A freshness rule that protects money already spent on good ingredients.
  3. Store olive oil in a dark, tightly sealed bottle, away from heat, light, and air. Light, heat, and air spend the oil’s protective compounds; a dark, sealed, cool bottle can double the oil’s useful life. Olive oil's polyphenols — the compounds behind tip-top-2 — are spent by light, heat, and air, the same enemies as any unsaturated fat. A dark, sealed, cool bottle can double the oil's useful life. Storage as preservation, nothing more mystical.
  4. Handle cooked and cooled starches safely. Moist, starchy food left at room temperature is bacterial habitat — so cooked potatoes and legumes get the rice rule: refrigerate promptly and reheat thoroughly. The rice rule (tip 10-1) is really a cooked-starch rule: moist, starchy, room-temperature food is bacterial habitat. Potatoes and legumes get the same prompt refrigeration and thorough reheating. One habit covers the class — learn it once.
  5. Use wood, parchment, or glass instead of plastic where food touches it. Plastic sheds microplastics into food, especially when heated or scratched — a wooden board, a parchment cover, or a glass container sheds none. The health effects of ingested microplastics are not yet established. [Limited] Plastic sheds particles, more when heated, scratched, or fatty — that much is measured. What those particles do in a body is not yet established, and this tip does not pretend otherwise. Wood, parchment, and glass cost little; treat the swap as cheap insurance, ranked accordingly.
  6. Never swallow chia dry. Chia seeds absorb roughly ten times their weight in water and swell into a gel — stir them into wet food or soak them first, because a dry spoonful can swell in the throat instead. [Moderate] A published case documents the hazard: a man with a swallowing disorder ate dry chia, drank water after, and the gel blocked his esophagus (the food tube). It is a rare, specific risk — ordinary eaters using chia in food face none of it. The same swelling is why chia works in puddings and drinks.
  7. Don't wash raw chicken. Rinsing raw poultry doesn't remove bacteria — it spreads them around the sink. In a USDA test-kitchen study, 60 percent of people who washed poultry had bacteria in their sink afterward; cooking to 165°F is what makes chicken safe. [Strong] The study seeded chicken with a harmless tracer microbe and watched where it traveled: a quarter of the washers carried it onto salad lettuce, and 14 percent of sinks still held it after cleaning. Pat chicken dry with paper towels instead, wash hands for 20 seconds, and keep raw poultry away from ready-to-eat food.
11. Cautions and Special Situations (6 notes)
  • Warfarin or other blood thinners: Keep vitamin K intake (leafy greens, broccoli) consistent rather than suddenly changing it, and talk to your prescriber.
  • Thyroid conditions: Very large amounts of raw cruciferous vegetables, sprouts, or concentrated supplements may affect thyroid function in susceptible people. Normal food portions are generally fine.
  • Kidney disease or kidney stones: Discuss protein, creatine, oxalate-rich foods (spinach, beets, nuts), and potassium with a clinician.
  • Pregnancy: Follow guidance on fish mercury, unpasteurized foods, and food safety.
  • Iron overload or low iron: Iron-absorption strategies matter differently depending on your situation.
  • Supplements: Whole foods first. Check interactions with medications.
Everyday Nutrition Foundation (8 foods)

Build your diet around:

  1. Cruciferous vegetables: broccoli, broccoli sprouts, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, cabbage.
  2. Polyphenol-rich fruits: blueberries, blackberries, raspberries, strawberries, cherries.
  3. Legumes: black lentils, red lentils, chickpeas, black beans.
  4. Healthy fats: extra virgin olive oil, walnuts, avocado, seeds.
  5. Seafood: salmon, sardines, oysters, mussels, trout.
  6. Quality protein: eggs, poultry, fish, wild game, Greek yogurt, beef in moderation.
  7. Fermented foods: kefir, plain yogurt, kimchi, sauerkraut.
  8. Herbs and spices: garlic, ginger, turmeric, rosemary, oregano, cinnamon.
Resources (5 sources)
  1. Eating on the Wild Side by Jo Robinson: produce selection, storage, and preparation.
  2. Rhonda Patrick / FoundMyFitness: sulforaphane, micronutrients, and omega-3s.
  3. Peter Attia: protein, metabolic health, and longevity nutrition.
  4. Andrew Huberman: meal timing and circadian rhythms.
  5. For a mainstream baseline, check Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health’s Nutrition Source and the Dietary Guidelines for Americans.

Guiding principle: Don’t just eat healthy foods. Choose good varieties, store them well, prepare them to preserve nutrients, and combine them intelligently. Prioritize variety over perfection. No single vegetable, supplement, or technique replaces a diverse, minimally processed, fiber-rich diet. Evidence varies by tip. Favor well-established dietary patterns over individual superfood claims, and check with a healthcare professional about your own situation.
